As with the p-value, we begin by tentatively assuming that \(H_0\) is true, using the boundary value of the null hypothesis (\(p = p_0\) for a proportion, \(\mu = \mu_0\) for a mean). Under this assumption each statistic — the count \(X\), the sample proportion \(\hat{p}\), or the sample mean \(\bar{X}\) — has a sampling distribution describing how it varies from sample to sample. We use that distribution to mark off the values that would be unusual under \(H_0\).






NoteThe Critical Region



The critical region (or rejection region) is the set of values of the statistic for which we reject \(H_0\). The value or values that separate “reject” from “fail to reject” are called critical values. The critical values are chosen so that, when \(H_0\) is true, the probability that the statistic falls in the critical region equals the significance level \(\alpha\).
Because the critical region is built to have probability \(\alpha\) under \(H_0\), rejecting \(H_0\) whenever the statistic lands in it guarantees that the probability of a Type I error is exactly \(\alpha\). This is what controls the error rate.


The shape of the critical region matches the direction of the alternative hypothesis: we reject \(H_0\) when the statistic falls in the direction that \(H_a\) predicts. We illustrate all three cases with the SAT example, where the boundary value is \(\mu_0 = 508\). The critical values shown are hypothetical, chosen only to illustrate; their actual computation is taken up in the later chapters.
Case 1: upper-tail alternative (\(H_a: \mu > 508\)). Large values of the sample mean support \(H_a\), so the critical region sits in the upper tail — reject \(H_0\) when the sample mean is at or above an upper critical value. In Figure 9.9 the critical value is \(535\), so the rejection region is every value at or above \(535\). The left panel shows an observed mean of \(542\), which falls inside the rejection region, so we reject \(H_0\); the right panel shows an observed mean of \(521\), which falls outside, so we fail to reject \(H_0\).






Figure 9.9: Case 1, \(H_a: \mu > 508\), with a critical value of \(535\). The rejection region (coral) is every value at or above \(535\). Left: observed mean \(542\) is inside the region — reject \(H_0\). Right: observed mean \(521\) is outside — fail to reject \(H_0\).



Case 2: lower-tail alternative (\(H_a: \mu < 508\)). Small values support \(H_a\), so the critical region sits in the lower tail — reject \(H_0\) when the sample mean is at or below a lower critical value. In Figure 9.10 the critical value is \(481\), so the rejection region is every value at or below \(481\). The left panel shows an observed mean of \(474\) (inside — reject \(H_0\)); the right panel shows an observed mean of \(495\) (outside — fail to reject \(H_0\)).






Figure 9.10: Case 2, \(H_a: \mu < 508\), with a critical value of \(481\). The rejection region (coral) is every value at or below \(481\). Left: observed mean \(474\) is inside the region — reject \(H_0\). Right: observed mean \(495\) is outside — fail to reject \(H_0\).



Case 3: two-sided alternative (\(H_a: \mu \neq 508\)). Extreme values in either direction support \(H_a\), so the critical region occupies both tails — reject \(H_0\) when the sample mean is at or below a lower critical value or at or above an upper critical value. Because rejection can happen on either side, the significance level is split evenly between the two tails, with probability \(\alpha/2\) assigned to each. In Figure 9.11 the critical values are \(481\) and \(535\), so the rejection region is every value at or below \(481\) together with every value at or above \(535\). The left panel shows an observed mean of \(542\), which falls in the upper tail (inside — reject \(H_0\)); the right panel shows an observed mean of \(515\), which falls in the middle (outside — fail to reject \(H_0\)).






Figure 9.11: Case 3, \(H_a: \mu \neq 508\), with critical values \(481\) and \(535\). The rejection region (coral) is both tails: at or below \(481\) or at or above \(535\). Left: observed mean \(542\) is in the upper tail — reject \(H_0\). Right: observed mean \(515\) is in the middle — fail to reject \(H_0\).









NoteDecision Rule Using the Critical Region



Construct the critical region so that, under \(H_0\), the probability the statistic falls in it equals \(\alpha\). Then:

If the observed statistic falls in the critical region, reject \(H_0\).
If the observed statistic falls outside the critical region, fail to reject \(H_0\).



Locating the critical values requires a sampling distribution, just as the p-value does, and the actual computation — carried out with Rguroo in the later chapters — depends on the statistic. The conceptual point that matters here is independent of those details: the critical region is a fixed target set up before the data are examined, and the decision is simply a matter of seeing whether the observed value lands inside it.
The two worked examples below show how a critical-region decision is read once the critical value has been found, without our performing the computation here.

Example 9.13 (Using the Critical Region: YouTube Use (Proportion)) For the YouTube test with \(H_0: p \leq 0.70\) versus \(H_a: p > 0.70\), suppose that for a sample of \(n = 20\) students and \(\alpha = 0.05\) the critical region is found to be \(X \geq 18\), where \(X\) is the count of daily users. The observed count is \(x_{\text{obs}} = 17\). State the decision.







Tip🔎 Solution





The critical region is \(X \geq 18\). The observed count \(x_{\text{obs}} = 17\) does not reach \(18\), so it falls outside the critical region. We therefore fail to reject \(H_0\): the data do not provide strong enough evidence that more than 70% of students use YouTube daily.





YouTube use example: observed count outside the critical region; fail to reject \(H_0.\)








Example 9.14 (Using the Critical Region: SAT Scores (Mean)) For the SAT test with \(H_0: \mu \leq 508\) versus \(H_a: \mu > 508\), suppose that for \(\alpha = 0.05\) the critical region is found to be \(\bar{X} \geq 535\). The observed sample mean is \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 542\). State the decision.







Tip🔎 Solution





The critical region is \(\bar{X} \geq 535\). The observed mean \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 542\) exceeds \(535\), so it falls inside the critical region. We therefore reject \(H_0\) in favor of \(H_a: \mu > 508\): the data provide evidence that the mean SAT score of incoming freshmen exceeds the national figure.





SAT scores example: observed mean inside the rejection region; reject \(H_0.\)







As with the p-value examples, the two differ only in their surface details. In both, the critical region is fixed in advance to have probability \(\alpha\) under \(H_0\), and in both the decision comes from checking whether the observed value lands inside it.

9.6.1 The Two Approaches Always Agree
The p-value approach and the critical region approach are two descriptions of one and the same test. They are guaranteed to reach the identical decision, because each is built from the same significance level \(\alpha\) and the same sampling distribution under \(H_0\).
The connection is easiest to see by picturing the boundary of the critical region. The observed statistic falls inside the critical region precisely when it is at least as extreme as the critical value — and that is exactly the situation in which the probability of a result this extreme or more so, the p-value, is at or below \(\alpha\). The two statements
\[
\text{the observed value lies in the critical region}
\qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad
\text{p-value} \leq \alpha
\]
are therefore equivalent, and the corresponding decisions always match.






NoteTwo Routes, One Decision



The critical region approach answers the question “for which values of the statistic would we reject \(H_0\)?” and checks whether the observed value is among them. The p-value approach answers the question “given the value we observed, how strong is the evidence against \(H_0\)?” and compares that strength to \(\alpha\). Both control the Type I error probability at \(\alpha\), and both always lead to the same conclusion. The p-value approach has the added advantage of quantifying how strong the evidence is, not merely whether it crosses the threshold.

title: 9  Foundations of Statistical Inference
section: 9.7 From Hypothesis Tests to Confidence Intervals
text:
9.7 From Hypothesis Tests to Confidence Intervals
A hypothesis test answers a yes-or-no question about a single candidate value of the parameter: is that value (call it the boundary value, \(p_0\) or \(\mu_0\)) consistent with the data, or not? Often, though, we want something more informative — not a verdict on one value, but a whole range of values that the data find plausible. This is the role of a confidence interval. The two tools answer different questions, but as we will see, they are built from exactly the same sampling distributions.
Before explaining how confidence intervals are constructed, let’s first see what one looks like and how to interpret it. Suppose we survey \(n = 400\) registered voters and find that \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} = 0.55\) support a proposed policy. Rather than testing a single hypothesized value of \(p\), we might instead ask: what range of values of \(p\) are plausible given our data? A method we will construct later in this section might give us the interval \((0.50, 0.60)\), along with a confidence level of 95%. We would report this as: “we are 95% confident that the true proportion of voters who support the policy is between 0.50 and 0.60.”
The same reasoning applies to a population mean. Instead of estimating a population proportion, suppose a sample of \(n = 50\) employees has an average commute time of \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 27.3\) minutes. A 95% confidence interval for the true mean commute time \(\mu\) might be \((25.1, 29.5)\) minutes — we are 95% confident that the true average commute time falls in this range.
Both examples report a 95% confidence interval. But what does “95% confident” actually mean here? The answer is subtler than it first appears, and we will make it precise shortly. For now, notice something familiar in both examples: each interval consists of the observed statistic (\(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} = 0.55\), \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 27.3\)) and extends some distance in each direction — a structure that will turn out to be closely connected to the hypothesis tests.
At first glance, confidence intervals and hypothesis tests may seem like different inferential tools. In reality, they are two sides of the same idea. The key realization is that we already possess everything needed to build such a range. A two-sided hypothesis test is, in effect, a consistency check for a proposed value: test the parameter against that single value, and if we fail to reject, the value is consistent with our data; if we reject, it is not. Nothing stops us from running that check not for one candidate value but for every candidate value. Collect all the values that survive — all the values we would fail to reject — and the resulting set is a confidence interval. This connection can be summarized in a simple rule, called inverting a test.






NoteConfidence Interval by Inverting a Test



A \((1-\alpha)\times 100\%\) confidence interval for a parameter (a proportion \(p\) or a mean \(\mu\)) consists of all candidate values that would not be rejected by a two-sided test of that value at significance level \(\alpha\).
The confidence level and the significance level are complementary: \(\alpha = 0.05\) corresponds to a 95% confidence interval, \(\alpha = 0.10\) to a 90% interval, and so on.


To picture the inversion, imagine sweeping a candidate value along the number line and testing each one, as in Figure 9.12. Consider the SAT example, where a sample of math SAT scores has an observed mean of \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 542\). Each dot marks a candidate value for the population mean \(\mu\). A two-sided test rejects candidate values far from 542 (coral) and fails to reject those close to it (teal). The stretch of non-rejected values between the two switching points — marked by the bracket — is the confidence interval: the band of mean values the data deem plausible. (No computation is shown here; the figure simply records, for a grid of candidate values, which ones a test would reject.)






Figure 9.12: A confidence interval as an inverted test, illustrated for the mean math SAT score.



This construction also explains what the confidence level means — and the idea is easy to misstate, so it’s worth stating carefully.






NoteInterpreting the Confidence Level



Imagine repeating the whole study many times: each time we draw a fresh random sample and build an interval by this method. Because of sampling variability, the intervals shift from sample to sample, and some capture the true parameter while others miss it. The confidence level is the long-run percentage of intervals that capture the true value. A 95% confidence interval comes from a method that succeeds in 95% of such repetitions.
In practice we collect a single sample and build a single interval. That one interval either contains the true parameter or it does not — we cannot know which. What we can say is that it was produced by a method with a known, high success rate over the long run.


Two consequences of this relationship between tests and intervals are worth highlighting, because they will reappear in both later chapters.
First, a confidence interval can stand in for a two-sided test. To test whether a particular value (say \(p_0\) or \(\mu_0\)) is consistent with the data at level \(\alpha\), simply check whether that value lies inside the \((1-\alpha)\times 100\%\) confidence interval. If the value falls outside the interval, it would have been rejected, so we reject \(H_0\). If it falls inside the interval, we fail to reject \(H_0\).
Second, the interval is generally more informative than the test alone. A test tells us only whether a single value is or is not consistent with the data. The interval reports the entire collection of consistent values, and so conveys both the likely magnitude and the direction of the effect — not merely whether an effect is present.


9.7.1 Homework for Section 9.5, Section 9.6, and Section 9.7
No computations are required for these problems; they ask you to reason with the concepts of this chapter.

In your own words, explain what a p-value measures. Why is a small p-value considered evidence against the null hypothesis?
A test of \(H_0: p = 0.50\) versus \(H_a: p \neq 0.50\) produces a p-value of \(0.21\). Using \(\alpha = 0.05\), state the decision and explain what it does and does not tell us about \(H_0\).
Two researchers test the same hypotheses on the same data at the same significance level. One uses the p-value approach and the other uses the critical region approach. Explain why they must reach the same decision.
For the SAT example (\(H_a: \mu > 508\)), describe in which tail the critical region lies and explain why. Do the same for the sleep example (\(H_a: \mu < 7\)) and the commute-time example (\(H_a: \mu \neq 26.8\)).
Explain the difference between a Type I error and a Type II error in terms of the decision rule “reject \(H_0\) when the p-value is at most \(\alpha\).” If you lowered \(\alpha\) from \(0.05\) to \(0.01\), which error becomes more likely and which becomes less likely?
A 95% confidence interval for a population mean \(\mu\) is reported as \((508, 576)\). Without doing any computation, state whether a two-sided test of \(H_0: \mu = 508\) at \(\alpha = 0.05\) would reject or fail to reject. Explain your reasoning. What about \(H_0: \mu = 600\)?
Explain the statement: “The confidence level describes the long-run behavior of the method, not the certainty of any single interval.” Why is it incorrect to say that a particular 95% confidence interval “has a 95% chance of containing \(\mu\)”?
Describe, in words and without formulas, how you could build a confidence interval for a parameter if all you had was the ability to carry out a two-sided hypothesis test at level \(\alpha\) for any candidate value.







NoteLooking Ahead



This chapter has laid out the logic that every inference procedure shares: a research question expressed as null and alternative hypotheses, the two types of error and the strategy of controlling the Type I error at a significance level \(\alpha\), the two equivalent decision rules based on the p-value and the critical region, and the construction of a confidence interval by inverting a test. None of this reasoning depends on the parameter being studied.
What remains is to fill in the parameter-specific machinery — the sampling distribution of the statistic under \(H_0\), the formulas for the p-value and the critical region, and the software steps to compute them. The next chapter does this for a population proportion \(p\), using the sampling distribution of the count \(X\), and the chapter after that does the same for a population mean \(\mu\), using the sampling distribution of the sample mean \(\bar{X}\). In each case the computations are new, but the framework is the one you have just learned.

title: 10  Inference for Population Proportions
text:
10.1 Hypothesis Testing: Concepts and Setup
Before you begin, click to expand the box below to review the process for importing a dataset.
In the foundations chapter, we developed the logic of statistical inference — null and alternative hypotheses, the two types of error, the significance level, the p-value and critical region approaches to making a decision, and the idea of a confidence interval — without performing any computations. That development and reasoning do not depend on which parameter we study. In this chapter we put it to work for a population proportion \(p,\) filling in the parameter-specific machinery the foundations chapter deferred: the statistics and their sampling distribution, the calculations that produce a p-value and a critical region, and the software steps to carry them out in Rguroo. We consider both one-population and two-population settings for proportions.
Because the conceptual framework is already in place, this chapter focuses on computation. We will recall each idea briefly as we use it, with a pointer back to the foundations chapter for the full discussion, and spend our effort on how the ideas are actually carried out for a proportion. The same pattern will repeat in the next chapter for a population mean: new computations, the same framework.
We begin with hypothesis testing for one population proportion.
In many real situations, we encounter numerical claims about population proportions: the proportion of teenagers who use a particular app, the proportion of adults who meet health guidelines, or the proportion of students who rely on social media for news. But how can we determine whether such claims are reasonable? When does sample evidence support a claim, and when should we question it?
To see how we might answer such questions, we will work through examples and develop the reasoning needed to evaluate claims and reach conclusions. We begin by establishing the framework and notation we will use throughout this chapter.

title: 10  Inference for Population Proportions
text:
10.1.1 Setting the Stage: A Running Example
Suppose we want to know what proportion of students at our university prefer online classes. The population is all students at our university. The response variable is class mode preference, a categorical variable (also called a factor) that classifies each student into one of two categories: prefers online classes or does not prefer online classes. We define “prefers online classes” as a success and the other category as a failure.
In statistics, the terms success and failure do not imply that one outcome is good and the other is bad. A success simply refers to the outcome we are interested in studying, while a failure refers to the other outcome. For example, if we are studying the proportion of manufactured parts that are defective, we might define a defective part as a success. Similarly, if we are studying the proportion of patients who experience a side effect from a medication, experiencing the side effect could be defined as a success. In both cases, “success” identifies the outcome of interest, not a desirable outcome.
The parameter of interest is the population proportion, denoted by \(p\)—the fraction of all students at our university who prefer online classes. Since we cannot survey every student, we collect data from a random sample and use it to learn about \(p.\)
This example illustrates the key elements of proportion inference:

A population with a characteristic we want to measure
A categorical response variable with two outcomes (success/failure)
A parameter \(p\) representing the true population proportion of successes
A sample from which we compute a statistic to estimate \(p\)

Let’s develop this framework more formally.


10.1.2 From Samples to Statistics
When we collect a sample of size \(n,\) we count how many individuals have a success outcome. Before the sample is collected, this count is unknown, so we treat it as a random variable and denote it by \(X.\) The corresponding sample proportion is also a random variable, given by \(\hat{p}=X/n\) (read “p-hat”).
After the data are collected, we observe the count of successes in our sample, which we denote by \(x_{\text{obs}}\) (read “x-observed”). The corresponding observed sample proportion is \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}=\frac{x_{\text{obs}}}{n}\) (read “p-hat-observed”) which provides an estimate of the population proportion \(p.\)
In our example of students who prefer online classes, suppose we randomly select \(n = 100\) students. Before we collect the sample, \(X\) represents the number of students who will say they prefer online classes in a random sample of \(n=100\) students. The value of \(X\) could be anywhere from 0 to 100. Correspondingly, \(\hat{p}\) represents the proportion of students in the sample who say that they prefer online classes. After we survey the students, suppose 62 say they prefer online classes. Then, the observed count is \(x_{\text{obs}} = 62\) and the observed proportion is \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} = 62/100 = 0.62\) or 62%. .






\(X\) is a random variable representing the number of successes across all possible samples; \(x_{\text{obs}}\) is the specific count from our actual sample. Similarly, \(\hat{p}=X/n\) is a random variable representing the sample proportion across all possible samples, while \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}=x_{\text{obs}}/n\) is the observed sample proportion from our actual sample. We use \(x_{\text{obs}},\) or equivalently \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}},\) to make decisions about \(p.\)









NoteNotation Summary



As we work through the examples in this chapter, it may be helpful to keep the following symbols and their meanings in mind.








Symbol
Name
Description




\(p\)
Population proportion
The true, unknown proportion in the population


\(n\)
Sample size
The number of individuals in the sample


\(X\)
Random variable (count)
The number of successes across all possible samples of size \(n\)


\(x_{\text{obs}}\)
Observed count
The actual number of successes in our sample


\(\hat{p}\)
Random variable (proportion)
The sample proportion \(X/n\) across all possible samples of size \(n\)


\(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}\)
Observed sample proportion
The proportion of success we observed in our sample; estimate of \(p\) computed as \(x_{\text{obs}}/n\)






Example 10.1 (Daily YouTube Use Among Teens) According to a Pew Research Center report, about 71% of U.S. teenagers say they visit YouTube every day (Pew Research Center, Teens, Social Media and Technology, 2023).
Suppose a school district claims that more than 70% of students in its district use YouTube daily. To examine this claim, a random sample of \(n=20\) students is selected, and 17 of them report that they use YouTube daily.
Describe or compute the following related to the claim:

The response variable and its possible categories
The success category of the response variable
The population of interest

The parameter of interest \(p\)
The sample
The statistic \(X\) and its observed value \(x_{\text{obs}}\)
The observed sample proportion \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}\) that is an estimate of \(p\)








Tip🔎 Solution






The response variable is Daily Use of YouTube with two possible response categories “Yes” and “No”.
The success category is “Yes”, that is if the student uses YouTube daily.
The population of interest is all students in the district.
The parameter of interest \(p\) is the proportion of students in the district who use YouTube daily.
The sample is the 20 students who were randomly selected and questioned about their YouTube use.
The statistic \(X\) is the number of students in a sample of size \(n = 20\) who use YouTube daily. From our sample, the observed value is \(x_{\text{obs}} = 17.\)
The observed sample proportion (an estimate of \(p\)) is

\[\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} = \frac{x_{\text{obs}}}{n}=\frac{17}{20} = 0.85.\]




Example 10.2 (Physical Inactivity Among Adults) The World Health Organization reports that approximately 31% of adults worldwide do not meet recommended levels of physical activity (World Health Organization, 2024).
Suppose a national health agency hopes that fewer than 35% of adults in its country are physically inactive. To examine this claim, a random sample of \(n=50\) adults is selected, and 10 of them are found to be physically inactive.
Describe, and when relevant compute, the following related to the claim:

The response variable and its possible categories
The success category of the response variable
The population of interest

The parameter of interest \(p\)
The sample
The statistic \(X\) and its observed value \(x_{\text{obs}}\)
The observed sample proportion \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}\) that is an estimate of \(p\)








Tip🔎 Solution






The variable of interest is Physical Activity, with possible categories of “Inactive” and “Active”.
The success category is “Inactive”, since we want to make inference about those who are physically inactive.
The population of interest is all adults in the country.
The parameter of interest \(p\) is the proportion of adults in the country who are physically inactive.
The sample is the 50 adults who were randomly selected and their physical activity levels were recorded.
The statistic \(X\) is the number of individuals in a sample of size \(n=50\) who are inactive, and its observed value is \(x_{\text{obs}} = 10.\)
The observed sample proportion (an estimate of \(p\)) is

\[\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} = \frac{x_{\text{obs}}}{n}=\frac{10}{50} = 0.20.\]




Example 10.3 (Social Media as a Primary News Source) According to a Pew Research Center report, 36% of U.S. adults ages 18–29 say they regularly get news from social media (Shearer, 2023).
Suppose the university administration is unsure whether the same percentage applies to students at their university and wants to determine whether the true proportion of students who get most of their news from social media differs from 36%.
To investigate this question, a random sample of \(n=15\) students is selected, and 9 of them report that they get most of their news from social media.
Describe, and when relevant compute, the following related to the claim:

The response variable and its possible categories
The success category of the response variable
The population of interest

The parameter of interest \(p\)
The sample
The statistic \(X\) and its observed value \(x_{\text{obs}}\)
The observed sample proportion \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}\) that is an estimate of \(p\)








Tip🔎 Solution






The response variable is regarding how students get their news, We call the variable “Use Social Media”, and the possible categories are “Yes”, and “No”.
The success category is “Yes”.
The population of interest is all students at the university.
The parameter of interest \(p\) is the proportion of students at the university who get most of their news from social media.
The sample is the 15 students who were randomly selected and surveyed about their primary news source.
The statistic \(X\) is the number of students in a sample of size \(n=15\) who get most of their news from social media, and its observed value is \(x_{\text{obs}} = 9.\)
The observed sample proportion (an estimate of \(p\)) is

\[\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} = \frac{x_{\text{obs}}}{n}=\frac{9}{15} = 0.60.\]



To use sample evidence to evaluate a claim about a population proportion, we first need to state clearly the claims we are considering. Because our decision is based on a sample rather than the entire population, there is always a possibility of reaching the wrong conclusion. As we saw in Chapter 8, we might reject a claim that is actually true, or we might fail to reject a claim that is actually false. These two possibilities correspond to Type I and Type II errors, which we will now consider in the context of inference for a population proportion.


10.1.3 Null and Alternative Hypotheses and Errors for a Proportion
The foundations chapter (Section 9.3) developed the null and alternative hypotheses, the three forms they take, and the two types of error in full. Here, we briefly review the notation for hypothesis tests involving a population proportion and then apply these ideas to our examples.
For a population proportion, the alternative hypothesis \(H_a\) is the claim we seek evidence for, and the null hypothesis \(H_0\) is its complement, the value or range we assume true unless the data force us to abandon it. Both are statements about the population proportion \(p,\) not about the sample, so they are written using \(p\) and not \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}.\) Writing \(p_0\) for the boundary value that separates the null from the alternative, the three forms are:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Case 1: }
&\begin{cases} H_0: p \leq p_0 \\ H_a: p > p_0 \end{cases}
\qquad
\text{Case 2: }
&\begin{cases} H_0: p \geq p_0 \\ H_a: p < p_0 \end{cases}
\\[1em]
\text{Case 3: }
&\begin{cases} H_0: p = p_0 \\ H_a: p \neq p_0 \end{cases}
\end{aligned}
\] Cases 1 and 2 are one-sided and Case 3 is two-sided, exactly as in Section 9.3.1.
Recall too the two ways a test can be wrong: a Type I error rejects \(H_0\) when \(H_0\) is in fact true, and a Type II error fails to reject \(H_0\) when \(H_a\) is in fact true (see Section 9.4.1). The following examples write the hypotheses and interpret both errors for our three proportion scenarios.

Example 10.4 (Daily YouTube Use Among Teens (continued)) Recall Example 10.1 where a school district was interested to test the claim that more than 70% of students in its district use YouTube daily.

State the null and alternative hypotheses in words.
Write the null and alternative hypotheses using mathematical notation.
Describe what happens if a Type I error occurs in the context of the problem.
Describe what happens if a Type II error occurs in the context of the problem.








Tip🔎 Solution






The null hypothesis states that 70% or fewer students in the district use YouTube daily. The alternative hypothesis states that more than 70% of students in the district use YouTube daily.
\[
\begin{cases}
H_0: p \leq 0.70 \\
H_a: p > 0.70
\end{cases}
\]
A Type I error occurs if we reject \(H_0\) and conclude that more than 70% of students in the district use YouTube daily when, in fact, the true proportion is 70% or less (\(H_0\) is true).
A Type II error occurs if we fail to reject \(H_0\) and therefore do not conclude that more than 70% of students in the district use YouTube daily when, in fact, the true proportion is greater than 70% (\(H_a\) is true).





Example 10.5 (Physical Inactivity Among Adults (continued)) Recall Example 10.2 where a national health agency wanted to examine the claim that fewer than 35% of adults in its country are physically inactive.

State the null and alternative hypotheses in words.
Write the null and alternative hypotheses using mathematical notation.
Describe what happens if a Type I error occurs in the context of the problem.
Describe what happens if a Type II error occurs in the context of the problem.








Tip🔎 Solution






The null hypothesis states that 35% or more adults in the country are physically inactive. The alternative hypothesis states that fewer than 35% of adults in the country are physically inactive.
\[
\begin{cases}
H_0: p \geq 0.35 \\
H_a: p < 0.35
\end{cases}
\]
A Type I error occurs if we reject \(H_0\) and conclude that fewer than 35% of adults in the country are physically inactive when, in fact, the true proportion is 35% or greater (\(H_0\) is true).
A Type II error occurs if we fail to reject \(H_0\) and therefore do not conclude that fewer than 35% of adults in the country are physically inactive when, in fact, the true proportion is less than 35% (\(H_a\) is true).





Example 10.6 (Social Media as a Primary News Source (continued)) Recall Example 10.3 where a university administration wanted to determine whether the true proportion of students who get most of their news from social media differs from 36% at their university.

State the null and alternative hypotheses in words.
Write the null and alternative hypotheses using mathematical notation.
Describe what happens if a Type I error occurs in the context of the problem.
Describe what happens if a Type II error occurs in the context of the problem.








Tip🔎 Solution






The null hypothesis states that 36% of students at the university get most of their news from social media. The alternative hypothesis states that the proportion of students at the university who get most of their news from social media is different from 36%.
\[
\begin{cases}
H_0: p = 0.36 \\
H_a: p \ne 0.36
\end{cases}
\]
A Type I error occurs if we reject \(H_0\) and conclude that the proportion of students at the university who get most of their news from social media is different from 36% when, in fact, the true proportion is 36% (\(H_0\) is true).
A Type II error occurs if we fail to reject \(H_0\) and therefore do not conclude that the proportion of students at the university who get most of their news from social media is different from 36% when, in fact, the true proportion is not 36% (\(H_a\) is true).






10.1.4 Homework for Section 10.1
For each of the following scenarios, describe or compute the items listed below as they relate to the research question:

The response variable and its possible categories
The success category of the response variable
The population of interest
The parameter of interest \(p\)
The sample
The statistic \(X\) and its observed value \(x_{\text{obs}}\)
The observed sample proportion \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}\) that is an estimate of \(p\)
State the null and alternative hypotheses in words.
Write the null and alternative hypotheses using mathematical notation.
Describe what happens if a Type I error occurs in the context of the problem.
Describe what happens if a Type II error occurs in the context of the problem.



Arizona Marijuana Legalization A poll conducted by The Arizona Republic/Morrison/Cronkite News, published on October 20, 2016, surveyed 779 registered voters in Arizona between October 10 and October 15, 2016. Of those surveyed, 390 reported favoring Proposition 205, which would legalize marijuana for adults (Sanchez, 2016). At the same time, 55% of Colorado residents supported the legalization of marijuana. Do Arizona registered voters differ from Colorado residents in their support for marijuana legalization?
Australian Unemployment Outlook In July 1997, 47% of Australians surveyed believed that unemployment would increase. In November 1997, the same question was asked again in a poll of 631 Australians, and 284 of them said they believed unemployment would increase (Morgan Gallup Poll, 2013). Did Australian sentiment about unemployment shift between July and November of 1997?
Arkansas Identity Theft Complaints According to the February 2008 Federal Trade Commission report on consumer fraud and identity theft, 23% of all complaints in 2007 were for identity theft. In that same year, Arkansas recorded 1,601 identity theft complaints out of a total of 3,482 consumer complaints (Consumer Fraud and, 2008). Was the proportion of identity theft complaints in Arkansas larger than the national figure of 23%?
Alaska Identity Theft Complaints According to the February 2008 Federal Trade Commission report on consumer fraud and identity theft, 23% of all complaints in 2007 were for identity theft. In that same year, Alaska recorded 321 identity theft complaints out of a total of 1,432 consumer complaints (Consumer Fraud and, 2008). Was Alaska’s proportion of identity theft complaints significantly less than the national proportion of 23%?
Kennedy Assassination Conspiracy Belief In 2001, a Gallup poll found that 81% of American adults believed there was a conspiracy behind the death of President Kennedy. In 2013, the same question was posed to a Gallup poll of 1,039 American adults, and 634 of them believed there was a conspiracy behind the assassination (Gallup News Service, 2013). Is there evidence that American belief in a conspiracy behind President Kennedy’s assassination changed between 2001 and 2013?
Autism Spectrum Disorder in Arizona In 2008, 507 out of 32,601 children in Arizona were diagnosed with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) (Autism and Developmental, 2008). Nationally, 1 in 88 children are diagnosed with ASD (CDC Features, 2013). Is the rate of ASD diagnosis among children in Arizona larger than the national rate?
Graduate Degree Attainment: GSS2024 According to the U.S. Census Bureau’s 2024 educational attainment data, approximately 15% of U.S. adults aged 25 and older have earned a graduate degree, defined as a master’s degree, professional degree, or doctoral degree (U.S. Census Bureau, 2025). The GSS2024 dataset contains responses from \(n = 388\) U.S. adults. The variable Degree records the highest degree earned by each respondent, and 33 of the 388 respondents reported a graduate degree as their highest level of education. Does the GSS2024 data provide evidence that the proportion of U.S. adults who hold a graduate degree differs from the 15% reported by the U.S. Census Bureau?


 The dataset for this exercise is available in the Rguroo dataset repository Intro to Stats with Rguroo, with the dataset name GSS2024.
Code book for Dataset GSS2024 is given here.

title: 10  Inference for Population Proportions
section: 10.2 Making a Decision about a Population Proportion
text:
10.2 Making a Decision about a Population Proportion
For a two-sided test, an observed sample proportion either above or below the null value can provide evidence against \(H_0.\) For example, in the social media example with \(H_0: p = 0.36\) versus \(H_a: p \neq 0.36,\) a sample proportion that differs from \(0.36\) in either direction could provide evidence in favor of \(H_a.\) However, simply observing that \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}\) differs from \(0.36\) is not enough to reject \(H_0.\) Some difference is expected because of random sampling variation. We need to perform a hypothesis test to determine whether the observed difference is large enough to provide sufficient evidence against \(H_0.\)
For a one-sided test, there is an additional consideration: the observed sample proportion must first be in the direction specified by \(H_a\) to provide evidence against \(H_0.\) For instance, in Example 10.1, the Daily YouTube Use Among Teens example, the hypotheses are \(H_0: p \leq 0.70\) versus \(H_a: p > 0.70.\) If a sample of \(n = 20\) students resulted in only \(x_{\text{obs}} = 12\) students reporting daily use, then \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} = \frac{12}{20} = 0.60.\) Since \(0.60\) falls within the values specified by \(H_0\) rather than in the direction of \(H_a,\) this sample result clearly does not provide evidence against \(H_0\) in favor of \(H_a.\)
On the other hand, if \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}\) were greater than \(0.70,\) being in the direction of \(H_a\) would not by itself be enough to reject \(H_0.\) We would still need to perform the hypothesis test to determine whether the observed result is sufficiently far from the null value to be unlikely to occur by random chance, assuming \(H_0\) is true.
Now consider sample results that point in the direction of \(H_a.\) For the YouTube example (\(H_a: p > 0.70\)), \(x_{\text{obs}} = 17\) out of \(n = 20\) gives \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} = 0.85,\) which is greater than \(0.70.\) For the physical inactivity example (\(H_a: p < 0.35\)), \(x_{\text{obs}} = 10\) out of \(n = 50\) gives \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} = 0.20,\) which is less than \(0.35.\) For the social media example (\(H_a: p \neq 0.36\)), \(x_{\text{obs}} = 9\) out of \(n = 15\) gives \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} = 0.60,\) which is noticeably different from \(0.36.\) Each of these results points in the direction of \(H_a.\) But is that enough to reject \(H_0\)?
Not necessarily!






NoteConsistency With \(H_a\) Is Not the Same as Strong Evidence in Favor of \(H_a\)



A sample result that points in the direction of \(H_a\) does not by itself constitute strong evidence in favor of \(H_a.\) Because of sampling variability, such a result can occur by chance even when \(H_0\) is true. The key question is whether the sample result would be unlikely to occur by chance if \(H_0\) were true. If so, we have strong evidence against \(H_0\) and in favor of \(H_a.\)


We now turn to actually carrying out a hypothesis test for a proportion. Recall from Section 9.4.2 that, because reducing one type of error tends to increase the other, we control the probability of a Type I error by holding it to a small, prespecified significance level \(\alpha.\) Recall also that there are two equivalent ways to reach a decision: the p-value approach and the critical region approach. These approaches always lead to the same decision.
There are two methods we will use to carry out a hypothesis test for one population proportion: a large-sample approach based on the normal distribution and an exact approach based on the binomial distribution. We begin with the large-sample approach in Section 10.3, which relies on the central limit theorem and requires a sufficiently large sample for the normal approximation to work well. We then consider the exact binomial approach in Section 10.5, which uses the binomial distribution directly and does not require a large sample.
It is important to distinguish these two methods from the p-value and critical region approaches. The large-sample and exact binomial methods determine how we calculate the probabilities for the test. The p-value and critical region approaches determine how we use those probabilities to make a decision about \(H_0.\)
The exact binomial method is an ideal choice when we want to avoid relying on a large-sample approximation because it uses the binomial distribution directly to calculate exact probabilities. It does not require a large sample for the normal approximation to be valid. Nevertheless, there are good reasons to begin with the large-sample approach. Most importantly, the basic ideas generalize naturally to other inference problems, such as comparing two population proportions and drawing inferences about population means. In addition, large-sample methods have historically been widely used, so you will frequently encounter them in published research. Finally, because the large-sample approach builds on the familiar normal distribution, it provides an accessible starting point for learning how hypothesis tests are carried out.

title: 10  Inference for Population Proportions
text:
10.3 Large Sample Hypothesis Testing
The large sample approach rests on the Central Limit Theorem (CLT), which you have already seen in Chapter 7. Recall that the CLT tells us that, for a sufficiently large sample, the sampling distribution of a sample mean is approximately normal, even when the population distribution itself is not normal. At first, this may seem unrelated to proportions: the CLT concerns sample means, while our interest here is in a sample proportion. However, as we will see next, a sample proportion can itself be viewed as a sample mean. This connection allows us to apply the CLT directly to sample proportions and provides the foundation for the large-sample approach.

10.3.1 A Sample Proportion Is a Mean
Suppose we record whether each individual in our sample has the characteristic of interest by assigning a value of 1 to each success and a value of 0 to each failure. For example, in the YouTube study (Example 10.1), a student who uses YouTube daily receives a 1, and a student who does not receives a 0. If our sample of \(n = 20\) students produced 17 daily users, the data would consist of 17 ones and 3 zeros. The sum of these 20 values is 17, and their average is
\[
\frac{17}{20} = 0.85,
\]
which is exactly the observed sample proportion, \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}.\)
More generally, if a sample of size \(n\) produces some number of successes, then
\[
\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} = \frac{\text{number of successes}}{n} = \frac{\text{sum of the 0/1 values}}{n}.
\]
Thus, when successes and failures are coded as 1 and 0, the observed sample proportion is simply the mean of the zeros and ones in the sample.
The same idea applies to any random sample of size \(n.\) For each possible sample, the sample proportion \(\hat{p}\) is the mean of its 0/1 values. Thus, a sample proportion is a special case of a sample mean: it is the mean of observations that can take only the values 0 and 1.
This connection allows us to apply the Central Limit Theorem (CLT) to sample proportions. Recall that the CLT tells us that, for a sufficiently large sample size, the sampling distribution of a sample mean is approximately normal. Since a sample proportion is a sample mean based on 0/1 observations, its sampling distribution is also approximately normal for a sufficiently large sample.


10.3.2 Applying the Central Limit Theorem to \(\hat p\)
Since \(\hat{p}\) is a sample mean of 0s and 1s, its sampling distribution follows the same general pattern as other sample means. For a population with proportion of successes \(p,\) the sampling distribution of \(\hat{p}\) has:

Mean: \(\mu_{\hat{p}}=p\)
Standard deviation: \(\sigma_{\hat{p}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}}\)

This standard deviation is often called the standard error of \(\hat{p}.\) It measures how much we expect \(\hat{p}\) to vary from sample to sample. By the CLT, when \(n\) is sufficiently large, \(\hat{p}\) follows approximately a normal distribution:
\[
\hat{p} \sim N\!\left(p,\; \sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}\right).
\]
Since \(p\) is unknown, we need to specify a value for it to use this result for inference. Recall that in hypothesis testing we assume the null hypothesis is true, and that the maximum Type I error occurs at the boundary value \(p_0\) of \(H_0\) (see Section 9.3.2). We therefore evaluate the sampling distribution of \(\hat{p}\) at \(p = p_0,\) giving:
\[
\hat{p} \sim N\!\left(p_0,\; \sqrt{\frac{p_0(1-p_0)}{n}}\right).
\]
We call this the null distribution of \(\hat{p},\) since it describes the behavior of \(\hat{p}\) at the boundary value \(p_0\) of the null hypothesis \(H_0,\) where the Type I error is at its maximum. This normal null distribution of \(\hat{p}\) is the foundation for decisions in hypothesis testing in the large sample method.
An option is to use a standardized statistic called the \(z\)-score, obtained by subtracting \(p_0\) from \(\hat{p}\) and dividing by the standard error:
\[
z = \frac{\hat{p} - p_0}{\sqrt{\dfrac{p_0(1-p_0)}{n}}}.
\]
This unit-less quantity is then compared to a standard normal distribution. In this textbook, we instead work directly with \(\hat{p}\) and compare it to its null distribution. This requires fewer computational steps and, more importantly, keeps our decisions on the original scale — conclusions are about a sample proportion rather than an abstract standardized value.


10.3.3 What is Considered a Large Sample Size?
What constitutes a large sample size for the normal approximation to hold? A common rule of thumb is to check the expected numbers of successes and failures. In particular, the approximation is typically considered reliable when \(np_0 \geq 10\) and \(n(1 - p_0) \geq 10.\) When both of these conditions are satisfied, the binomial distribution tends to be reasonably symmetric, and the normal model provides a good fit.






NoteLarge Sample Condition: The 10-10 Rule



The normal approximation for \(\hat{p}\) is considered reliable when both of the following hold:
\[np_0 \geq 10 \qquad \text{and} \qquad n(1-p_0) \geq 10.\]
These conditions ensure that the sample is large enough for the CLT to provide a good approximation. If either condition fails, the exact binomial method (see Section 10.5.2 and Section 10.5.3) is the appropriate choice.


To illustrate the 10–10 rule, consider the YouTube Daily Use example, where \(n=20\) and \(p_0=0.70\):

Expected successes: \(np_0 = 20\times 0.70 = 14\)
Expected failures: \(n(1-p_0) = 20\times 0.30 = 6\)

Since the expected number of failures is less than 10, the 10–10 rule is not satisfied. Therefore, the normal approximation may not be reliable for this example.
In contrast, for the Physical Inactivity example, where \(n=50\) and \(p_0=0.35\):

Expected successes: \(np_0 = 50\times 0.35 = 17.5\)
Expected failures: \(n(1-p_0) = 50\times 0.65 = 32.5\)

Since both values exceed 10, the 10–10 rule is satisfied. Therefore, the normal approximation is appropriate for the Physical Inactivity example.


10.3.4 Decision Based on a p-value
We explained the idea behind the p-value approach in Section 9.5. In this section we show how p-values are computed using the large sample method for a population proportion.
To compute a p-value, we first need to identify which possible sample results provide at least as much support for \(H_a\) as the result we actually observed. For this purpose, we define what we call the \(H_a\) support.
The \(H_a\) support is the set of all possible values of the sample proportion \(\hat{p}\) that are at least as favorable to \(H_a\) as the observed sample proportion \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}.\)
For one-sided tests, this is straightforward: as shown in Figure 10.1, if \(H_a: p > p_0,\) larger values of \(\hat{p}\) are more favorable to \(H_a,\) so the \(H_a\) support consists of \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}\) and all values above it. Symmetrically, for \(H_a: p < p_0,\) the \(H_a\) support consists of \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}\) and all values below it.








Figure 10.1: One-tailed p-value regions. Top: right-tailed test, p-value is the area where p-hat is greater than or equal to the observed value. Bottom: left-tailed test, p-value is the area where p-hat is less than or equal to the observed value





For the two-sided test \(H_a: p \neq p_0,\) the \(H_a\) support consists of values in both tails of the null distribution that are at least the same distance \(d\) from \(p_0\) as \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}\) (see Figure 10.2). Because the normal null distribution is symmetric about \(p_0,\) these values are symmetrically positioned about \(p_0\) . If \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} > p_0,\) the \(H_a\) support is the set of values \(\hat{p} \geq \hat{p}_{\text{obs}}\) together with their mirror image relative to \(p_0\) in the left tail. If \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} < p_0,\) the \(H_a\) support is the set of values \(\hat{p} \leq \hat{p}_{\text{obs}}\) together with their mirror image relative to \(p_0\) in the right tail.








Figure 10.2: The \(H_a\) support for a two-sided test. The shaded segments show the values of \(\hat{p}\) that are as favorable or more favorable to \(H_a\) than \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}.\) The dashed tick marks the mirror image of \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}\) relative to \(p_0,\) each being a distance \(d\) from \(p_0.\)





Once the \(H_a\) support has been identified, the p-value is the probability, assuming \(H_0\) is true, that \(\hat{p}\) falls in the \(H_a\) support. For the large-sample method, we compute this probability using the normal null distribution at the boundary value \(p=p_0.\) Thus, \[
\text{p-value} = P(\hat{p} \text{ is in the } H_a \text{ support}), \text{ assuming that } p=p_0.
\] Recall from Section 9.3.2 why we use the boundary value \(p=p_0.\) A more detailed explanation is provided in the optional Section 10.7.






Notep-value for the Large Sample Test



All probabilities are computed using the null distribution \(\hat{p} \sim N\!\left(p_0,\, \sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}\right).\)








Alternative Hypothesis
\(H_a\) Support
p-value




\(H_a: p > p_0\)
\(\hat{p} \geq \hat{p}_{\text{obs}}\)
\(P(\hat{p} \geq \hat{p}_{\text{obs}})\)


\(H_a: p < p_0\)
\(\hat{p} \leq \hat{p}_{\text{obs}}\)
\(P(\hat{p} \leq \hat{p}_{\text{obs}})\)


\(H_a: p \neq p_0,\) if \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} > p_0\)
\(\hat{p} \geq \hat{p}_{\text{obs}}\) and its mirror relative to \(p_0\)
\(2 \times P(\hat{p} \geq \hat{p}_{\text{obs}})\)


\(H_a: p \neq p_0,\) if \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} < p_0\)
\(\hat{p} \leq \hat{p}_{\text{obs}}\) and its mirror relative to \(p_0\)
\(2 \times P(\hat{p} \leq \hat{p}_{\text{obs}})\)





As explained in Section 9.5, we compare the p-value to the significance level \(\alpha\) to make our decision: \[
\text{If p-value} \leq \alpha, \text{ reject } H_0. \qquad \text{If p-value} > \alpha, \text{ fail to reject } H_0.
\] Recall that a small p-value means that \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}\) and values at least as supportive of \(H_a\) would be unlikely to occur if \(H_0\) were true. Thus, a small p-value provides evidence against \(H_0\) and in favor of \(H_a.\)
The p-value approach also indicates the strength of the evidence: a very small p-value indicates strong evidence against \(H_0,\) while a p-value just below \(\alpha\) indicates weaker evidence.

Example 10.7 (Physical Inactivity Among Adults - p-value Approach) Recall Example 10.2. A national health agency hopes that fewer than 35% of adults in its country are physically inactive. A random sample of \(n = 50\) adults was selected and \(x_{\text{obs}} = 10\) were found to be physically inactive. The hypotheses are: \[
\begin{cases}
H_0: p \geq 0.35 \\
H_a: p < 0.35
\end{cases}
\]

Check the 10-10 rule to see whether the conditions for the normal approximation hold.
Determine the \(H_a\) support.
Write a probability statement that describes the p-value.
Use Rguroo’s Proportion Inference function to obtain the p-value, and state your conclusion in the context of the problem using significance level of \(\alpha=0.05.\)








Tip🔎 Solution





a. To check the large sample condition, we compute the expected number of successes and failures under \(H_0.\) Using the boundary value \(p_0 = 0.35\):
\[np_0 = 50 \times 0.35 = 17.5 \geq 10\]
\[n(1 - p_0) = 50 \times 0.65 = 32.5 \geq 10.\]
Both conditions are satisfied, so the large sample normal approximation is appropriate for this example.
b. We have \(x_{\text{obs}}=10\) and \(n=50,\) which gives \[
\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}=\frac{10}{50}=0.20.
\] Since the alternative hypothesis is \(H_a: p<0.35,\) smaller values of \(\hat{p}\) provide stronger evidence in favor of \(H_a.\) Therefore, the \(H_a\) support consists of all sample proportions less than or equal to the observed value:
\[
\textbf{H}_a\ \textbf{Support:}\;\; \hat{p} \le 0.20.
\]








Figure 10.3: One-sided \(H_a\) support for \(p_0=0.35\) and \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} = 0.20.\)





c. The p-value is computed as \[
\text{p-value} = P\left(\hat{p} \le 0.2),\; \text{ assuming }  p=0.35\right.
\]

The red colored area corresponds to the \(H_a\) support, consisting of all sample proportions \(\hat{p} \le 0.20.\) The area under the curve over this region is the p-value, 0.01308. Example 10.8 (Social Media as a Primary News Source - p-value Approach) Recall Example 10.3, where a Pew Research Center report stated that 36% of U.S. adults ages 18–29 say they regularly get news from social media. A university administration was unsure whether the same percentage applied to students at their university. Thus, they set out to test the hypotheses \[
\begin{cases}
H_0: p = 0.36 \\
H_a: p \neq 0.36.
\end{cases}
\] To investigate this claim, the university initially took a sample of \(n=15\) students. However, they realized that this sample was too small to apply the large-sample test. So, they increased their sample to \(n=35\) students. In their sample of \(n=35\) students, they found that 21 students stated that they regularly get news from social media.

Check the 10-10 rule to determine whether the conditions for the normal approximation hold.
Determine the \(H_a\) support.
Write a probability statement that describes the p-value.
Use Rguroo’s Proportion Inference function to obtain the p-value, and state your conclusion in the context of the problem using significance level of \(\alpha=0.01.\)








Tip🔎 Solution





a. To check the large sample condition, we compute the expected number of successes and expected number of failures under \(H_0.\) Using the boundary value \(p_0 = 0.36\):
\[np_0 = 35 \times 0.36 = 12.6 \geq 10\]
\[n(1 - p_0) = 35 \times 0.64 = 22.4 \geq 10.\]
Both conditions are satisfied, so the large sample normal approximation is appropriate for this example.
b. We have \(x_{\text{obs}}=21\) and \(n=35,\) which gives \[
\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}=\frac{21}{35}=0.60.
\] Since this is a two-sided alternative, values of \(\hat{p}\) far from \(p_0\) in either direction count as evidence against \(H_0.\) The observed proportion \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}=0.60\) lies \(0.60-0.36=0.24\) above \(p_0,\) so a value equally far below \(p_0\) — namely \(0.36-0.24=0.12\) — provides just as much evidence against \(H_0.\) Since \(p_0=0.36,\) and \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}=0.60,\) the \(H_a\) support is given by
\[
\textbf{H}_a\ \textbf{Support:}\;\; \hat{p} \geq 0.60 \text{ or } \hat{p} \leq 0.12.\]








Figure 10.6: Two-sided \(H_a\) support for \(p_0=0.36\) and \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} = 0.60.\)





c. The p-value is computed as \[
\begin{aligned}
\text{p-value}
&= P\left(\hat{p} \le 0.12\right) + P\left(\hat{p} \ge 0.60\right) \\
&= 2\times P\left(\hat{p} \ge 0.60\right), \qquad \text{assuming } p=0.36.
\end{aligned}\] The last equalty holds, since the normal distribution is symmetric about \(p_0=0.36,\)

Using Raw Data
So far, we have performed proportion inference using a summary of the sample, namely the sample size \(n\) and the observed count \(x_{\text{obs}}.\) In practice, however, we often work directly with a raw dataset rather than a pre-computed summary. Now, we show how to perform proportion inference from raw data using Rguroo.
We illustrate this using data from the General Social Survey (GSS), one of the longest-running and most widely used surveys in the United States. Conducted by NORC at the University of Chicago, the GSS has collected data on the attitudes, behaviors, and characteristics of American adults since 1972, covering topics such as social values, political views, religion, and lifestyle. The dataset that we use here, GSS2024, is a subset of the 2024 GSS data. After removing observations with missing values, the dataset contains \(n = 388\) respondents.

\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}=\frac{282}{388}\approx 0.727.
\] Since the alternative hypothesis is \(H_a: p>0.70,\) larger values of \(\hat{p}\) provide stronger evidence in favor of \(H_a.\) Therefore, the \(H_a\) support consists of all sample proportions greater than or equal to the observed value: \[
\textbf{H}_a\ \textbf{Support:}\;\; \hat{p} \ge 0.727.
\]

\text{p-value} = P\left(\hat{p} \ge 0.727\right), \text{assuming } p=0.70.
\]

10.3.5 Decision Based on a Critical Region
We now turn to the critical region approach, the other standard way to reach a decision. Recall from Section 9.6 that the critical region is the set of values of the statistic for which we reject \(H_0\) in favor of \(H_a.\) Whereas the p-value approach summarizes the evidence with a probability computed from the observed proportion \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}},\) the critical region approach decides in advance which values of \(\hat{p}\) are extreme enough to reject \(H_0,\) and then simply checks whether \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}\) falls in the critical region.
The decision is governed by a decision rule: a rule that specifies which values of \(\hat{p}\) lead to rejecting \(H_0.\) For a one-sided test with \(H_a: p > p_0,\) large values of \(\hat{p}\) favor the alternative hypothesis, so the critical region lies in the right tail of the null distribution. To determine the critical region, we use the distribution of \(\hat{p}\) under the null hypothesis \(p=p_0,\) namely \[
\hat{p}\sim N\left(p_0, \sqrt{\frac{p_0(1-p_0)}{n}}\right).
\] We choose the critical value so that the probability of falling in the critical region when \(H_0\) is true equals the significance level \(\alpha.\) The shape of the critical region — right tail, left tail, or both — depends on the alternative hypothesis, as shown in Figure 10.12.








Figure 10.12: Critical regions for right-tailed, left-tailed, and two-tailed tests on the null distribution of \(\hat{p}.\)





For the right-tailed test, we find the critical value \(c\) so that there is probability \(\alpha\) in the right tail: \[
P(\hat{p} \geq c)=\alpha.
\] We then reject \(H_0\) if the observed sample proportion satisfies \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} \geq c.\)
Similarly, for a one-sided test with \(H_a: p < p_0,\) small values of \(\hat{p}\) favor the alternative hypothesis, so the critical region lies in the left tail. We find \(c\) such that \[
P(\hat{p} \leq c)=\alpha,
\] and reject \(H_0\) if \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} \leq c.\)
For a two-sided test with \(H_a: p \neq p_0,\) both unusually small and unusually large values of \(\hat{p}\) favor the alternative hypothesis. The critical region therefore lies in both tails. We find lower and upper critical values, \(c_1\) and \(c_2,\) that leave probability \(\alpha/2\) in each tail: \[
P\left(\hat{p} \leq c_1 \right)=\frac{\alpha}{2}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
P\left(\hat{p} \geq c_2 \right)=\frac{\alpha}{2}.
\] We reject \(H_0\) if \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} \leq c_1\) or \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} \geq c_2.\)






NoteCritical Region for the Large Sample Test



All critical values are found using the null distribution \(\hat{p} \sim N\!\left(p_0,\, \sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}\right).\)








Alternative Hypothesis

\(H_a: p > p_0\)

\(H_a: p < p_0\)
\(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} \leq c\)
\(P(\hat{p} \leq c) = \alpha\)


\(H_a: p \neq p_0\)
\(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} \leq c_1\) or \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} \geq c_2\)
\(P(\hat{p} \leq c_1) = P(\hat{p} \geq c_2) = \alpha/2\)

title: 10  Inference for Population Proportions
text:
10.5 Exact Binomial Hypothesis Testing
In the previous section, we used the large-sample method to carry out a hypothesis test for a population proportion. This method uses the normal distribution to approximate the sampling distribution of \(\hat{p}\) and works well when the sample is sufficiently large. We now consider the exact binomial method, which uses the binomial distribution directly and therefore does not require a large-sample approximation. The basic reasoning of the hypothesis test remains the same: we determine how unusual the observed sample result would be if \(H_0\) were true and use either the p-value or critical region approach to make a decision. The main difference is the statistic we use. With the large-sample method, we worked with the sample proportion \(\hat{p}.\) With the exact binomial method, we work directly with \(X,\) the number of successes in the sample. Since \(\hat{p}=X/n,\) these two statistics contain the same information; we are simply expressing the sample result in a different way.

10.5.1 The Distribution of \(X\)
To use \(X\) for inference, we need to know its probability distribution. Since we are sampling from a population and counting successes, the binomial distribution provides the appropriate model. Recall from Section 6.2 that a random variable follows a binomial distribution when:

The number of trials \(n\) is fixed
Each trial results in one of two outcomes: success or failure
The probability of success \(p\) is the same for every trial
The trials are independent of one another

In our sampling context, each individual in the sample either has the characteristic of interest (success) or does not (failure). Since the sample is selected randomly, the trials are practically independent. The probability of success \(p\) is constant—it equals the population proportion. (Strictly speaking, sampling without replacement causes \(p\) to change slightly with each draw, but when the sample is small relative to the population, this change is negligible and we treat \(p\) as constant.)
Therefore, \[
X \sim \text{Binomial}(n, p).
\]
This distribution will be the foundation for computing probabilities and making decisions about \(p.\)


10.5.2 Decision Based on a p-Value
The p-value approach measures how unusual the observed count \(x_{\text{obs}}\) would be if the null hypothesis were true, and rejects \(H_0\) when the data are sufficiently unusual under \(H_0.\) To make this concrete for a proportion, we evaluate probabilities at the boundary value \(p_0\) (see Section 9.3.2), using the binomial distribution of the count \(X.\)
Using the definition of \(H_a\) support from Section 9.5, the \(H_a\) support for the exact binomial method consists of the values of \(X\) that are at least as supportive of \(H_a\) as the observed value \(x_{\text{obs}}.\) The p-value then is the probability, assuming \(p=p_0,\) that \(X\) takes a value in the \(H_a\) support:
\[
\text{p-value} = P(X \text{ is a value in the } H_a \text{ support),  assuming }  p = p_0.
\]
A small p-value is evidence against \(H_0.\)
What counts as “the \(H_a\) support” depends on the form of the alternative hypothesis.






NoteCase 1: \(H_a: p > p_0\) (e.g., \(H_a: p > 0.70\))



Larger values of \(X\) are more supportive of \(H_a.\) The \(H_a\) support consists of \(x_{\text{obs}}\) and all values larger than \(x_{\text{obs}},\) so the p-value is \[
\text{p-value} = P(X \geq x_{\text{obs}}), \text{ assuming } p = p_0.
\]


To understand Case 1, note that a larger value of \(X\) means more successes in the sample, which corresponds to a higher sample proportion \(\hat{p}.\) A higher sample proportion is less consistent with \(H_0\) and more supportive of the claim that the true population proportion exceeds \(p_0.\) For example, in the YouTube example where \(x_{\text{obs}} = 17\) out of \(n = 20,\) the \(H_a\) support consists of the values \(\{17, 18, 19, 20\}\) — the observed count and every larger possibility.






NoteCase 2: \(H_a: p < p_0\) (e.g., \(H_a: p < 0.35\))



Smaller values of \(X\) are more supportive of \(H_a.\) The \(H_a\) support consists of \(x_{\text{obs}}\) and all values smaller than \(x_{\text{obs}},\) so the p-value is \[
\text{p-value} = P(X \leq x_{\text{obs}}), \text{ assuming } p = p_0.
\]


Case 2 is the mirror image of Case 1: a smaller value of \(X\) means fewer successes in the sample, which corresponds to a lower sample proportion \(\hat{p}.\) A lower sample proportion is less consistent with \(H_0\) and more supportive of the claim that the true population proportion is less than \(p_0.\) For example, in the Physical Inactivity example where \(x_{\text{obs}} = 10\) out of \(n = 50,\) the \(H_a\) support is \(\{0, 1, 2, \ldots, 9, 10\}\) — the observed count and every smaller possibility.






NoteCase 3: \(H_a: p \neq p_0\) (e.g., \(H_a: p \neq 0.36\))



A value \(x\) is in the \(H_a\) support if it is at least as unlikely as the observed value \(x_{\text{obs}}\) under \(H_0,\) that is, \[
P(X = x) \leq P(X = x_{\text{obs}}), \text{ assuming } p = p_0.
\]
Such values can occur in either tail of the distribution.


The two-sided case is easiest to see in a picture. For the Social Media News example with \(x_{\text{obs}} = 9\) out of \(n = 15\) and \(p_0 = 0.36,\) Figure 10.17 shows the binomial distribution of \(X\) under \(H_0,\) where \(X \sim \text{Binomial}(15, 0.36).\)








Figure 10.17: Two-sided p-value for the Social Media example; shaded regions represent outcomes at least as unlikely as x_obs = 9 under H0, when p = 0.36.





The \(X\) values corresponding to the orange bars are the values of \(X\) whose probability under \(H_0\) is at most equal to \(P(X = 9).\) Therefore, the \(H_a\) support appears in both tails: large values \(9, 10, 11, \ldots\) on the right and small values \(0, 1\) on the left. The p-value is the total probability of the orange bars.
The decision rule using the p-value is the same as the one introduced in Section 9.5 and used with the large-sample method: we reject \(H_0\) when the p-value is less than or equal to the significance level \(\alpha.\) The interpretation is also the same. A small p-value means that the observed result and results at least as supportive of \(H_a\) would be unlikely if \(H_0\) were true. The difference is that with the exact binomial method, we express the observed result as the number of successes \(x_{\text{obs}}\) and calculate the p-value directly from the binomial distribution of \(X.\)






NoteDecision Rule Using the p-Value



When testing at significance level \(\alpha,\) \[
\text{If p-value} \leq \alpha, \text{ reject } H_0. \qquad \text{If p-value} > \alpha, \text{ fail to reject } H_0.
\]


In practice, we use statistical software such as Rguroo to compute p-values. Rguroo’s One-Population Proportion inference function carries out a complete hypothesis test from the inputs \(n,\) \(x_{\text{obs}},\) and the form of \(H_a\) (including \(p_0\)). The next four examples illustrate how to obtain the p-value and reach a decision, using our three running examples plus the raw-dataset example from the GSS.

Example 10.12 (Daily YouTube Use Among Teens (continued)) Recall Example 10.1. A school district claims that more than 70% of students in its district use YouTube daily, that is, \(H_a: p > 0.70.\) A random sample of \(n = 20\) students is selected, and \(x_{\text{obs}} = 17\) of them report daily YouTube use. The hypotheses are \[
\begin{cases}
H_0: p \leq 0.70 \\
H_a: p > 0.70
\end{cases}
\]
Use Rguroo’s One-Population Proportion inference function to obtain the p-value, and use it to make a decision at significance level \(\alpha = 0.05.\)







Tip🔎 Solution





Our sample of \(n = 20\) students yielded \(x_{\text{obs}} = 17\) daily users, giving \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} = 17/20 = 0.85.\) We use Rguroo to compute the p-value and decide whether this result is statistically significant.

Figure 10.19 shows the p-value graph from the Rguroo output. The p-value is approximately \(0.107,\) with \(H_a\) support \(X \geq 17,\) highlighted by the red bars. Since the p-value \(0.107 > \alpha = 0.05,\) we fail to reject \(H_0.\) The data do not provide sufficient evidence at the \(5\%\) significance level to conclude that more than 70% of students in the district use YouTube daily.








Figure 10.19: Binomial distribution under the null hypothesis with observed count 17. The red bars show the \(H_a\) support, and their total probability is the p-value.










Example 10.13 (ESP Card-Guessing Experiment - Exact Binomial (P-value)) In a classic test of extrasensory perception (ESP), a participant tries to identify which of five symbols (a star, a circle, a square, a cross, or wavy lines) appears on a hidden card, without seeing it. If the participant has no real ability to sense the symbol and is simply guessing, the probability of a correct guess on any single trial is \(p = 0.20\).
A researcher wants to test whether a particular participant performs worse than random guessing, a phenomenon some parapsychology researchers have called “psi-missing” and attributed to an unconscious avoidance of the correct answer. The participant completes \(n = 20\) trials, and \(x_{\text{obs}} = 1\) of the guesses is correct. Test, at the \(\alpha = 0.05\) level, whether these results provide evidence that the participant’s true probability of a correct guess is below \(0.20\).







Tip🔎 Solution





The null and alternative hypotheses are \[
H_0: p \ge 0.20 \quad \text{vs.} \quad H_a: p < 0.20.
\]
Since \(np_0 = 20 \times 0.20 = 4 < 10\), the sample is too small to rely on the normal approximation, so we use the exact binomial method. Because we are only given the sample size and the number of successes rather than raw data for each trial, we enter the information using summary statistics rather than a raw dataset, following the same instructions as in the solution of the YouTube example.
In the summary-statistics entry dialog, since there is no dataset to select variables and levels from, we instead type in our own labels:

Factor label: Guess Outcome
Success label: Correct
Failure label: Incorrect

along with the sample size (\(n = 20\)), the number of successes (\(x_{\text{obs}} = 1\)), the hypothesized proportion (\(p_0 = 0.20\)), the direction of the alternative hypothesis (\(p < 0.20\)), and the exact binomial method.
The Rguroo dialog for this example is shown below.








Figure 10.20: Rguroo dialog for the one-proportion exact binomial test, entered using summary statistics for the ESP card-guessing experiment.





Click to expand the box below to see the Rguroo output.






TipRguroo output: One-Population Proportion Inference — ESP Test






 




The exact binomial p-value is \(0.069\). This is the probability, computed under \(H_0\) (i.e., assuming \(p = 0.20\)), of observing a result at least as favorable to \(H_a\) as the one obtained — that is, \(X \le 1\) success out of 20 trials.








Figure 10.21: P-value graph for the exact binomial test of the ESP card-guessing experiment.





Since the p-value is greater than \(\alpha = 0.05\), we fail to reject \(H_0\). There is not sufficient evidence at the 5% significance level that the participant’s true probability of a correct guess is below 0.20, i.e., the results are not sufficient to conclude that psi-missing occurred.




Example 10.14 (Social Media as a Primary News - Source Exact Binomial (P-value)) Recall Example 10.3. A university administration wants to determine whether the proportion of students who get most of their news from social media differs from 36%, that is, \(H_a: p \neq 0.36.\) A random sample of \(n = 15\) students is selected, and \(x_{\text{obs}} = 9\) report using social media as their primary news source. The hypotheses are \[
\begin{cases}
H_0: p = 0.36 \\
H_a: p \neq 0.36
\end{cases}
\]
Use Rguroo’s One-Population Proportion inference function to obtain the p-value, and use it to make a decision at significance level \(\alpha = 0.10.\)







Tip🔎 Solution

10.5.3 Decision Based on a Critical Region
Recall from Section 9.6 that the critical region approach identifies, in advance, the values of the statistic that lead us to reject \(H_0.\) We used this same approach with the large-sample method. For the exact binomial method, the reasoning is unchanged; the difference is that the critical region is now defined in terms of the possible values of \(X,\) the number of successes. As before, the location of the critical region is determined by the direction of the alternative hypothesis \(H_a\):






\[\text{Reject } H_0 \text{ if }
\begin{cases}
X \geq c & \text{when } H_a: p > p_0 \\
X \leq c & \text{when } H_a: p < p_0 \\
X \leq c_1 \text{ or } X \geq c_2 & \text{when } H_a: p \neq p_0
\end{cases}\] The values \(c,\) \(c_1,\) and \(c_2\) are called critical values, and the corresponding values of \(X\) form the critical region (also called the rejection region).



To find the critical values, we use the null distribution \[
X\sim\text{Binomial}(n,p_0).
\] We choose the largest critical region for which the probability of a Type I error does not exceed the significance level \(\alpha.\)






NoteSometimes the Actual Significance Level Is Less Than \(\alpha\)



Because the binomial distribution is discrete, \(X\) takes only whole-number values. As a result, changing a critical value causes the probability of the critical region to change in steps rather than continuously. Therefore, we often cannot find a critical region with a probability exactly equal to \(\alpha.\)
Rguroo returns the largest critical region whose probability under \(H_0\) is at or below \(\alpha.\) The probability of this critical region is the actual significance level of the test and is reported as the Exact Significance Level in the Rguroo output.
For example, if we choose \(\alpha = 0.05,\) Rguroo might return a critical region with an actual significance level \(0.0476\) or \(0.0342.\) In either case, the probability of a Type I error is below the chosen significance level of \(0.05.\)


In practice, we use Rguroo’s One-Population Proportion inference function to find this critical region.

10.6 State your conclusion in the context of the problem.


Airport Security Screening: An airport reports that 5% of randomly selected passengers require additional security screening. In a random sample of \(n = 40\) passengers at a particular terminal, \(x_{\text{obs}} = 5\) required additional screening. Defective Computer Chips: A manufacturer claims that 4% of the computer chips it produces are defective. A quality-control inspector randomly selects \(n = 50\) chips and finds that \(x_{\text{obs}} = 5\) are defective. Is there evidence that the true proportion of defective chips is greater than 4%?
