Online Order Returns: A small online retailer has historically had 8% of its orders returned. After changing its product descriptions, the retailer randomly examines \(n = 30\) recent orders and finds that \(x_{\text{obs}} = 1\) was returned. Is there evidence that the proportion of orders being returned has decreased from 8%? Use \(\alpha = 0.05.\)
Free-Throw Shooting: A basketball player has historically made 85% of her free throws. During a randomly selected set of \(n = 20\) free throws, she makes \(x_{\text{obs}} = 14\). Is there evidence that her true free-throw success rate differs from 85%? Use \(\alpha = 0.05.\)
Rare Side Effect: A commonly used medication is known to produce a particular side effect in 2% of patients. Among a random sample of \(n = 60\) patients receiving the medication at a clinic, \(x_{\text{obs}} = 4\) experience the side effect. Is there evidence that the proportion of patients experiencing the side effect at this clinic differs from 2%? Use \(\alpha = 0.05.\)

title: 10  Inference for Population Proportions
section: 10.7 A Closer Look at Critical Regions and p-values (Optional)
text:
10.7 A Closer Look at Critical Regions and p-values (Optional)






Note



This section is optional. The material here is not required for performing hypothesis tests, but it is highly recommended for readers who want a firmer conceptual grasp of what is happening behind the procedures.


In the previous sections, you learned two equivalent approaches for testing a hypothesis about a population proportion: the critical region approach and the p-value approach. In both approaches, we computed probabilities for our decisions using the boundary value of the null hypothesis, and we relied on Rguroo’s Proportion Infrence function to produce the critical region or the p-value automatically.
This section is intended to deepen your understanding of why these procedures work the way they do. Specifically, we address two questions:

Why do we use the boundary value of \(H_0\) when computing probabilities required for our decisions? The null hypothesis in many tests is a statement such as \(H_0: p \leq p_0\) or \(H_0: p \geq p_0,\) which encompasses many possible values of \(p.\) Yet we always use the single boundary value \(p_0\) in our calculations. There is a principled reason for this, and understanding it clarifies what a hypothesis test is really doing.
How are critical regions and p-values actually obtained from a probability distribution? Rguroo’s Proportion Inference function returns these quantities directly, but doing so hides the underlying probability calculation. By using Rguroo’s probability calculator instead, we can see exactly which area under a sampling distribution corresponds to the critical region or the p-value.


10.7.1 Why Use the Boundary Value in \(H_0\)? **
In this section we explain why we use the boundary value of \(H_0\) when computing the probability of a Type I error. The front-half discussion stated this as a fact: for a composite \(H_0\) such as \(H_0: p \leq p_0,\) the maximum Type I error probability over the values allowed by \(H_0\) occurs at the boundary \(p_0,\) so controlling the error there automatically controls it everywhere in \(H_0.\) Here we demonstrate this empirically: we compute the probability of a Type I error for several specific values of \(p\) within \(H_0,\) for one decision rule, and observe that the maximum occurs at the boundary. A formal account, including worked examples and the underlying mathematics, is given in Jamshidian and Jamshidian (2026).

Example 10.20 (Daily YouTube Use Among Teens (continued)) Recall Example 10.1 where a school district claimed that more than 70% of students in its district use YouTube daily, and a random sample of \(n = 20\) students was selected. The null and alternative hypotheses are: \[
\begin{cases}
H_0: p \leq 0.70 \\
H_a: p > 0.70
\end{cases}
\]
Consider the critical region: Reject \(H_0\) if \(X \geq 17.\)
For this critical region, compute \(P(\text{Type I error})\) when

\(p = 0.60\)
\(p = 0.65\)
\(p = 0.70.\)

In each case, interpret the probability in the context of the problem.







Tip🔎 Solution





a. Since the sample size is \(n = 20\) and \(p = 0.60,\) we have \(X \sim \text{Binomial}(20, 0.60).\) Using Rguroo’s probability calculator, we compute \[P(\text{Type I error}) = P(\text{Reject } H_0 \mid H_0 \text{ is true})\] \[= P(X \geq 17 \mid p = 0.60).\]
Click to expand the box below to see how to calculate the probability of Type I error.






Note Calculating Type I Error Probability






Open the Probability-Simulation toolbox in Rguroo.

From the Probability dropdown, select Probability Calculator –> Discrete.
(Optional) In the Calculation textbox, type a name for the calculation (e.g., Type I error).

In the Distribution dropdown, select Binomial.
In the No. of Trials textbox, enter 20.
In the Prob. of Success textbox, enter 0.60.
In the next dropdown menu, select Above, and in the textbox next to it, enter 17.
(Optional) Select the Graph checkbox to see a graph showing calculation details.
Click the preview icon  to see the result.
(Optional) In the  textbox, enter the name TypeI_Error to save this calculation to your Rguroo account.







TipClick here to see the Rguroo dialog








Probability calculator dialog for computing Type I error probability











Figure 10.38 shows the Rguroo Probability Calculator output for \(X \sim \text{Binomial}(20, 0.60),\) giving






\[P(\text{Type I error}) = P(X \geq 17\mid p=0.60) \approx 0.016.\]



That is, if the true proportion of students in the district who use YouTube daily is \(p = 0.60,\) and our decision rule is to reject \(H_0\) whenever \(X \geq 17\) in a sample of \(n = 20\) students, then there is only a \(1.6\%\) chance of committing a Type I error; that is, incorrectly concluding that more than 70% of students in the district use YouTube daily.








Figure 10.38: Binomial distribution for \(X \sim \text{Binomial}(n = 20, p = 0.60)\) showing the Type I error probability as the upper-tail area \(P(X \geq 17) = 0.016.\)





b. To compute the probability of Type I error for the critical region \(X \geq 17\) when \(p = 0.65,\) we follow the same steps as in the part (a), but enter 0.65 in the Prob. of Success box. The Rguroo output gives






\[P(\text{Type I error}) = P(X \geq 17\mid p=0.65) \approx 0.044.\]



That is, if the true proportion of students in the district who use YouTube daily is \(p = 0.65,\) and our decision rule is to reject \(H_0\) whenever \(X \geq 17\) in a sample of \(n = 20\) students, then there is approximately a \(4.4\%\) chance of committing a Type I error; that is, incorrectly concluding that more than 70% of students in the district use YouTube daily.
c. Entering 0.70 in the Prob. of Success box gives






\[P(\text{Type I error}) = P(X \geq 17\mid p=0.70) \approx 0.107.\]



That is, if the true proportion of students in the district who use YouTube daily is \(p = 0.70,\) and our decision rule is to reject \(H_0\) whenever \(X \geq 17\) in a sample of \(n = 20\) students, then there is approximately a \(10.7\%\) chance of committing a Type I error; that is, incorrectly concluding that more than 70% of students in the district use YouTube daily.

Example 10.21 (Physical Inactivity Among Adults (continued)) Recall Example 10.2 where a national health agency claimed that fewer than 35% of adults in its country are physically inactive, and a random sample of \(n = 50\) adults was selected. The null and alternative hypotheses are: \[
\begin{cases}
H_0: p \geq 0.35 \\
H_a: p < 0.35
\end{cases}
\]
Consider the critical region: Reject \(H_0\) if \(X \leq 13.\)
For this critical region, compute \(P(\text{Type I error})\) when

\(p = 0.35\)
\(p = 0.40\)
\(p = 0.50.\)

In each case, interpret the probability in the context of the problem.







Tip🔎 Solution





a. Since the sample size is \(n = 50\) and \(p = 0.35,\) we have \(X \sim \text{Binomial}(50, 0.35).\) Using Rguroo’s probability calculator, we compute \[P(\text{Type I error}) = P(\text{Reject } H_0 \mid H_0 \text{ is true})\] \[= P(X \leq 13 \mid p = 0.35).\]
Use the same Rguroo Probability Calculator steps as in the YouTube example, with No. of Trials = 50, Prob. of Success = 0.35, and the direction set to Below with value 13:






TipClick here to see the Rguroo dialog








Probability calculator dialog for computing Type I error probability





Figure 10.39 shows the Rguroo Probability Calculator output for \(X \sim \text{Binomial}(50, 0.35),\) giving






\[P(\text{Type I error}) = P(X \leq 13\mid p=0.35) \approx 0.1163.\]



That is, if the true proportion of inactive adults in the population is \(p = 0.35,\) and our decision rule is to reject \(H_0\) whenever \(X \leq 13\) in a sample of \(n = 50\) adults, then there is approximately an \(11.63\%\) chance of committing a Type I error; that is, incorrectly concluding that fewer than 35% of adults in the population are physically inactive.








Figure 10.39: Binomial distribution for \(X \sim \text{Binomial}(n = 50, p = 0.35)\) showing the Type I error probability as the lower-tail area \(P(X \leq 13) = 0.1163.\)





 
b. Entering 0.40 in the Prob. of Success box gives






\[P(\text{Type I error}) = P(X \leq 13\mid p=0.40) \approx 0.028.\]



That is, if the true proportion of inactive adults in the population is \(p = 0.40,\) and our decision rule is to reject \(H_0\) whenever \(X \leq 13\) in a sample of \(n = 50\) adults, then there is approximately a \(2.8\%\) chance of committing a Type I error; that is, incorrectly concluding that fewer than 35% of adults in the population are physically inactive.
c. Entering 0.50 in the Prob. of Success box gives






\[P(\text{Type I error}) = P(X \leq 13\mid p=0.50) \approx 0.00046.\]



That is, if the true proportion of inactive adults in the population is \(p = 0.50,\) and our decision rule is to reject \(H_0\) whenever \(X \leq 13\) in a sample of \(n = 50\) adults, then there is approximately a \(0.046\%\) chance of committing a Type I error; that is, incorrectly concluding that fewer than 35% of adults in the population are physically inactive.



Now that we have computed the probability of a Type I error at various values of \(p,\) let us look back at what we observed in our examples.
For the one-sided cases, there is a range of values of \(p\) in \(H_0,\) and we computed the probability of a Type I error at several of them. You may have noticed a pattern: in both the YouTube example and the Physical Inactivity example, the probability of a Type I error was largest at the value of \(p\) where \(H_0\) and \(H_a\) meet, the boundary value of \(p\) in \(H_0\). For the YouTube example, this is \(p = 0.70,\) and for the Physical Inactivity example, this is \(p = 0.35.\) Is this a coincidence that the probability of a Type I error is largest at the boundary value?
The answer is, it is not a coincident. Figure 10.40 shows the probability of a Type I error across a range of values of \(p\) in \(H_0,\) for the two examples that we considerd here and for three different decision rules in each case.








Figure 10.40: Type I error probabilities for binomial tests as a function of \(p.\) Panel (a) shows \(X \sim \text{Binomial}(20, p)\) with \(P(X \geq 16, 17, 18)\); panel (b) shows \(X \sim \text{Binomial}(50, p)\) with \(P(X \leq 11, 12, 13).\) The red dashed line marks \(\alpha = 0.05.\) The gray dotted line shows the boundary of \(H_0.\)





In panel (a), for the YouTube example, the null hypothesis is \(H_0: p \leq 0.70,\) so the boundary value is \(p = 0.70.\) The three curves correspond to the decision rules \(X \geq 16,\) \(X \geq 17,\) and \(X \geq 18.\) For all three rules, the probability of a Type I error increases as \(p\) gets closer to the boundary value of \(0.70,\) and reaches its maximum at \(p = 0.70.\)
In panel (b), for the Physical Inactivity example, the null hypothesis is \(H_0: p \geq 0.35,\) so the boundary value is \(p = 0.35.\) The three curves correspond to the decision rules \(X \leq 11,\) \(X \leq 12,\) and \(X \leq 13.\) Again, for all three rules, the probability of a Type I error is largest at the boundary value \(p = 0.35\) and decreases as \(p\) moves away from it.






NoteKey Result: Maximum Type I Error Occurs at the Boundary Value



For the one-sided tests, the probability of a Type I error is largest at the boundary value of \(H_0.\)


Notice also that the horizontal dashed red line in each panel is drawn at \(0.05.\) This represents a commonly chosen upper bound for the probability of a Type I error — that is, the significance level \(\alpha = 0.05.\) As discussed in the previous sections, the decision rule (critical region) that we use is chosen to satisfy two requirements:

At the boundary value of \(H_0,\) the probability of a Type I error does not exceed the desired significance level \(\alpha.\)
Among all critical regions satisfying (1), we choose the one containing the largest number of \(X\) values, so that the probability of a Type II error is as small as possible.

Therefore, as shown in Figure 10.40, the critical region corresponding to the significance level \(\alpha = 0.05\) for the YouTube example is \(X\geq 18,\) and that for the Physical Inactivity example is \(X\leq 11.\)


10.7.2 Obtaining Critical Regions and p-values Using Rguroo’s Probability Calculator
In this subsection, we revisit examples from earlier in the chapter, but instead of using Rguroo’s Proportion Inference function, we compute critical values and p-values directly from the sampling distribution under \(H_0\) using Rguroo’s Probability Calculator function. This approach makes visible the area-under-the-curve interpretation of both quantities.

10.7.2.1 Using Inverse Probability to Find the Critical Region
When using a probability calculator, we could find a critical region by trying different candidate decision rules and checking their Type I error probabilities one at a time, as illustrated in Figure 10.40. For example, we might check whether the rule “\(X \ge 17\)” has a Type I error probability close to 0.05, then try “\(X \ge 18,\)” and so on. While this trial-and-error approach works, there is a more direct method.
Many calculators provide an inverse probability function. A probability function starts with a value of \(X\) and returns the corresponding probability. An inverse probability function works in the opposite direction: we provide a probability, such as \(\alpha=0.05,\) and it returns the value of \(X\) that creates that probability. This allows us to find the rejection-region boundary directly rather than testing several possible decision rules one at a time.
To find the critical region, we use the binomial distribution with the boundary value of \(p\) from \(H_0\) as the probability of success and \(n\) as the number of trials. Instead of providing a value of \(X\) and asking for a probability, we provide the significance level \(\alpha\) as the probability. The inverse probability function then returns the corresponding boundary value of \(X,\) which we use to determine the critical region. Below, we show how this is done in Rguroo using its built-in probability calculator.

Example 10.22 (YouTube Use: Finding the Critical Region) In the YouTube Use example (Example 10.1), we are testing \(H_0: p \leq 0.70\) versus \(H_a: p > 0.70,\) where \(p\) is the true proportion of students in the district who use YouTube daily. Using a sample of \(n = 20\) students and a significance level of \(\alpha = 0.05,\) find the critical region for this test.







Tip🔎 Solution





Since the alternative hypothesis is \(H_a: p > 0.70,\) large values of \(X\) provide evidence in favor of \(H_a.\) Therefore, we need a critical region in the upper tail of the binomial distribution. We use Rguroo’s Probability Calculator and the significance level \(\alpha\) to find the boundary value of \(X\) that defines this region.
Click to expand the box below to see how to use the Probability Calulator function in Rguroo.






Note Critical Region Using Calculator — YouTube example






Open the Probability-Simulation toolbox
Select Probability \(\Rightarrow\) Values to use the inverse probability function.
In the Distribution dropdown, set the distribution to Binomial.
Set the No. of Trials to 20 and the Prob. of Success to 0.70.
From the dropdown, select Upper Tail and enter \(0.05\) as the significance level \(\alpha.\)
Select the checkbox Graph to see a detailed output.







TipRguroo Discrete Probability Calculator dialog













Figure 10.41: Rguroo Probability Calculator Settings for the YouTube Critical Region Example











The output, shown in Figure 10.42, gives \[
P(X \geq 17)=0.1071 > 0.05
\quad\text{and}\quad
P(X \geq 18)=0.03548 < 0.05.
\]








Figure 10.42: Rguroo Probability Calculator Output for the YouTube Critical Region Example





Thus, the decision rule \(X \geq 17\) would produce a Type I error probability greater than our significance level and cannot be used. However, the decision rule \(X \geq 18\) has a Type I error probability below 0.05 and therefore satisfies the significance-level requirement.
Therefore, the critical region at significance level \(\alpha=0.05\) is \[
X \geq 18.
\] In other words, if 18 or more of the \(n=20\) students in the sample report daily YouTube use, we reject \(H_0\) in favor of \(H_a: p>0.70.\)




Example 10.23 (Physical Inactivity: Finding the Critical Region) In the Physical Inactivity example (Example 10.5), we are testing \(H_0: p \geq 0.35\) versus \(H_a: p < 0.35,\) where \(p\) is the true proportion of adults in the population who are physically inactive. Using a sample of \(n = 50\) adults and a significance level of \(\alpha = 0.05,\) find the critical region for this test.







Tip🔎 Solution





Since the alternative hypothesis is \(H_a: p < 0.35,\) small values of \(X\) provide evidence in favor of \(H_a.\) Therefore, we are looking for a critical region in the lower tail of the binomial distribution. We use Rguroo’s Discrete Distributions Probability Calculator with the settings shown in Figure 10.43:

Set the No. of Trials to 50 and the Prob. of Success to 0.35, the boundary value of \(p\) in \(H_0.\)
From the dropdown, select Lower Tail and enter \(0.05\) as the significance level \(\alpha.\)

Because we are using the inverse probability function, the calculator returns the boundary value of \(X\) that leaves probability \(0.05\) in the lower tail. We then use this value to determine the critical region.








Figure 10.43: Rguroo Probability Calculator Settings for the Physical Inactivity Critical Region Example





The output, shown in Figure 10.44, gives \[P(X \leq 12) = 0.06613 \geq 0.05 \quad \text{and} \quad
P(X \leq 11) = 0.03423 \leq 0.05.\]
we reject \(H_0\) in favor of \(H_a: p < 0.35.\)








Figure 10.44: Rguroo Probability Calculator Output for the Physical Inactivity Critical Region Example





This means that the decision rule \(X \leq 12\) exceeds our significance level, while the decision rule \(X \leq 11\) satisfies it. Therefore, the rejection region at significance level \(\alpha = 0.05\) is \[X \leq 11.\] That is, if we observe 11 or fewer inactive adults in our sample of \(n = 50,\)




Example 10.24 (Social Media as a Primary News Source: Finding the Critical Region) In the Social Media as a Primary News Source example (Example 10.6), we are testing \(H_0: p = 0.36\) versus \(H_a: p \neq 0.36,\) where \(p\) is the true proportion of students who use social media as their primary news source. Using a sample of \(n = 15\) students and a significance level of \(\alpha = 0.05,\) find the critical region for this test.







Tip🔎 Solution





Since the alternative hypothesis is \(H_a: p \neq 0.36,\) both unusually small and unusually large values of \(X\) provide evidence in favor of \(H_a.\) Therefore, we are looking for a two-sided critical region. For a two-sided test at significance level \(\alpha = 0.05,\) we split the significance level equally between the two tails, allocating \(0.025\) to each tail so that the total Type I error probability is \(0.05.\)
We use Rguroo’s Discrete Distributions Probability Calculator with the settings shown in Figure 10.45:

Set the No. of Trials to 15 and the Prob. of Success to 0.36, the value of \(p\) specified by \(H_0.\)
From the dropdown, select Outside Tails and enter \(0.025\) in each tail box.

Because we are using the inverse probability function, the calculator returns the boundary values of \(X\) that leave probability \(0.025\) in each tail. These boundaries determine the two-sided critical region.








Figure 10.45: Rguroo Probability Calculator Settings for the Social Media Critical Region Example





The output, shown in Figure 10.46, gives \[P(X \leq 2) + P(X \geq 9) = 0.1032 \geq 0.05,\] with the additional note that \[P(X \leq 2) = 0.05281, \quad P(X \geq 9) = 0.05038,\] \[P(X \leq 1) = 0.01168, \quad P(X \geq 10) = 0.01545.\]








Figure 10.46: Rguroo Probability Calculator Output for the Social Media Critical Region Example





The decision rule \(X \leq 2\) or \(X \geq 9\) exceeds our significance level of \(\alpha = 0.05.\) Moving one step further in each tail, the decision rule \(X \leq 1\) or \(X \geq 10\) satisfies our significance level since \[P(X \leq 1) + P(X \geq 10) = 0.01168 + 0.01545 = 0.02713 \leq 0.05.$
Therefore, the critical region at significance level $\alpha = 0.05$ is \]X X .$$ That is, if we observe 1 or fewer, or 10 or more students in our sample of \(n = 15\) who use social media as their primary news source, we reject \(H_0\) in favor of \(H_a: p \neq 0.36.\)





10.7.2.2 Using Probability Calculator to Compute the p-Value
We now illustrate how to compute the p-value and use it to make a decision, starting with the two one-sided examples that we have seen.

Example 10.25 (YouTube Use: Computing the p-Value and Making a Decision) In the YouTube Use example (Example 10.1), we are testing \(H_0: p \leq 0.70\) versus \(H_a: p > 0.70,\) where \(p\) is the true proportion of students in the district who use YouTube daily. A random sample of \(n = 20\) students is selected and \(x_{\text{obs}} = 17\) report daily YouTube use.

Obtain the \(H_a\) support.
Compute the p-value.
At significance level \(\alpha = 0.05,\) make a decision and state your conclusion in the context of the problem.








Tip🔎 Solution





a. Obtain the \(H_a\) support.
Since \(H_a: p > 0.70,\) values of \(X\) that are at least as supportive of \(H_a\) as \(x_{\text{obs}} = 17\) are values greater than or equal to 17. Therefore the \(H_a\) support is \(\{17, 18, 19, 20\}.\)
b. Compute the p-value.
The p-value is computed at the boundary value \(p_0 = 0.70\): \[\text{p-value} = P(X \geq 17 \mid p = 0.70).\]
We compute this probability using Rguroo’s Discrete Distributions Probability Calculator with \(X \sim \text{Binomial}(20, 0.70).\)
Figure 10.47 shows the Rguroo dialog and the output, giving






\[\text{p-value} = P(X \geq 17 \mid p = 0.70) \approx 0.1071.\]












Rguroo dialog for computing the p-value









Rguroo output showing the p-value







Figure 10.47: Rguroo setup (left) and p-value output (right) for the YouTube example.



c. Make a decision.
Since the p-value \(0.1071 > \alpha = 0.05,\) we fail to reject \(H_0.\) The data do not provide sufficient evidence at the 5% significance level to conclude that more than 70% of students in the district use YouTube daily. Note that this conclusion is consistent with the critical region approach: \(x_{\text{obs}} = 17\) does not fall in the critical region \(X \geq 18\) determined in Example 10.22.




Example 10.26 (Physical Inactivity: Computing the p-Value and Making a Decision) In the Physical Inactivity example (Example 10.2), we are testing \(H_0: p \geq 0.35\) versus \(H_a: p < 0.35,\) where \(p\) is the true proportion of adults in the population who are physically inactive. A random sample of \(n = 50\) adults is selected and \(x_{\text{obs}} = 10\) are found to be physically inactive.

Obtain the \(H_a\) support.
Compute the p-value.
At significance level \(\alpha = 0.05,\) make a decision and state your conclusion in the context of the problem.








Tip🔎 Solution





a. Obtain the \(H_a\) support.
Since \(H_a: p < 0.35,\) values of \(X\) that are at least as supportive of \(H_a\) as \(x_{\text{obs}} = 10\) are values less than or equal to 10. Therefore the \(H_a\) support is \(\{0, 1, \ldots, 10\}.\)
b. Compute the p-value.
The p-value is computed at the boundary value \(p_0 = 0.35\): \[\text{p-value} = P(X \leq 10 \mid p = 0.35).\]
We compute this probability using Rguroo’s Discrete Probability Calculator with \(X \sim \text{Binomial}(50, 0.35).\) Figure 10.48 shows the Rguroo dialog setup (left panel) and the Rguroo output (right panel) giving






\[\text{p-value} = P(X \leq 10 \mid p = 0.35) \approx 0.0160.\]












Rguroo dialog for computing the p-value









Rguroo output showing the p-value







Figure 10.48: Rguroo setup (left) and p-value output (right) for the Physical Inactivity example.



c. Make a decision.
Since the p-value \(0.0160 < \alpha = 0.05,\) we reject \(H_0\) in favor of \(H_a: p < 0.35.\) The data provide sufficient evidence at the 5% significance level to conclude that fewer than 35% of adults in the population are physically inactive. Note that this conclusion is consistent with the critical region approach: \(x_{\text{obs}} = 10\) falls in the critical region \(X \leq 11\) determined in Example 10.23.



The two-sided case requires a bit more care. Since \(H_a: p \neq p_0\) does not specify a direction, evidence against \(H_0\) can come from either tail of the distribution. Recall from Case 3 that a value \(x\) is in the \(H_a\) support if \(P(X = x \mid p = p_0) \leq P(X = x_{\text{obs}} \mid p = p_0),\) that is, if it is at least as unlikely as \(x_{\text{obs}}\) under \(H_0.\)

Example 10.27 (Social Media as a Primary News Source: Computing the p-Value and Making a Decision) In the Social Media as a Primary News Source example (Example 10.3), we are testing \(H_0: p = 0.36\) versus \(H_a: p \neq 0.36,\) where \(p\) is the true proportion of students who use social media as their primary news source. A random sample of \(n = 15\) students is selected and \(x_{\text{obs}} = 9\) report using social media as their primary news source.

Obtain the \(H_a\) support.
Compute the p-value.
At significance level \(\alpha = 0.05,\) make a decision and state your conclusion in the context of the problem.








Tip🔎 Solution





a. Obtain the \(H_a\) support.
Since \(H_a: p \neq 0.36,\) values of \(X\) that are at least as supportive of \(H_a\) as the observed value \(x_{\text{obs}} = 9\) are those that are at least as unlikely as \(x_{\text{obs}} = 9\) under \(H_0.\) That is, the \(H_a\) support consists of \(x_{\text{obs}} = 9\) and all values \(x\) for which \[
P(X = x \mid p = 0.36) \leq P(X = 9 \mid p = 0.36).
\]
Figure Figure 10.50 shows the Rguroo dialog and output used to compute \(P(X = x \mid p = 0.36).\) The probability of the observed value is \(P(X = 9 \mid p = 0.36) \approx 0.0349.\) Therefore, any value of \(x\) with probability less than or equal to \(0.0349\) is included in the \(H_a\) support, in addition to \(x_{\text{obs}} = 9.\)
From the graph, the \(H_a\) support consists of \(\{0, 1\}\) in the left tail and \(\{9, 10, 11, \ldots, 15\}\) in the right tail.
Note that the graph is truncated at \(X = 12,\) since the probabilities for values greater than 12 are extremely small.









Rguroo dialog









Rguroo output







Figure 10.49: Rguroo setup (left) and Rguroo output for \(P(X=9)\) (right) for the Social Media example.



b. Compute the p-value.
The p-value is computed at the boundary value \(p_0 = 0.36.\) Using Rguroo’s Discrete Probability Calculator with \(X \sim \text{Binomial}(15, 0.36),\) we compute the probability that \(X\) falls in the \(H_a\) support.
Recall that the \(H_a\) support consists of the values \(\{0, 1, 9, 10, 11, \ldots, 15\}.\) Therefore, the p-value is the total probability of these values under \(H_0.\)
Figure Figure 10.50 shows the Rguroo output, giving






\[
\text{p-value} = P\left(X \text{ is a value in the } H_a \text{ support}
\mid p = 0.36\right) \approx 0.0621.
\]












Rguroo dialog









Rguroo output







Figure 10.50: Rguroo setup (left) and Rguroo output (right) for computing the p-value for the Social Media example.



c. Make a decision.
Since the p-value \(0.0621 > \alpha = 0.05,\) we fail to reject \(H_0\) in favor of \(H_a: p \neq 0.36.\) The data do not provide sufficient evidence at the 5% significance level to conclude that the proportion of students who use social media as their primary news source differs from 0.36.
This conclusion is consistent with the critical region approach: the observed value \(x_{\text{obs}} = 9\) does not fall in the critical region \(X \leq 1\) or \(X \geq 10\) determined in Example 10.24.

title: 10  Inference for Population Proportions
section: 10.8 Confidence Interval for a Population Proportion
text:
10.8 Confidence Interval for a Population Proportion
Recall from Section 9.7 that a confidence interval gives us a range of plausible values for a population parameter. In this section, our parameter is the population proportion \(p,\) and we use the sample proportion \(\hat{p}\) as our estimate of it. Because \(\hat{p}\) varies from sample to sample, we do not expect it to equal \(p\) exactly. Instead, we use the observed sample proportion \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}\) to construct an interval of plausible values for \(p.\)
As discussed in Section 9.7, the confidence level describes the long-run success rate of the method used to construct the interval. For example, a 95% confidence interval comes from a method that captures the true value of \(p\) in about 95% of repeated samples. In practice, however, we collect one sample and construct one interval.






NoteConfidence Level



Imagine that we repeatedly take random samples from the same population and construct a confidence interval for \(p\) using the same method each time. Because the samples differ, the intervals will also differ. Some intervals will contain the true population proportion \(p,\) while others will not.
The confidence level tells us the percentage of these intervals that we expect to contain the true value of \(p.\) For example, a 95% confidence level means that, over many repeated samples, about 95% of the intervals constructed using this method would contain the true population proportion \(p.\)


Recall from Section 9.7 that we can construct a confidence interval by inverting a two-sided hypothesis test. For a population proportion, we consider different candidate values \(p_0\) and test \(H_0: p=p_0\) versus \(H_a:p\neq p_0\).
If we fail to reject \(H_0,\) our data are consistent with \(p_0,\) so we consider \(p_0\) a plausible value for \(p.\) If we reject \(H_0,\) we do not consider \(p_0\) plausible. We repeat this process for different values of \(p_0.\) The collection of all values for which we fail to reject \(H_0\) forms our confidence interval.






NoteConfidence Interval by Test Inversion



A \((1-\alpha) \times 100\%\) confidence interval for \(p\) consists of all candidate values \(p_0\) for which we fail to reject
\[
H_0:p=p_0
\]
in a two-sided hypothesis test at significance level \(\alpha.\)


The following example illustrates this idea by testing a grid of values of \(p_0\) and identifying which ones are consistent with the observed data.

Example 10.28 (Daily YouTube Use Among Teens: Building a Confidence Interval from a Grid) Recall Example 10.1. A sample of \(n = 20\) students produced \(x_{\text{obs}} = 17\) daily YouTube users, giving an observed sample proportion of \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} = 17/20 = 0.85.\)
For each candidate value of \(p_0\) shown in the grid below, carry out the two-sided hypothesis test \(H_0: p = p_0\) versus \(H_a: p \neq p_0\) at significance level \(\alpha = 0.05,\) using the binomial distribution with \(n = 20\) and \(x_{\text{obs}} = 17.\) Based on the results, identify the range of values of \(p_0\) for which we fail to reject \(H_0.\)
















Tip🔎 Solution





For each candidate value of \(p_0\) in the grid, we compute the two-sided p-value using the binomial distribution \(X \sim \text{Binomial}(20, p_0).\) The p-value is the probability of observing values of \(X\) that are at least as supportive of \(H_a\) as the observed value \(x_{\text{obs}}=17,\) assuming \(H_0\) is true. We then compare each p-value to \(\alpha = 0.05\) to decide whether to reject or fail to reject \(H_0.\)

As shown in the table and the graph, we fail to reject \(H_0\) for candidate values of \(p_0\) ranging from 0.65 to 0.95, and reject \(H_0\) for the candidate values 0.55, 0.60 and 0.99. Based on this grid, the range of plausible values for \(p\) is approximately \(0.65\) to \(0.95.\)
This gives us an approximate 95% confidence interval based on the candidate values in our grid. If we tested more closely spaced values of \(p_0,\) we could locate the endpoints of the confidence interval more precisely.



The confidence interval that we obtained in the example above is an approximation to the collection of values of \(p_0\) that are consistent with our observed data at significance level \(\alpha = 0.05.\) Notice that the interval is not symmetric around \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} = 0.85\): it extends further below \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}\) (down to approximately 0.65) than above it (up to approximately 0.95). This asymmetry is not surprising when the sample proportion is close to 0 or 1. Recall the large-sample condition from Section 10.3. Using \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} = 0.85\) as our estimate of \(p,\) we compute: \[n\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} = 20 \times 0.85 = 17 \geq 10,\] but \[n(1-\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}) = 20 \times 0.15 = 3 < 10.
\]
The large-sample condition fails because there are 3 observed failures. With a relatively small sample and a sample proportion close to 1, the binomial distribution can be noticeably skewed rather than approximately normal. As a result, an exact confidence interval need not be symmetric around \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}.\) A method based on a symmetric normal approximation may not work well in this situation.
This example illustrates that the choice of method for constructing a confidence interval matters. In the subsections that follow, we study two methods in detail. We begin in Section 10.8.1 with the large-sample method, which uses the normal approximation and produces a confidence interval that is symmetric around \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}.\) We consider this method first because it is widely used in practice and builds directly on the large-sample methods we have already developed for hypothesis testing. When the large-sample condition is satisfied, the normal approximation generally works well; however, it may be misleading when the condition is not satisfied, as in this example.
We then consider the exact binomial method in Section 10.8.2. This method does not rely on the normal approximation and can produce an asymmetric confidence interval. It is particularly useful when the large-sample condition is not satisfied.






TipSymmetry of the Normal-Approximation Interval



Because the normal distribution is symmetric, the large-sample confidence interval we will construct is symmetric around \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}.\) In contrast, an exact binomial confidence interval does not need to be symmetric. This difference can be especially noticeable when the sample size is small or \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}\) is close to 0 or 1.



10.8.1 Confidence Interval Based on the Large Sample Normal Approximation
We begin with the large-sample method for constructing a confidence interval for a population proportion. This method uses the normal approximation to the sampling distribution of \(\hat{p}\) and is one of the most commonly used methods for confidence intervals for a proportion. It also builds directly on the large-sample methods we used earlier for hypothesis testing.
Recall from Section 10.3 that when the large sample condition is satisfied, the sampling distribution of \(\hat{p}\) is approximately normal. We can use this normal distribution to determine how far we should extend on either side of the observed sample proportion \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}\) to obtain a range of plausible values for \(p.\)
To construct the interval, we first need to estimate the variability of \(\hat{p}.\) Recall that the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of \(\hat{p}\) is \[\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}.\] Because the population proportion \(p\) is unknown, we use the observed sample proportion \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}\) in its place. The resulting estimate of the standard deviation is called the standard error of \(\hat{p}\): \[\text{SE}(\hat{p}) = \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}(1 - \hat{p}_{\text{obs}})}{n}}.\]
For a confidence interval, we check the large sample condition using \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}\): \[n\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} \geq 10 \qquad \text{and} \qquad
n(1-\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}) \geq 10.\]
When this condition is satisfied, the \((1-\alpha) \times 100\%\) confidence interval for \(p\) takes the form
\[\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} \pm z^* \times \text{SE}(\hat{p}),\]
where \(z^*\) is the critical value from the standard normal distribution corresponding to the desired confidence level.
The quantity \(z^* \times \text{SE}(\hat{p})\) is called the margin of error. It tells us how far we extend below and above \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}\) when constructing the interval. A larger margin of error produces a wider interval and reflects greater uncertainty in our estimate of \(p.\)

NoteLarge Sample Confidence Interval for a Population Proportion



When the large sample condition \(n\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} \geq 10\) and \(n(1-\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}) \geq 10\) is satisfied, an approximate \((1-\alpha) \times 100\%\) confidence interval for \(p\) is:
\[\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} \pm \underbrace{z^* \times
\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}(1-\hat{p}_{\text{obs}})}{n}}}_{\text{margin of error}},\]
which gives the interval
\[\left(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} - z^* \times
\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}(1-\hat{p}_{\text{obs}})}{n}},\;
\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} + z^* \times
\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}(1-\hat{p}_{\text{obs}})}{n}}\right).\]
This interval is always symmetric around \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}.\) When the large sample condition is satisfied, the normal approximation generally works well; when it is not, the resulting confidence interval may be misleading.

As we saw in Example 10.30, the 95% confidence interval did not contain the null value \(p_0=0.36,\) and the corresponding two-sided hypothesis test at \(\alpha=0.05\) rejected \(H_0:p=0.36.\) This is not a coincidence. Recall from Section 9.7 that a confidence interval can be constructed by inverting a two-sided hypothesis test.
More generally, a \((1-\alpha)\times100\%\) confidence interval and a two-sided hypothesis test at significance level \(\alpha\) lead to the same decision. If the null value \(p_0\) is inside the confidence interval, it is a plausible value for \(p\) based on the observed data, and we fail to reject \(H_0.\) If \(p_0\) is outside the confidence interval, it is not a plausible value for \(p,\) and we reject \(H_0.\)






NoteUsing a Confidence Interval to Make a Decision



For a two-sided hypothesis test \[
H_0:p=p_0
\qquad\text{versus}\qquad
H_a:p\neq p_0,
\] at significance level \(\alpha,\) use the corresponding \((1-\alpha)\times100%\) confidence interval: If \(p_0\) is inside the confidence interval, fail to reject \(H_0.\) If \(p_0\) is outside the confidence interval, reject \(H_0.\) For example, a two-sided test at \(\alpha=0.05\) corresponds to a 95% confidence interval.

10.8.2 Confidence Interval Based on the Exact Binomial Method
As we saw in Example 10.28, we can construct a confidence interval for the population proportion \(p\) by testing a grid of null hypotheses \(H_0: p = p_0\) and collecting all values of \(p_0\) for which we fail to reject \(H_0.\) When this approach uses the exact binomial distribution to carry out each test, the resulting interval is called the exact binomial confidence interval. As we noted in that example, this method has an important advantage: it correctly reflects any asymmetry in the data, which can occur when the large sample condition fails and the binomial distribution is skewed.
Of course, testing every conceivable value of \(p_0\) between 0 and 1 is not practical. Fortunately, efficient algorithms can locate the exact endpoints of the interval directly, without testing each value one by one. These algorithms are implemented in Rguroo, making it straightforward to obtain the exact binomial confidence interval in practice. The following example illustrates how.

The sample consisted of \(n = 1{,}432\) complaints, of which \(x_{\text{obs}} = 321\) were for identity theft.

Check whether the large sample condition is satisfied using the 10-10 rule. Based on your answer, determine whether the large sample normal approximation confidence interval is appropriate.
Use Rguroo’s One-Population Proportion inference function with the Large Sample z option to obtain a 95% confidence interval for \(p.\) Interpret the interval in the context of the problem.

Use your confidence interval to test \(H_0: p = 0.23\) versus \(H_a: p \neq 0.23\) at the \(\alpha = 0.05\) significance level. Is there evidence that Alaska’s proportion of identity theft complaints differs from the national proportion?

Check whether the large sample condition is satisfied using the 10-10 rule. Based on your answer, determine whether the large sample normal approximation confidence interval is appropriate.

The sample consisted of \(n = 1{,}039\) adults, of whom \(x_{\text{obs}} = 634\) believed in a conspiracy.

Use your confidence interval to test \(H_0: p = 0.81\) versus \(H_a: p \neq 0.81\) at the \(\alpha = 0.05\) significance level. Is there evidence that American belief in a conspiracy changed between 2001 and 2013?

The sample consisted of \(n = 388\) adults, of whom \(x_{\text{obs}} = 33\) reported a graduate degree as their highest level of education.

title: 10  Inference for Population Proportions
text:
10.9 Hypothesis Testing for Two Proportions
Many important research questions require comparing proportions between two groups. In medical research, clinical trials compare treatment outcomes between patients receiving a new therapy and those receiving a placebo or standard care. In the social sciences, researchers investigate differences between demographic groups. In educational research, teachers evaluate whether new instructional methods outperform traditional approaches. Understanding how to compare two population proportions allows us to evaluate whether observed differences in sample data reflect genuine population differences or are due to chance variation.
Consider a few recent examples: A Phase 3 trial of the mRNA-1273 vaccine (Moderna) with over 30,000 participants found that 0.4% of the vaccinated group developed symptomatic COVID-19 compared to 4.9% in the placebo group—a substantial difference. A 2022 study examining 1,166 articles in Political Psychology found that 35.1% of lead authors were women compared to 64.9% men, highlighting a gender gap in academic publishing. In each case, researchers collected data from two independent samples, observed different sample proportions, and found statistical evidence that the population proportions differed.
While these large-scale studies demonstrate striking differences, many research questions involve smaller samples and more subtle effects where the statistical evidence is less clear-cut. In this section, we develop the concepts and tools for comparing two population proportions by working with examples where the answer is not immediately obvious and careful statistical reasoning is required.
We extend the hypothesis testing framework from one proportion to two proportions. The same core concepts—null and alternative hypotheses, test statistics, p-values, Type I and Type II errors, and significance levels—continue to apply. However, we now focus on the difference between two population proportions rather than a single proportion.

10.9.1 The Null and Alternative Hypotheses
To develop these concepts and tools, we’ll work with four examples: an educational intervention comparing instructional approaches for teaching proportional reasoning, a health behavior study evaluating text message reminders for medication adherence, a workplace wellness program assessing nicotine patches for smoking cessation, and an analysis of gender differences in attitudes toward marijuana legalization from the General Social Survey.
When comparing two population proportions, we focus on the difference between them. We have two populations—let’s call one population 1 and the other population 2. It does not matter which population you designate as population 1 and which as population 2, as long as you clearly define your choice. We denote the population proportion for population 1 by \(p_1\) and the population proportion for population 2 by \(p_2.\) Our goal is to make inferences about the difference between these proportions: \(p_1 - p_2.\) To do this, we begin by formulating hypotheses about this difference.
Just as in the one-population case, we can formulate both one-sided and two-sided tests. The three cases are:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Case 1: }
&\begin{cases}
H_0: p_1 \leq p_2 \\
H_a: p_1 > p_2
\end{cases}
\qquad
\text{Case 2: }
\begin{cases}
H_0: p_1 \geq p_2 \\
H_a: p_1 < p_2
\end{cases} \\
\\
\text{Case 3: }
&\begin{cases}
H_0: p_1 = p_2 \\
H_a: p_1 \neq p_2
\end{cases}
\end{aligned}
\]
We can equivalently write these hypotheses in terms of the difference \(p_1 - p_2\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Case 1: }
&\begin{cases}
H_0: p_1 - p_2 \leq 0 \\
H_a: p_1 - p_2 > 0
\end{cases}
\qquad
\text{Case 2: }
\begin{cases}
H_0: p_1 - p_2 \geq 0 \\
H_a: p_1 - p_2 < 0
\end{cases} \\
\\
\text{Case 3: }
&\begin{cases}
H_0: p_1 - p_2 = 0 \\
H_a: p_1 - p_2 \neq 0
\end{cases}
\end{aligned}
\]
Cases 1 and 2 are one-sided tests, while Case 3 is a two-sided test. In practice, the choice of case depends on the research question—specifically, whether we are testing for an increase, a decrease, or any difference. Let’s see how to set up the hypotheses for each of our examples.

Example 10.35 (Schema-Based Instruction: Stating Hypotheses) Researchers want to know whether a new schema-based instructional approach improves seventh-grade students’ mastery of proportional reasoning compared to traditional instruction. They randomly assign \(n_1=50\) students to the new approach and \(n_2=50\) students to traditional instruction. Let \(p_1\) represent the proportion of all students who would achieve mastery under the new approach, and \(p_2\) represent the proportion who would achieve mastery under traditional instruction. State the appropriate null and alternative hypotheses to address the research question.







Tip🔎 Solution





Since the researchers want to know whether the new approach improves mastery (that is, whether \(p_1 > p_2\)), this is a Case 1 situation. The hypotheses are:
\[
\begin{cases}
H_0: p_1 \leq p_2 \quad \text{or equivalently} \quad H_0: p_1 - p_2 \leq 0\\
H_a: p_1 > p_2 \quad \text{or equivalently} \quad H_a: p_1 - p_2 > 0
\end{cases}
\]
The null hypothesis states that the new approach is no better than (or is worse than) traditional instruction. The alternative hypothesis states that the new approach produces a higher mastery rate.




Example 10.36 (Text Message Reminders: Stating Hypotheses) Researchers are piloting a text message reminder system for diabetes patients. They want to know whether daily text reminders improve medication adherence compared to standard care, but they’re also open to the possibility that the reminders might perform worse (perhaps by being annoying or overwhelming). They randomly assign \(n_1=40\) patients to receive text reminders and \(n_2=50\) patients to receive standard care. Let \(p_1\) represent the proportion of all patients who would have good adherence with text reminders, and \(p_2\) represent the proportion who would have good adherence with standard care. State the appropriate null and alternative hypotheses.







Tip🔎 Solution





Since the researchers have no strong directional prediction and want to detect a difference in either direction, this is a Case 3 situation. The hypotheses are:
\[
\begin{cases}
H_0: p_1 = p_2 \quad \text{or equivalently} \quad H_0: p_1 - p_2 = 0\\
H_a: p_1 \neq p_2 \quad \text{or equivalently} \quad H_a: p_1 - p_2 \neq 0
\end{cases}
\]
The null hypothesis states that the difference between the two population proportions, \(p_1\) and \(p_2,\) is zero. A difference of zero means that the two population proportions are equal, so there is no difference in adherence rates between the two approaches. The alternative hypothesis states that the difference is not zero, meaning that the adherence rates differ between the two approaches.




Example 10.37 (Smoking Cessation: Stating Hypotheses) A workplace wellness program is comparing two approaches to smoking cessation. Employees are randomly assigned to either receive free nicotine patches (60 employees - Group 1) or participate in a self-guided quitting program (60 employees - Group 2). However, the researchers believe that the self-guided approach might actually be more effective because it emphasizes personal commitment and doesn’t rely on external aids. Let \(p_1\) represent the proportion of all employees who would quit smoking with nicotine patches, and \(p_2\) represent the proportion who would quit with the self-guided approach. State the appropriate null and alternative hypotheses to test whether the self-guided approach is more effective.







Tip🔎 Solution





Since the researchers want to test whether the self-guided approach is more effective than nicotine patches (that is, whether \(p_2 > p_1,\) or equivalently \(p_1 < p_2\)), this is a Case 2 situation. The hypotheses are:
\[
\begin{cases}
H_0: p_1 \geq p_2 \quad \text{or equivalently} \quad H_0: p_1 - p_2 \geq 0\\
H_a: p_1 < p_2 \quad \text{or equivalently} \quad H_a: p_1 - p_2 < 0
\end{cases}
\]
The null hypothesis states that nicotine patches are at least as effective as (or more effective than) the self-guided approach. The alternative hypothesis states that the self-guided approach produces a higher quit rate.




Example 10.38 (GSS 2024: Gender and Marijuana Legalization) The General Social Survey (GSS) is a long-running national survey that monitors societal change and studies the growing complexity of American society. In a representative sample from the GSS 2024 data, there are \(n_1=204\) females and \(n_2=184\) males who were asked whether they support the legalization of marijuana. Of the 204 females, 142 said they support legalization. Of the 184 males, 140 said they support legalization. Researchers want to know whether this sample provides evidence that the proportion of females who support legalization differs from the proportion of males who support legalization. Let \(p_1\) represent the proportion of females in the population who support legalization, and \(p_2\) represent the proportion of males who support legalization. State the appropriate null and alternative hypotheses.







Tip🔎 Solution





Since the researchers want to know whether the proportions differ (in either direction) without specifying which gender should have higher support, this is a Case 3 situation. The hypotheses are:
\[
\begin{cases}
H_0: p_1 = p_2 \quad \text{or equivalently} \quad H_0: p_1 - p_2 = 0\\
H_a: p_1 \neq p_2 \quad \text{or equivalently} \quad H_a: p_1 - p_2 \neq 0
\end{cases}
\]
The null hypothesis states that females and males support marijuana legalization at the same rate. The alternative hypothesis states that the support rates differ between the two groups.





10.9.2 Data, Statistic, and Sampling Distribution
To make inferences about \(p_1 - p_2,\) we collect a sample of size \(n_1\) from population 1 and a sample of size \(n_2\) from population 2. Note that these sample sizes don’t have to be equal—researchers often work with unequal group sizes due to practical constraints or deliberate design choices.
Let \(X_1\) denote the number of successes (favorable outcomes) in our sample from population 1, and let \(X_2\) denote the number of successes in our sample from population 2. Although we could compare the counts through \(X_1-X_2,\) differences in counts are difficult to analyze and can be misleading when the sample sizes differ. Instead, we compare sample proportions and rely on the Central Limit Theorem for large samples.
The sample proportions are \(\hat{p}_1 = X_1/n_1\) and \(\hat{p}_2 = X_2/n_2.\) These are our point estimates of \(p_1\) and \(p_2,\) respectively. To make inferences about the difference \(p_1 - p_2,\) we naturally use the difference in sample proportions: \(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2.\)
The Sampling Distribution of \(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2\)
When the sample sizes \(n_1\) and \(n_2\) are both sufficiently large, the Central Limit Theorem tells us that the sampling distribution of \(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2\) is approximately normal. The rule of thumb for “sufficiently large” is that each group must have at least 10 successes and 10 failures: \(n_1\hat{p}_1 \geq 10,\) \(n_1(1-\hat{p}_1) \geq 10,\) \(n_2\hat{p}_2 \geq 10,\) and \(n_2(1-\hat{p}_2) \geq 10.\)
When these conditions are met, the sampling distribution of \(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2\) is approximately normal with mean \(p_1 - p_2\) and standard error
\[
\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \sim N\left(p_1 - p_2, \; \text{SE}(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2)\right),
\] where \[
\text{SE}(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2) = \sqrt{\frac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n_1} + \frac{p_2(1-p_2)}{n_2}}.
\]
Notice that the variability depends on both sample sizes and population proportions.
Simplification Under the Null Hypothesis
Recall that when testing hypotheses, we work at the boundary of the null hypothesis, since the Type I error is maximized there. For all three cases above, the boundary value is \(p_1 - p_2 = 0,\) which means \(p_1 = p_2.\)
At this boundary, the two population proportions are equal. We denote their common value by \(p,\) so that \(p_1=p_2=p.\) As a result, the standard error simplifies to:
\[
\text{SE}(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2)
= \sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n_1} + \frac{p(1-p)}{n_2}}
= \sqrt{p(1-p)\left(\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}\right)}.
\]
Therefore, under the null hypothesis, the sampling distribution of \(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2\) is:
\[
\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \sim N\left(0, \; \sqrt{p(1-p)\left(\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}\right)}\right).
\]
This is the distribution we will use for hypothesis testing.
Estimating the Common Proportion
There is one practical issue: we do not know \(p,\) the common population proportion under \(H_0.\) Because \(H_0\) assumes that \(p_1=p_2,\) we treat the two samples as coming from populations with the same proportion. We therefore combine the number of successes from both samples and divide by the combined sample size. This gives us an estimate of the common population proportion called the pooled sample proportion: \[\hat{p} = \frac{X_1 + X_2}{n_1 + n_2}.\]
Using \(\hat{p}\) in place of \(p\) gives the estimated standard error:
\[
\widehat{\text{SE}}(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2)
= \sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})\left(\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}\right)}.
\]
This estimated standard error is used in our test statistic and in determining critical regions and p-values, just as we did in the one-population case.
The following example works through all of these computations for one of our four studies. The remaining three are summarized in Table 10.3.

Example 10.39 (Schema-Based Instruction: Computing the Key Quantities) In the schema-based instruction study, \(n_1=50\) students were assigned to the new approach and \(n_2=50\) to traditional instruction. After the intervention, 34 students in the new approach group achieved mastery, while 24 students in the traditional instruction group achieved mastery.

Compute the sample proportions \(\hat{p}_1\) and \(\hat{p}_2\) and their difference.
Verify the large sample conditions.
Compute the pooled sample proportion \(\hat{p}.\)
Compute the estimated standard error of \(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2.\)








Tip🔎 Solution





a. Sample proportions.
\[\hat{p}_1 = \frac{34}{50} = 0.68, \qquad \hat{p}_2 = \frac{24}{50} = 0.48, \qquad \hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 = 0.20.\]
The new approach shows a 20 percentage point higher mastery rate in the sample. We will test whether this provides sufficient evidence that \(p_1 > p_2\) or whether it could reasonably arise by chance when both approaches are equally effective.
b. Large sample conditions.
We check whether each group has at least 10 successes and 10 failures.
For Group 1 (new approach):
\[n_1 \hat{p}_1 = 50 \times 0.68 = 34, \qquad n_1(1 - \hat{p}_1) = 50 \times 0.32 = 16.\]
For Group 2 (traditional instruction):
\[n_2 \hat{p}_2 = 50 \times 0.48 = 24, \qquad n_2(1 - \hat{p}_2) = 50 \times 0.52 = 26.\]
All four counts are at least 10, so the large-sample conditions are satisfied and the Central Limit Theorem applies.
c. Pooled sample proportion.
\[\hat{p} = \frac{34 + 24}{50 + 50} = \frac{58}{100} = 0.58.\]
Under the null hypothesis, we estimate that 58% of students would achieve mastery if both approaches were equally effective.
d. Estimated standard error.
\[
\widehat{\text{SE}}(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2)
= \sqrt{0.58 \times 0.42 \times \left(\frac{1}{50} + \frac{1}{50}\right)}
= \sqrt{0.009744}
\approx 0.0987.
\]
This is the typical sample-to-sample variability in \(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2\) if the null hypothesis is true.



The same computations for all four studies are summarized in Table 10.3. We will refer back to this table when working through hypothesis tests in the next subsection.

The pooled sample proportion, used under \(H_0: p_1 = p_2,\) is \[\hat{p} = \frac{X_1 + X_2}{n_1 + n_2}.\]
Large Sample Conditions
The normal approximation is appropriate when each sample has at least 10 successes and 10 failures: \[n_1\hat{p}_1 \geq 10, \quad n_1(1-\hat{p}_1) \geq 10, \quad n_2\hat{p}_2 \geq 10, \quad n_2(1-\hat{p}_2) \geq 10.\]
Null Distribution Under \(H_0: p_1 = p_2\)
When \(H_0\) is true and the large-sample conditions hold, \[\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \sim N\left(0, \; \sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})\left(\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}\right)}\right).\]
The estimated standard error is \[\widehat{\text{SE}}(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2) = \sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})\left(\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}\right)}.\]
This distribution and its standard error are used to compute critical regions and p-values for all three forms of \(H_a\) (right-tailed, left-tailed, two-tailed).




10.9.3 Hypothesis Testing: p-Value and Critical Region Approaches
As we explained earlier, there are two equivalent approaches to making decisions in hypothesis testing: the p-value approach and the critical region approach. We now apply both approaches to testing hypotheses about the difference between two population proportions, \(p_1-p_2,\) and show how to carry them out using Rguroo.
Recall that we developed the sampling distribution of \(\hat{p}_1-\hat{p}_2\) at the null boundary \(p_1-p_2=0\) in the previous section. When the large-sample conditions are satisfied, we use this approximately normal distribution, together with the pooled sample proportion, to carry out the test. Both the p-value and critical region approaches use this same sampling distribution to determine whether the observed difference \(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2\) provides sufficient evidence against \(H_0\) and favors \(H_a.\)






NoteA Note on Notation



In the one-sample sections, we used \(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}\) to distinguish the observed sample proportion from the random variable \(\hat{p}.\) For two proportions, that notation becomes cumbersome — we would need \(\hat{p}_{1,\text{obs}}\) and \(\hat{p}_{2,\text{obs}}.\) To keep the notation simpler, we use \(\hat{p}_1\) and \(\hat{p}_2\) for both meanings. The context will make the meaning clear: when discussing sampling distributions or probabilities, they represent random variables; when working with the observed data or making a decision, they represent the observed sample proportions.


The p-value approach asks: “How much support does the observed difference provide for \(H_a\)?” The critical region approach asks: “Does the observed difference fall in the critical region?” Both approaches lead to the same conclusion, and we will use Rguroo to carry out both approaches.
Let’s examine each case in detail.

10.9.3.1 Case 1: Right-Tailed Test (\(H_a: p_1 - p_2 > 0\))
In this case, we want to test whether \(p_1 > p_2.\) The alternative hypothesis \(H_a: p_1 - p_2 > 0\) is supported when \(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2\) is positive, with larger positive differences providing stronger support for \(H_a.\) Values near zero or negative provide little or no support for \(H_a.\)
p-Value Approach:
The p-value measures he strength of the evidence against \(H_0\) and in favor of \(H_a.\) For a right-tailed test, the p-value is the probability of observing a difference that provides at least as much support for \(H_a\) as our observed difference, assuming \(p_1=p_2\):
\[\text{p-value}
=
P\left(\hat{p}_1-\hat{p}_2
\geq \text{observed difference}\right),\;
\text{assuming } p_1=p_2.\]
This is the area to the right of the observed difference under the \(N\left(0, \sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})\left(\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}\right)}\right)\) distribution. A small p-value indicates strong evidence against \(H_0\) and in favor of \(H_a,\) while a large p-value indicates that the data do not provide strong evidence against \(H_0.\)
Decision Rule:

Reject \(H_0\) if p-value \(< \alpha\) (observed difference strongly support \(H_a\)).
Fail to reject \(H_0\) if p-value \(\geq \alpha\) (data do not strongly support \(H_a\)).

Critical Region Approach:
The critical region consists of values in the upper tail of the sampling distribution. These are the values of \(\hat{p}_1-\hat{p}_2\) that are sufficiently large to lead us to reject \(H_0\) in favor of \(H_a: p_1-p_2>0.\) We find the critical value \(c\) o that the probability of falling in the critical region is equal to the significant level \(\alpha,\) assuming \(p_1=p_2\):
\[P\left(\hat{p}_1-\hat{p}_2 \geq c\right) = \alpha,\;
\text{assuming }p_1=p_2.\]
Using the sampling distribution under this assumption,
\[\hat{p}_1-\hat{p}_2\sim N\left(0, \sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})\left(\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}\right)}\right)\]
we choose \(c\) so that the area to the right of \(c\) is \(\alpha.\) We reject \(H_0\) if the observed difference \(\hat{p}_1-\hat{p}_2\) falls in this critical region.
Decision Rule:

Reject \(H_0\) if \(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 > c\) (observed difference strongly supports \(H_a\)).
Fail to reject \(H_0\) if \(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \leq c\) (observed difference does not strongly support \(H_a\)).









Figure 10.51: Critical region and p-value for a right-tailed test






Example 10.40 (Schema-Based Instruction: Hypothesis Test - p-Value Example) For the schema-based instruction study, we want to test whether the new approach has a higher mastery rate than the traditional approach. Recall:

\(n_1 = 50,\) \(X_1 = 34,\) \(\hat{p}_1 = 0.68\)
\(n_2 = 50,\) \(X_2 = 24,\) \(\hat{p}_2 = 0.48\)
\(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 = 0.20\)
\(\hat{p} = 0.58\)

Hypotheses: \[
\begin{cases}
H_0: p_1 - p_2 \leq 0\\
H_a: p_1 - p_2 > 0.
\end{cases}
\]

Give a probability statement that describes the p-value.
Use Rguroo to obtain the p-value for the test and state your conclusion based on the significance level \(\alpha = 0.05.\)








Tip🔎 Solution

10.9.3.2 Case 2: Left-Tailed Test (\(H_a: p_1 - p_2 < 0\))
Case 2 is the mirror of Case 1. Small (negative) values of \(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2\) support \(H_a,\) so the p-value and critical region lie in the lower tail of the null distribution.






p-value: \(\quad \text{p-value} = P(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \leq \text{observed difference} \mid p_1 = p_2)\)
Critical value \(c\): \(\quad P(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \leq c \mid p_1 = p_2) = \alpha\)
Decision: Reject \(H_0\) if p-value \(< \alpha,\) equivalently if \(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \leq c.\)











Figure 10.54: Critical region and p-value for a left-tailed test





Critical Region Approach:
The critical region consists of values in the lower tail of the sampling distribution—these are the values that strongly support \(H_a: p_1 - p_2 < 0.\) We find the critical value \(c\) such that at the boundary where \(p_1 = p_2\):
\[P(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 < c \mid p_1 = p_2) = \alpha\]
Using the sampling distribution at the boundary, we find \(c\) from \(N\left(0, \sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})\left(\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}\right)}\right)\) such that the area to the left equals \(\alpha.\)
Decision Rule:

Reject \(H_0\) if \(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 < c\) (observed difference strongly supports \(H_a\)).
Fail to reject \(H_0\) if \(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \geq c\) (observed difference does not strongly support \(H_a\)).

10.9.3.3 Case 3: Two-Tailed Test (\(H_a: p_1 - p_2 \neq 0\))
In Case 3, \(H_a\) is supported when \(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2\) is far from zero in either direction. The p-value is therefore a two-tail probability, and the critical region occupies both tails with \(\alpha/2\) in each.






p-value: \(\quad \text{p-value} = P(|\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2| \geq |\text{observed difference}| \mid p_1 = p_2)\)
Critical values \(c_1, c_2\): \(\quad P(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \leq c_1 \mid p_1 = p_2) = P(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \geq c_2 \mid p_1 = p_2) = \alpha/2\)
Decision: Reject \(H_0\) if p-value \(< \alpha,\) equivalently if \(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \leq c_1\) or \(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \geq c_2.\)











Figure 10.59: Critical region and p-value for a two-tailed test





Critical Region Approach:
The critical region consists of values in both tails of the sampling distribution—these are the values that strongly support \(H_a: p_1 - p_2 \neq 0.\) We find two critical values, \(c_1\) and \(c_2,\) such that at the boundary where \(p_1 = p_2\):
\[P(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 < c_1 \text{ or } \hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 > c_2 \mid p_1 = p_2) = \alpha\]
We split \(\alpha\) equally between the two tails (\(\alpha/2\) in each tail). Using the sampling distribution at the boundary:

\(c_1\) is the value with area \(\alpha/2\) to its left
\(c_2\) is the value with area \(\alpha/2\) to its right

Decision Rule:

Reject \(H_0\) if \(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 < c_1\) or \(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 > c_2\) (observed difference strongly supports \(H_a\)).
Fail to reject \(H_0\) if \(c_1 \leq \hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \leq c_2\) (observed difference does not strongly support \(H_a\)).

So far, in the examples above, we have performed two-population proportion inference using summarized data—namely, the sample sizes and the number of successes for each group. In practice, however, we often begin with raw data rather than pre-computed summaries. By raw data, we mean datasets where each individual observation is recorded as a separate row, with variables indicating group membership and the outcome for each case. The following example demonstrates how we can carry out two-population proportion inference directly from raw data using Rguroo.

Calculate the observed sample proportions \(\hat{p}_1\) and \(\hat{p}_2\) and their difference \(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2.\) Based on this observed difference, does the sample data appear consistent with the alternative hypothesis?
Compute the pooled sample proportion \(\hat{p}\) and use it to obtain an estimate of the standard error of \(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2.\)
Check whether the large sample test is valid by verifying that \(n_1\hat{p} \geq 10,\) \(n_1(1-\hat{p}) \geq 10,\) \(n_2\hat{p} \geq 10,\) and \(n_2(1-\hat{p}) \geq 10.\) If these conditions are not satisfied, stop here and note that the large sample test is not appropriate for this scenario and skip parts e, f, and g.
Use Rguroo to conduct the test of hypothesis using the critical region approach. Does the observed sample difference fall in the critical region? Based on this, do you reject \(H_0\) at the 5% significance level?
Use Rguroo to obtain the \(p\)-value for the test of hypothesis. Is the \(p\)-value less than 0.05? Based on the \(p\)-value, do you reject \(H_0\)?
Write your conclusion in the context of the problem, stating what the results tell you about the scenario.



A researcher wants to determine whether male college students have a higher smoking rate than female college students. In a survey of 120 male students, 18 reported being regular smokers. Among 150 female students, 12 reported being regular smokers. Is there enough evidence to show that the proportion of male smokers is higher than the proportion of female smokers among college students? Test at the \(\alpha=0.05\) level.
A school district is evaluating whether a new reading program is more effective for students with previous tutoring than for those without. Of 85 students with previous tutoring, 68 passed the reading assessment. Of 92 students without previous tutoring, 59 passed the assessment. Is there enough evidence to show that the proportion of students passing the assessment is higher for those with previous tutoring than for those without? Test at the \(\alpha=0.05\) level.
A small clinic wants to compare the effectiveness of two different treatments for a skin condition. In a trial, 8 out of 25 patients receiving Treatment A showed improvement, while 12 out of 28 patients receiving Treatment B showed improvement. Is there enough evidence to show that the proportion of patients improving differs between the two treatments? Test at the \(\alpha=0.05\) level.
A coffee shop owner wants to know if customer satisfaction is higher during the morning shift than the evening shift. Of 45 morning customers surveyed, 38 reported being satisfied with their service. Of 52 evening customers surveyed, 35 reported being satisfied. Is there enough evidence to show that the proportion of satisfied customers is higher in the morning than in the evening? Test at the \(\alpha=0.05\) level.
Many high school students take the AP tests in different subject areas. In 2007, of the 211,693 students who took the calculus AB exam, 102,598 of them were female and 109,095 of them were male (“AP exam scores,” 2013). Is there enough evidence to show that the proportion of female students taking the calculus AB exam is different from the proportion of male students taking the calculus AB exam? Test at the \(\alpha=0.05\) level.
Are there more children diagnosed with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) in states that have larger urban areas than in states that are mostly rural? In the state of Pennsylvania, a fairly urban state, there are 245 eight-year-olds diagnosed with ASD out of 18,440 eight-year-olds evaluated. In the state of Utah, a fairly rural state, there are 45 eight-year-olds diagnosed with ASD out of 2,123 eight-year-olds evaluated (“Autism and developmental,” 2008). Is there enough evidence to show that the proportion of children diagnosed with ASD in Pennsylvania is higher than the proportion in Utah? Test at the \(\alpha=0.01\) level.
A child dying from an accidental poisoning is a terrible incident. Is it more likely that a male child will get into poison than a female child? To find this out, data was collected that showed that out of 1,830 children between the ages of one and four who died from poisoning, 1,031 were males and 799 were females (Flanagan, Rooney & Griffiths, 2005). Do the data show that the proportion of male children dying of poisoning is higher than the proportion of female children? Test at the \(\alpha=0.01\) level.
Many high school students take the AP tests in different subject areas. In 2007, of the 144,796 students who took the biology exam, 84,199 of them were female. In that same year, of the 211,693 students who took the calculus AB exam, 102,598 of them were female (“AP exam scores,” 2013). Is there enough evidence to show that the proportion of female students taking the biology exam is different from the proportion of female students taking the calculus AB exam? Test at the \(\alpha=0.05\) level.
The General Social Survey (GSS) collects data through different survey modes, including in-person interviews and telephone interviews. Researchers want to investigate whether the survey mode affects responses to sensitive questions. Using the GSS2024 dataset, test whether the proportion of respondents who support the legalization of marijuana differs between those surveyed in person and those surveyed by phone. The variable Mode indicates the survey mode (In Person or Phone), and the variable Grass indicates support for marijuana legalization (Yes or No). Test at the 5% level. Note: The Mode variable in the GSS2024 dataset includes three categories: In Person, Phone, and Web. When you select only the In Person and Phone groups in Rguroo for your analysis, Rguroo will automatically exclude respondents who completed the survey via the Web.

title: 10  Inference for Population Proportions
section: 10.10 Confidence Interval for the Difference Between Two Population Proportions
text:
10.10 Confidence Interval for the Difference Between Two Population Proportions
In Section 10.9, we learned how to test whether two population proportions differ. For example, in the schema-based instruction study (Example 10.40), we found strong evidence that the new instructional approach produced higher mastery rates than traditional instruction. The hypothesis test told us that a difference exists, but it didn’t tell us how large that difference might be. Does the new approach improve mastery by 5 percentage points? 20 percentage points? 35 percentage points? The hypothesis test alone cannot answer this question.
This is where confidence intervals become valuable. A confidence interval for \(p_1 - p_2\) provides a range of plausible values for the true difference between the two proportions, addressing the question “How large is the difference?” It tells us not just that a difference exists, but also gives us insight into the magnitude and direction of that difference. For instance, a confidence interval might tell us: “We are 95% confident that the new approach improves mastery rates by somewhere between 4 and 36 percentage points compared to traditional instruction.” This additional information helps researchers, educators, and policymakers make more informed decisions.
Just as in the one-population case (Section 10.8), a confidence interval for \(p_1 - p_2\) can be derived by inverting hypothesis tests: given the observed difference \(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2,\) the \((1-\alpha) \times 100\%\) interval consists of all values \(d\) for which we would fail to reject \(H_0: p_1 - p_2 = d\) in a two-sided test at significance level \(\alpha.\) And as in the one-population case, the confidence level describes the long-run behavior of the construction method, not any single interval — a 95% method captures the true difference in 95% of repeated samples. In practice we use a direct formula based on the normal approximation rather than carrying out the test inversion by hand, but the logic is the same.

10.10.1 Large Sample Confidence Interval for \(p_1 - p_2\)
When the large sample conditions are satisfied, we can construct a confidence interval for \(p_1 - p_2\) using the normal approximation. Recall from Section 10.9.2 that when both samples are sufficiently large, the difference in sample proportions \(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2\) follows an approximately normal distribution.
However, there is an important difference between constructing a confidence interval and conducting a hypothesis test. In hypothesis testing, we assumed \(H_0: p_1 = p_2\) was true, which allowed us to use a pooled estimate \(\hat{p}\) for the common proportion. When constructing a confidence interval, we do not assume the proportions are equal—in fact, we’re trying to estimate how different they are! Therefore, we cannot use the pooled proportion.
Instead, for a confidence interval, we estimate the standard error using the individual sample proportions \(\hat{p}_1\) and \(\hat{p}_2\):
\[\text{SE}(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2) = \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}_1(1-\hat{p}_1)}{n_1} + \frac{\hat{p}_2(1-\hat{p}_2)}{n_2}}.\]
This is called the unpooled standard error, or simply the standard error, because we do not pool the two samples together.






NotePooled vs. Unpooled Standard Error



The two-proportion confidence interval uses the unpooled standard error, based on \(\hat{p}_1\) and \(\hat{p}_2\) separately: \[\text{SE}(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2) = \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}_1(1-\hat{p}_1)}{n_1} + \frac{\hat{p}_2(1-\hat{p}_2)}{n_2}}.\]
The two-proportion hypothesis test, by contrast, uses the pooled standard error, based on the common proportion \(\hat{p}\) under \(H_0: p_1 = p_2\) (see Section 10.9.2): \[\widehat{\text{SE}}(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2) = \sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})\left(\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}\right)}.\]
The reason is the assumption being made. The hypothesis test assumes \(p_1 = p_2,\) so we pool. The confidence interval makes no such assumption — we’re trying to estimate the difference, not assume it away — so we estimate each proportion’s variance from its own sample.


The large sample conditions for a confidence interval are the same as those for hypothesis testing. We need at least 10 successes and at least 10 failures in each group:
\[n_1\hat{p}_1 \geq 10, \quad n_1(1-\hat{p}_1) \geq 10, \quad n_2\hat{p}_2 \geq 10, \quad n_2(1-\hat{p}_2) \geq 10.\]
When these conditions are satisfied, the \((1-\alpha) \times 100\%\) confidence interval for \(p_1 - p_2\) takes the form:
\[(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2) \pm z^* \times \text{SE}(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2),\]
where \(z^*\) is the critical value from the standard normal distribution corresponding to the desired confidence level, just as in the one-population case.






NoteLarge Sample Confidence Interval for \(p_1 - p_2\)



When the large sample conditions are satisfied, an approximate \((1-\alpha) \times 100\%\) confidence interval for \(p_1 - p_2\) is:
\[(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2) \pm \underbrace{z^* \times \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}_1(1-\hat{p}_1)}{n_1} + \frac{\hat{p}_2(1-\hat{p}_2)}{n_2}}}_{\text{margin of error}}.\]
That is, the lower endpoint is \((\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2) - z^* \cdot \text{SE}\) and the upper endpoint is \((\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2) + z^* \cdot \text{SE},\) where \(\text{SE}\) is the unpooled standard error given above.


Common critical values remain the same:
