Let’s see how to construct and interpret confidence intervals for the difference between two proportions using our earlier examples.


10.10.2 Relationship Between Confidence Intervals and Hypothesis Tests
There is an important connection between confidence intervals and two-sided hypothesis tests. A \((1-\alpha)\times100%\) confidence interval and a two-sided hypothesis test at significance level \(\alpha\) lead to the same decisions about the null value \(p_1-p_2=0\):

If a \((1-\alpha) \times 100\%\) confidence interval for \(p_1 - p_2\) does not contain 0, then 0 is not a plausible value for \(p_1-p_2,\) and we reject \(H_0: p_1 - p_2 = 0\) at significance level \(\alpha\) in a two-sided test.
If a \((1-\alpha) \times 100\%\) confidence interval for \(p_1 - p_2\) contains 0, 0 is a plausible value for \(p_1-p_2,\) and we fail to reject \(H_0: p_1 - p_2 = 0\) at significance level \(\alpha\) in a two-sided test.

This relationship provides a quick way to connect the confidence interval to the corresponding two-sided hypothesis test. As noted, however, confidence intervals provide more information than hypothesis tests alone. They tell us not just whether the data provide evidence of a difference, but also which values are plausible for the size and direction of the difference.
This direct relationship applies only to two-sided hypothesis tests. For a one-sided hypothesis test, you should not use this confidence interval rule to determine whether to reject \(H_0.\)

Example 10.47 (Schema-Based Instruction: Confidence Interval) Recall Example 10.40. In the schema-based instruction study, \(n_1=50\) students were assigned to the new approach and \(n_2=50\) to traditional instruction. After the intervention, 34 students in the new approach group achieved mastery (\(\hat{p}_1 = 0.68\)), while 24 students in the traditional instruction group achieved mastery (\(\hat{p}_2 = 0.48\)).

Check whether the large sample conditions are satisfied for constructing a confidence interval.
Use Rguroo’s Two-Population Proportion inference function to construct a 95% confidence interval for the true difference in mastery rates between the two approaches, and interpret the interval in the context of the problem.








Tip🔎 Solution





a. We check the large sample conditions using the individual sample proportions:

Group 1 (new approach): \(n_1\hat{p}_1 = 50 \times 0.68 = 34 \geq 10\) and \(n_1(1-\hat{p}_1) = 50 \times 0.32 = 16 \geq 10\)
Group 2 (traditional): \(n_2\hat{p}_2 = 50 \times 0.48 = 24 \geq 10\) and \(n_2(1-\hat{p}_2) = 50 \times 0.52 = 26 \geq 10\)

All four conditions are satisfied, so the large-sample normal approximation is appropriate for constructing the confidence interval.
b. Click to expand the box below to see how to use the Proportion Inference function in Rguroo to obtain a large sample confidence interval for this problem.






Note Two-population large sample confidence interval - Schema example






Open the Analytics toolbox in Rguroo.
From the Analysis dropdown, select Proportion Inference → Two Populations. This opens the Two Population Proportion Inference dialog.
In the Response/Success section of the dialog, enter the same information as in Example 10.40:

Response Label: Improves Mastery
Success Label: Yes
Failure Label: No

In the Population section, enter Seventh Graders.
In the Data Summary tab, enter the data for both populations:

Population 1: Label: New, Sample Size: 50, # of Successes: 34
Population 2: Label: Traditional, Sample Size: 50, # of Successes: 24

Click on the Confidence Interval tab and specify the following:

In the Confidence Level textbox, enter 0.95. This is the default value corresponding to 95% confidence.
In the Methods section, select the checkbox Large Sample z.

Click the preview icon  to view the output.
Click the  button and save the result as SchemaCI.







TipRguroo Two-Population Proportion dialog for Schema-Based Instruction confidence interval










Rguroo dialog for constructing a confidence interval










Click to expand the box below to see the Rguroo output.






TipRguroo output: Two-Population Proportion Confidence Interval - Schema-Based Instruction






 




From the Rguroo output, the 95% confidence interval for \(p_1 - p_2\) is approximately \((0.0105, 0.3895).\)
Interpretation: We are 95% confident that the true difference in mastery rates (new approach minus traditional instruction) is between about 0.011 and 0.379, or between about 1.1 and 38.9 percentage points. Since the entire interval is positive the data suggest that the mastery rate is higher for the new instructional approach than for traditional instruction.




Example 10.48 (Text Message Reminders: Confidence Interval) Recall Example 10.44. In the text message reminder study, \(n_1=40\) patients received text reminders and \(n_2=50\) received standard care. After three months, 32 patients in the text reminder group had good adherence (\(\hat{p}_1 = 0.80\)), while 28 patients in the standard care group had good adherence (\(\hat{p}_2 = 0.56\)).

Check whether the large sample conditions are satisfied for constructing a confidence interval.
Use Rguroo’s Two-Population Proportion inference function to construct a 95% confidence interval for the true difference in adherence rates between the two approaches, and interpret the interval in the context of the problem.
Compare this confidence interval to the hypothesis test result in Example 10.44. Are they consistent?








Tip🔎 Solution





a. We check the large sample conditions using the individual sample proportions:

Group 1 (text reminders): \(n_1\hat{p}_1 = 40 \times 0.80 = 32 \geq 10\) and \(n_1(1-\hat{p}_1) = 40 \times 0.20 = 8 < 10\)
Group 2 (standard care): \(n_2\hat{p}_2 = 50 \times 0.56 = 28 \geq 10\) and \(n_2(1-\hat{p}_2) = 50 \times 0.44 = 22 \geq 10\)

The condition \(n_1(1-\hat{p}_1) \geq 10\) is not satisfied. We have only 8 observed failures in the text reminder group. Therefore, the 10-10 rule is not fully satisfied, and we should use caution when applying the large-sample normal approximation. We will proceed with the large-sample method here so that we can examine the resulting interval.
b. Follow the same Rguroo instructions as shown in Example 10.47. The following is a screenshot of the Two Population Proportion Inference dialog for obtaining the large sample confidence interval for this example.





Rguroo dialog for constructing a confidence interval for the text message study




Click to expand the box below to see the Rguroo output.






TipRguroo output: Two-Population Proportion Confidence Interval - Text Message Reminders






 




From the Rguroo output, the 95% confidence interval for \(p_1 - p_2\) is \((0.0548067, 0.425193).\)
Interpretation: We are 95% confident that the true difference in adherence rates (text message reminders minus standard care) is between 0.0548067 (about 5.5 percentage points) and 0.425193 (about 42.5 percentage points).
c. Since the entire interval is positive, the data suggest that the adherence rate is higher for the text message reminder group than for the standard care group. This is consistent with the two-sided hypothesis test in Example 10.44, where we rejected \(H_0: p_1 - p_2 = 0\) at significance level \(\alpha=0.05.\) The value 0 lies outside the 95% confidence interval.
As expected, the two-sided test at \(\alpha=0.05\) and the corresponding 95% confidence interval lead to the same conclusion.




Example 10.49 (Smoking Cessation: Confidence Interval) Recall Example 10.42. In the smoking cessation study, \(n_1=60\) employees received nicotine patches and \(n_2=60\) participated in the self-guided program. After six months, 24 employees in the nicotine patch group had quit smoking (\(\hat{p}_1 = 0.40\)), while 30 in the self-guided group had quit (\(\hat{p}_2 = 0.50\)).

Check whether the large sample conditions are satisfied for constructing a confidence interval.
Use Rguroo’s Two-Population Proportion inference function to construct a 95% confidence interval for the true difference in quit rates between the two approaches, and interpret the interval in the context of the problem.








Tip🔎 Solution





a. We check the large sample conditions using the individual sample proportions:

Group 1 (nicotine patches): \(n_1\hat{p}_1 = 60 \times 0.40 = 24 \geq 10\) and \(n_1(1-\hat{p}_1) = 60 \times 0.60 = 36 \geq 10\)
Group 2 (self-guided): \(n_2\hat{p}_2 = 60 \times 0.50 = 30 \geq 10\) and \(n_2(1-\hat{p}_2) = 60 \times 0.50 = 30 \geq 10\)

All conditions are satisfied, so tthe large-sample normal approximation is appropriate for constructing the confidence interval.
b. The following is a screenshot of the Two Population Proportion Inference dialog for obtaining the large sample confidence interval for this example.





Rguroo dialog for constructing a confidence interval for the smoking cessation study




Click to expand the box below to see the Rguroo output.






TipRguroo output: Two-Population Proportion Confidence Interval - Smoking Cessation






 




From the Rguroo output, the 95% confidence interval for \(p_1 - p_2\) is \((-0.277121, 0.0771212).\)
Interpretation: We are 95% confident that the true difference in quit rates (nicotine patches minus self-guided) is between \(-0.2771\) (about \(-27.7\) percentage points) and \(0.07712\) (about \(7.7\) percentage points). Negative values indicate a higher quit rate for the self-guided approach, while positive values indicate a higher quit rate for the nicotine patch approach. Because the interval includes 0, the data are consistent with no difference in the population quit rates.




Example 10.50 (GSS 2024: Gender and Marijuana Legalization - Confidence Interval Using Raw Data) Recall Example 10.46. The GSS 2024 sample included \(n_1=204\) females, of whom 142 support marijuana legalization (\(\hat{p}_1 \approx 0.696\)), and \(n_2=184\) males, of whom 140 support legalization (\(\hat{p}_2 \approx 0.761\)).

Check whether the large sample conditions are satisfied for constructing a confidence interval.
Use Rguroo’s Two-Population Proportion inference function with the GSS2024 dataset to construct a 95% confidence interval for the true difference in support for marijuana legalization between females and males, and interpret the interval in the context of the problem.
Compare this confidence interval to the hypothesis test result in Example 10.46. Are they consistent?


 The dataset for this example is available in the Rguroo dataset repository Intro to Stats with Rguroo, with the dataset name GSS2024.
Code book for Dataset GSS2024 is given here.








Tip🔎 Solution





a. We check the large sample conditions using the individual sample proportions:

Group 1 (females): \(n_1\hat{p}_1 = 204 \times 0.696 \approx 142 \geq 10\) and \(n_1(1-\hat{p}_1) = 204 \times 0.304 \approx 62 \geq 10\)
Group 2 (males): \(n_2\hat{p}_2 = 184 \times 0.761 \approx 140 \geq 10\) and \(n_2(1-\hat{p}_2) = 184 \times 0.239 \approx 44 \geq 10\)

All conditions are comfortably satisfied, the large-sample normal approximation is appropriate for constructing the confidence interval.
b. Click to expand the box below to see how to use the Proportion Inference function in Rguroo to obtain a confidence interval from raw data.






Note Two-population confidence interval using raw data - GSS example





Before you begin: Make sure you have already imported the GSS2024 dataset into your Rguroo account, as shown here.

Open the Analytics toolbox in Rguroo.
From the Analysis dropdown, select Proportion Inference → Two Populations. This opens the Two Population Proportion Inference dialog.
From the Dataset dropdown, select the dataset GSS2024.
Fill in the Response/Success section of the dialog as follows:

From the Response dropdown, select the factor Grass.
From the Success dropdown, select the success level Yes.
In the Failure textbox, enter No.
(Optional) In the Response Label textbox, enter Legalize Marijuana.

In the Population section of the dialog, from the Population dropdown, select the variable Sex.
In the Data Summary tab, select Female from the Level dropdown for population 1, and Male from the Level dropdown for population 2. Then click the refresh icon  to display the summary statistics for each group.
Click on the Confidence Interval tab and specify the following:

In the Confidence Level textbox, enter 0.95.
In the Methods section, select the checkbox Large Sample z.

Click the preview icon  to view the output.
Click the  button and save the result as GSS2024CI.







TipRguroo Two-Population Proportion dialog for GSS2024 confidence interval










Rguroo dialog for constructing a confidence interval from raw data










Click to expand the box below to see the Rguroo output.






TipRguroo output: Two-Population Proportion Confidence Interval - GSS 2024 Marijuana Legalization






 




From the Rguroo output, the 95% confidence interval for \(p_1 - p_2\) is \((-0.153008, 0.0234262).\)
Interpretation: We are 95% confident that the true difference in support for marijuana legalization (females minus males) is between \(-0.1530\) (about \(-15.3\) percentage points) and \(0.0234\) (about \(2.3\) percentage points). Negative values indicate lower support among females than males, while positive values indicate higher support among females. Since the interval includes 0, the data are consistent with no difference in the population proportions who support marijuana legalization between females and males.
Note that the observed difference was \(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \approx -0.065,\) meaning the sample showed about 6.5 percentage points lower support among females. However, the confidence interval indicates that plausible values for the true difference range from about 15 percentage points lower support among females to about 2 percentage points higher support among females.
c. This confidence interval is consistent with our hypothesis test result in Example 10.46. In that test, we failed to reject \(H_0: p_1 - p_2 = 0\) at significance level \(\alpha=0.05,\) with a p-value of 0.153. The value 0 lies inside the 95% confidence interval, which corresponds to failing to reject \(H_0\) in the corresponding two-sided test. Both the hypothesis test and the confidence interval lead us to the same conclusion: the data do not provide sufficient evidence that support for marijuana legalization differs between females and males.

For each of the scenarios described below, answer the following:

Autism Spectrum Disorder: Pennsylvania vs. Utah Recall Problem 6 from Section 10.9. In Pennsylvania, 245 eight-year-olds were diagnosed with ASD out of 18,440 evaluated. In Utah, 45 eight-year-olds were diagnosed with ASD out of 2,123 evaluated. Construct a 99% confidence interval for the difference in ASD diagnosis rates between Pennsylvania and Utah.

Of the 211,693 students who took the calculus AB exam, 102,598 were female. Construct a 95% confidence interval for the difference in the proportion of female students between these two exams. (Note: For this problem, let \(p_1\) represent the proportion of biology test-takers who are female, and \(p_2\) represent the proportion of calculus AB test-takers who are female.)

Additional Practice Problems:
For the following problems, construct the specified confidence interval and interpret it in context:

Vaccine Effectiveness Study A clinical trial randomly assigned 500 participants to receive a new vaccine and 500 to receive a placebo. After exposure, 12 vaccinated participants developed the disease, while 48 placebo recipients developed the disease. Construct a 95% confidence interval for the difference in disease rates between the two groups.
Online vs. In-Person Course Success A university compared success rates for a statistics course offered online versus in-person. Of 180 online students, 126 earned a grade of C or better. Of 220 in-person students, 165 earned a grade of C or better. Construct a 90% confidence interval for the difference in success rates between the two delivery methods.

title: 11  Statistical Inference for Means
text:
11.1 Basics of Hypothesis Testing for a Population Mean
Before you begin, click to expand the box below to review the process for importing a dataset.
In this chapter we develop methods for drawing inferences about a population mean \(\mu\) (read mu). Examples of population means abound in practice: the mean SAT math score among incoming freshmen at a particular university, the mean nightly sleep hours among college students, the mean one-way commute time in a metropolitan area, and the mean flipper length of Adélie penguins in the Palmer Archipelago. These are four of the running examples we use throughout the chapter, and many other applications follow the same pattern.
The framework established in the Foundations of Inference chapter applies here unchanged. We still begin with a research question about a population parameter — now \(\mu.\) We collect a random sample, compute a statistic from it, and study how that statistic varies from sample to sample through its sampling distribution (Section 9.1). We test claims by examining where our observed statistic falls within the null distribution(Section 9.3), and make decisions using p-values (Section 9.5) or critical regions (Section 9.6). Confidence intervals (Section 9.7), significance levels, Type I and Type II errors (Section 9.4.1), and confidence levels all retain the meanings established in the foundations chapter.
How do we tell, in a real-world problem, whether the parameter of interest is a mean or a proportion? As discussed in Section 9.3.3, the key is the variable measured on each individual in the population. If the variable is numerical — a score, a quantity, a measurement — the parameter is a population mean \(\mu.\) All the examples in this chapter are of this type: SAT scores in points, sleep duration in hours, commute time in minutes, flipper length in millimeters. If instead the variable is categorical (success/failure, yes/no), the parameter is a population proportion \(p,\) and the methods from the previous chapter apply.
For numerical data, the statistic we use to estimate the population mean \(\mu\) is the sample mean, the arithmetic average of the numerical measurements in the sample. As a random variable—that is, before we collect data—we denote it by \(\bar{X}.\) Once we have collected the data, we obtain a specific numerical value of this average, which we denote by \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}}\) and call the observed sample mean. To make inferences about \(\mu,\) we determine where our observed statistic \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}}\) lies within the sampling distribution of \(\bar{X}.\)
We assume the variable under study has a normal distribution in the population. In Section 11.7, we will see when the sample size is large, many of the same methods remain valid even when the population distribution is not normal. We will cover both one-population and two-population settings. In the one-population setting we draw inferences about a single population mean \(\mu.\) In the two-population setting we compare two population means \(\mu_1\) and \(\mu_2\) through their difference \(\mu_1 - \mu_2.\) We begin with the one-population case.
In this section we set up the elements common to all hypothesis tests for a population mean: the form of the null and alternative hypotheses, and the null distribution of \(\bar{X}.\) The specifics of this null distribution depend on what we assume about the population, leading to two cases that we develop in the subsections that follow.

title: 11  Statistical Inference for Means
text:
11.1.1 Null and Alternative Hypotheses
As established in Section 9.3.1, the null and alternative hypotheses always come in one of three forms, depending on the nature of the research question. For a population mean \(\mu,\) with \(\mu_0\) denoting a specific value, the three cases are:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Case 1: }
&\begin{cases}
H_0: \mu \leq \mu_0 \\
H_a: \mu > \mu_0
\end{cases}
\qquad
\text{Case 2: }
\begin{cases}
H_0: \mu \geq \mu_0 \\
H_a: \mu < \mu_0
\end{cases} \\
\\
\text{Case 3: }
&\begin{cases}
H_0: \mu = \mu_0 \\
H_a: \mu \neq \mu_0
\end{cases}
\end{aligned}
\]
The value \(\mu_0\) is the boundary value of \(H_0\) — the value at which the Type I error probability is maximized for one-sided tests (Section 9.3.2).
Recall from Section 9.3.1 that in Cases 1 and 2, the alternative hypothesis claims that \(\mu\) is either greater than \((>)\) or less than \((<)\) \(\mu_0,\) pointing in a single direction. These are called one-sided (or one-tailed) hypotheses. In Case 3, the alternative hypothesis claims only that \(\mu\) is different from \((\neq)\) \(\mu_0,\) without specifying a direction. This is called a two-sided (or two-tailed) hypothesis. The form of the hypotheses determines how we set up our decision rules.
Let’s begin with a few examples.

Example 11.1 (SAT Math Scores at CSUF) According to the College Board, the mean score on the math portion of the SAT for the high school graduating class of 2025 was 508 points, with a standard deviation of 113 points. These figures are computed from the more than 2 million high school students who took the exam that year.
We wish to investigate whether the mean math SAT score among incoming freshmen in fall 2025 at California State University, Fullerton (CSUF) is higher than the national mean. Since CSUF does not require the SAT for admission, the exact population mean for the CSUF students is not available, so we take a random sample of \(n = 40\) incoming CSUF freshmen and record their SAT math scores. The sample mean of these SAT scores is \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 542\) points. Using this information, answer the following questions:

What is the population of interest?
Describe the parameter \(\mu\) in words.
Write the null and alternative hypotheses.








Tip🔎 Solution





a. The population of interest is all incoming freshmen in fall 2025 at California State University, Fullerton (CSUF).
b. \(\mu\) is the mean math SAT score for all incoming freshmen in fall 2025 at CSUF.
c. The research question asks whether the mean math SAT score among incoming CSUF freshmen is higher than the national mean of 508. Because “higher than” points in the greater-than direction, the alternative hypothesis is \(H_a: \mu > 508.\) The null hypothesis includes the opposite situation, together with equality, so it is \(H_0: \mu \leq 508.\) The null and alternative hypotheses are therefore: \[
\begin{cases}
H_0: \mu \leq 508 \\
H_a: \mu > 508
\end{cases}
\]




Example 11.2 (Sleep Hours Among University Students) The National Sleep Foundation and the American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommend that young adults sleep between 7 and 9 hours per night, with 7 hours often cited as the minimum needed for healthy cognitive and physical functioning. There is widespread concern, however, that college students fall short of this recommendation.
We wish to investigate whether the mean nightly sleep among students at our university is less than 7 hours. We take a random sample of \(n = 15\) students and ask each student how many hours they slept the previous night. The resulting sample has a mean of \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 6.4\) hours and a standard deviation of \(s=1.2\) hours. Using this information, answer the following questions:

What is the population of interest?
Describe the parameter \(\mu\) in words.
Write the null and alternative hypotheses.








Tip🔎 Solution





a. The population of interest is all students at our university.
b. \(\mu\) is the mean nightly sleep, in hours, for all students at our university.
c. For this example, the research question asks whether the mean nightly sleep among students at our university is less than 7 hours. Because “less than” points in the lower-than direction, the alternative hypothesis is \(H_a: \mu < 7.\) The null hypothesis includes the opposite situation, together with equality, so it is \(H_0: \mu \geq 7.\)
The null and alternative hypotheses are therefore:
\[
\begin{cases}
H_0: \mu \geq 7 \\
H_a: \mu < 7
\end{cases}
\]




Example 11.3 (Commute Time in a Metropolitan Area) According to the U.S. Census Bureau’s American Community Survey, the mean one-way commute time for U.S. workers in 2023 was 26.8 minutes. Local commuting patterns can differ substantially from the national average, however, because of differences in population density, transportation infrastructure, and the prevalence of remote work.
We wish to investigate whether the mean one-way commute time among workers in our metropolitan area differs from the national mean. We take a random sample of \(n = 15\) commuters from the area and record each person’s one-way commute time. The sample has a mean of \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 24.8\) minutes and a standard deviation of \(s = 9.6\) minutes. Using this information, answer the following questions:

What is the population of interest?
Describe the parameter \(\mu\) in words.
Write the null and alternative hypotheses.








Tip🔎 Solution





a. The population of interest is all workers in our metropolitan area.
b. \(\mu\) is the mean one-way commute time, in minutes, for all workers in our metropolitan area.
c. For this example, the research question asks whether the mean one-way commute time among workers in our metropolitan area differs from the national mean of 26.8 minutes. Because “differs from” does not specify whether the local mean is higher or lower, the alternative hypothesis is two-sided: \(H_a: \mu \neq 26.8.\) The null hypothesis says there is no difference from the national mean, so it is \(H_0: \mu = 26.8.\)
The null and alternative hypotheses are therefore:
\[
\begin{cases}
H_0: \mu = 26.8 \\
H_a: \mu \neq 26.8
\end{cases}
\]




Example 11.4 (Flipper Length of Adélie Penguins) The Palmer Penguins dataset contains body measurements collected between 2007 and 2009 on 342 penguins from three species — Adélie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo — at three islands in the Palmer Archipelago, Antarctica. The data were assembled by Dr. Kristen Gorman and the Palmer Station Long Term Ecological Research (LTER) program and have since become a widely used dataset in introductory statistics and data science. Among Adélie penguins, flipper length is an important morphological measurement used in studies of body condition and adaptation, and a commonly cited reference value for the mean flipper length of Adélie penguins is 188 mm.
We wish to investigate whether the mean flipper length among Adélie penguins in the Palmer Archipelago differs from this reference value. Rather than working from summary statistics, in this example we use the raw flipper length measurements of \(n = 151\) Adélie penguins with recorded flipper lengths in the palmerpenguins_Adelie dataset available in this textbook repository. Using this information, answer the following questions:

What is the population of interest?
Describe the parameter \(\mu\) in words.
Write the null and alternative hypotheses.


 The dataset for this exercise is available in the Rguroo dataset repository Intro to Stats with Rguroo, with the dataset name PalmerPenguins_Adelie.
Code book for Dataset PalmerPenguins_Adelie is given here.








TipCode book for Dataset PalmerPenguins_Adelie





Dataset Name: PalmerPenguins_Adelie
This dataset contains measurements collected from Adélie penguins observed near Palmer Station, Antarctica, as part of the Palmer Penguins study. The original PalmerPenguins dataset includes \(n = 342\) penguins from three species; this subset includes only the Adélie penguins.
The variable Species is included in this dataset, but all observations have the value Adélie.
The variables included in this dataset are described below.
Species: Penguin species

Adélie

Island: Island where the penguin was observed

Biscoe

Dream

Torgersen

Penguin Anatomy and Measurements





BillLength: Bill length of the penguin (in millimeters)
BillDepth: Bill depth of the penguin (in millimeters)
FlipperLength: Flipper length of the penguin (in millimeters)
BodyMass: Body mass of the penguin (in grams)
Sex: Sex of the penguin

Male

Female

Year: Year in which the observation was recorded

2007

2008

2009

Source
Horst, A. M., Hill, A. P., & Gorman, K. B. palmerpenguins: Palmer Archipelago (Antarctica) penguin data.










Tip🔎 Solution





a. The population of interest is all Adélie penguins in the Palmer Archipelago.
b. \(\mu\) is the mean flipper length, in millimeters, of all Adélie penguins in the Palmer Archipelago.
c. For this example, the research question asks whether the mean flipper length among Adélie penguins in the Palmer Archipelago differs from the reference value of 188 mm. Because “differs from” does not specify whether the mean flipper length is greater than or less than 188 mm, the alternative hypothesis is two-sided: \(H_a: \mu \neq 188.\) The null hypothesis says there is no difference from the reference value, so it is \(H_0: \mu = 188.\)
The null and alternative hypotheses are therefore:
\[
\begin{cases}
H_0: \mu = 188 \\
H_a: \mu \neq 188
\end{cases}
\]





11.1.2 Homework for Section 11.1
For each problem, answer the following questions:

What is the population of interest?

Describe the parameter \(\mu\) in words.

Write the null and alternative hypotheses.



CO2 Emissions The Kyoto Protocol, signed in 1997, required participating countries to begin reducing their carbon emissions; it became enforceable in February 2005. In 2004, the mean CO2 emission was 4.87 metric tons per capita, computed by averaging each country’s per-capita emission rate across countries. A researcher wants to determine whether the mean CO2 emission per capita across countries in 2010 differs from the 2004 mean.
Mercury Concentration The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) sets 1.0 mg/kg as the allowable amount of mercury in fish that is consumed. To assess whether fish in Florida lakes meet this standard, largemouth bass were collected from 53 different lakes and for each lake a standardized estimate of the mercury concentration in a three-year-old bass was computed from the fish sampled there. A researcher wants to determine whether the mean standardized mercury concentration across Florida lakes differs from the allowable amount of 1.0 mg/kg.
Cereal Sugar The amount of sugar in a Krispy Kreme glazed donut is 10 g. Many people feel that cereal is a healthier alternative to glazed donuts for children. A researcher wants to determine whether the mean amount of sugar in children’s cereal differs from the 10 g found in a glazed donut.
Pulse Rate The mean pulse rate after running in place for one minute among females who do not drink alcohol is 97 beats per minute. A researcher wants to determine whether the mean pulse rate after running, among females who do drink alcohol, is higher than this value.
Economic Dynamism Economic dynamism is an index of productive growth, measured on a scale from 0 (worst) to 100 (best). Countries that are considered high-income have a mean economic dynamism of 60.29. A researcher wants to determine whether the mean economic dynamism of middle-income countries is less than the high-income mean.
Prenatal Care In 1999, the mean percentage of women who received prenatal care per country was 80.1%, computed by averaging each country’s percentage across countries. A researcher wants to determine whether the mean percentage of women receiving prenatal care across countries in 2009 differs from the 1999 mean.
Maintaining Balance Maintaining balance may become harder with age. In a study of steadiness, elderly subjects stood on a force platform and reacted to an unpredictable noise while the platform measured how much they swayed, in millimeters, in the forward/backward direction. The mean forward sway of younger people under the same conditions is 18.125 mm. A researcher wants to determine whether the elderly sway more than this value, on average.


 The dataset for this exercise is available in the Rguroo dataset repository Intro to Stats with Rguroo, with the dataset name sway_elderly.
Code book for Dataset sway_elderly is given here.

title: 11  Statistical Inference for Means
section: 11.2 The Null Distribution of the Sample Mean
text:
11.2 The Null Distribution of the Sample Mean
As we noted in Section 9.1, to make inferences about \(\mu,\) we use the sample mean \(\bar{X}\) as our statistic, and we work with its sampling distribution.
To make this distribution concrete, we will assume that the variable under study has a normal distribution in the population. Two reasons motivate this assumption. First, the normal distribution provides a reasonable model for many naturally occurring numerical variables, including adult heights, weights, exam scores, and a wide range of biological and physical measurements. Second, under this assumption, the sampling distribution of \(\bar{X}\) takes a clean, exact form that allows us to focus on the main ideas of inference without the distraction of approximations or special cases. In Section 11.6 we discuss how to assess this assumption graphically with a statistical test and normal probability plot, and in Section 11.7 we show that the methods developed under the normality assumption remain approximately valid for large samples even when the population is not normal.
The sampling distribution of \(\bar{X}\) depends on the unknown population mean \(\mu\) — the very quantity we want to make an inference about. As in foundations (Section 9.3.2), we proceed by evaluating the sampling distribution at the boundary value of \(H_0\): the value \(\mu_0\) where the Type I error probability is maximized. For two-sided tests, \(H_0\) specifies \(\mu = \mu_0\) directly. For one-sided tests, \(\mu_0\) is the boundary of the range of \(\mu\) values allowed by \(H_0.\)






NoteThe Null Distribution



The null distribution of \(\bar{X}\) is the sampling distribution of \(\bar{X}\) evaluated at \(\mu = \mu_0,\) the boundary value of \(H_0.\) This is the distribution we use for hypothesis testing — to compute p-values and to determine critical regions.


Under the normality assumption introduced above, the form of this null distribution depends on whether the population standard deviation \(\sigma\) is known. When \(\sigma\) is known, the null distribution is exactly normal. When \(\sigma\) is unknown — the typical situation in practice — we estimate it from the sample, and the resulting null distribution is a Student \(t\) distribution. The subsections that follow develop each case in turn.

11.2.1 When \(\sigma\) Is Known
In practice, the population standard deviation \(\sigma\) is rarely known exactly. There are, however, situations in which a value of \(\sigma\) has been established from extensive prior data and can reasonably be treated as known. The SAT example in Example 11.1 is one such case: the standard deviation of \(\sigma = 113\) points is computed from the scores of more than 2 million students who took the exam in 2025, a population large enough that we can reasonably treat this value as known when investigating the mean score among a particular subgroup such as incoming CSUF freshmen.
Beyond examples of this kind, beginning with the known-\(\sigma\) case is helpful pedagogically because it allows us to focus on the main ideas of statistical inference while working with a simpler sampling distribution. Once these ideas are established, we will turn to the more realistic setting in which \(\sigma\) is unknown and must be estimated from the sample data.
Let’s pause to clarify a phrase that will appear repeatedly throughout this chapter.






NoteA Convention on “When \(H_0\) Is True”



For a two-sided test of a population mean, the null hypothesis is \(H_0: \mu = \mu_0,\) so the phrase “when \(H_0\) is true” is unambiguous: it means \(\mu = \mu_0.\)
For a one-sided test, however, the null hypothesis allows a range of possible values. For example, if \(H_0: \mu \leq \mu_0,\) then any value \(\mu \leq \mu_0\) is included in the null hypothesis; similarly, if \(H_0: \mu \geq \mu_0,\) then any value \(\mu \geq \mu_0\) is included. Thus, “when \(H_0\) is true” could in principle refer to any value in that range. As established in Section 9.3.2, the boundary value \(\mu_0\) is the value within \(H_0\) at which the Type I error probability is maximized; controlling the error rate at \(\mu_0\) automatically controls it at every other value of \(\mu\) allowed under \(H_0.\)
Convention. For the remainder of this chapter, whenever we say “when \(H_0\) is true,” “under $H_0,” or “assuming the null hypothesis,” we mean at the boundary value \(\mu_0\).


Under the assumptions introduced earlier, the sample mean \(\bar{X}\) has a normal distribution when \(H_0\) is true. This distribution serves as the null distribution for hypothesis testing about the population mean \(\mu.\)






NoteThe Null Distribution



Under the assumptions that

the variable under study has a normal distribution in the population,
the population standard deviation \(\sigma\) is known,
the sample size is \(n,\) and
the boundary value specified by \(H_0\) is \(\mu = \mu_0,\)

the null distribution of the sample mean \(\bar{X}\) is
\[
\bar{X} \sim N\left(\mu_0,\ \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right).
\]


The result above tells us that, when \(H_0\) is true, the sample mean \(\bar{X}\) is centered at \(\mu_0\) and varies around it with standard deviation \(\sigma/\sqrt{n}.\) For instance, in the SAT example with hypothesis \(H_0: \mu \leq 508,\) the random variable \(\bar{X}\) has a normal distribution centered at 508 with standard deviation \(113/\sqrt{40} \approx 17.87\) points.
Sometimes, the sample mean is standardized by subtracting its null-hypothesis center \(\mu_0\) and dividing by its standard deviation \(\sigma/\sqrt{n}\):
\[
Z = \frac{\bar{X} - \mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}.
\]
When \(H_0\) is true, this standardized statistic has the standard normal distribution,
\[
Z \sim N(0,1),
\]
and for this reason the procedure is commonly called the \(z\)-test. Rguroo reports critical regions and p-values using both the standardized statistic \(Z\) and the sample mean \(\bar{X}\) on its original scale.
In this text, we will primarily use the null distribution of \(\bar{X}\) directly rather than its standardized version. Working on the original scale of the data allows us to interpret critical regions and p-values more naturally in the context of the problem and avoids the additional step of converting observations to standardized scores. In the SAT example, for instance, it is easier to reason about a sample mean of 542 points relative to a hypothesized population mean of 508 points than to translate everything into the unitless \(z\) scale.

Example 11.5 (SAT Math Scores at CSUF) Recall the SAT Math Scores at CSUF example. The national mean math SAT score for the high school graduating class of 2025 was 508 points, with population standard deviation \(\sigma = 113\) points. We wish to investigate whether the mean math SAT score among incoming CSUF freshmen is higher than the national mean.
The hypotheses are
\[
\begin{cases}
H_0: \mu \leq 508 \\
H_a: \mu > 508
\end{cases}
\]
Suppose we take a random sample of \(n = 40\) incoming CSUF freshmen. Assume that SAT math scores are normally distributed in the population and that the population standard deviation is known.
What is the null distribution of \(\bar{X}\)?







Tip🔎 Solution





Because \(H_0: \mu \leq 508,\) the boundary value is \(\mu_0 = 508.\) Since the population standard deviation is known, we use the normal distribution for the null distribution of \(\bar{X}.\)
Thus,
\[
\bar{X} \sim N\left(\mu_0,\ \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right).
\]
Substituting \(\mu_0 = 508,\) \(\sigma = 113,\) and \(n = 40,\) we get
\[
\bar{X} \sim N\left(508,\ \frac{113}{\sqrt{40}}\right).
\]
Since
\[
\frac{113}{\sqrt{40}} \approx 17.87,
\]
the null distribution is approximately
\[
\bar{X} \sim N(508,\ 17.87).
\]
So, when \(H_0\) is true at the boundary value \(\mu = 508,\) sample means from samples of size 40 are normally distributed with center 508 and standard deviation approximately 17.87 points.





11.2.2 When \(\sigma\) Is Unknown
In practice, only in rare cases do we know the population standard deviation \(\sigma.\) For example, in the sleep-hours example, we have data from only a sample of students, not from all students at our university, so we do not know the population standard deviation of nightly sleep hours. Similarly, in the commute-time and Adélie penguin examples, we have data from only samples, so the population standard deviation must be estimated from the data.
The good news is that the sample standard deviation \(s\) gives us a way to estimate the unknown population standard deviation \(\sigma.\) The key point is that this estimate adds uncertainty: from sample to sample, both the sample mean \(\bar{X}\) and the sample standard deviation \(s\) can vary.
To handle this extra uncertainty, we use a closely related distribution called the Student \(t\) distribution (or simply \(t\) distribution). The assumption is still about the individual measurements: we assume that the variable under study has a normal distribution in the population. But because \(\sigma\) is unknown and must be estimated by \(s,\) the sampling distribution we use for \(\bar{X}\) is a \(t\) distribution rather than a normal distribution.
The name Student was the pen name of William Sealy Gosset, a statistician working for Guinness Brewery in Ireland in the early 1900s. At the time, Guinness restricted employees from publishing research under their own names in order to protect company information and trade secrets. As a result, Gosset published his work under the pseudonym Student. His research led to the development of the \(t\) distribution, which allows us to make reliable inferences about population means when the population standard deviation is unknown.
The standard Student \(t\) distribution is similar in shape to the standard normal distribution: both are symmetric, bell-shaped, and centered at 0. Unlike the standard normal distribution, however, the \(t\) distribution depends on a shape parameter called the degrees of freedom, denoted \(\text{df},\) with different values of \(\text{df}\) producing slightly different shapes. When the degrees of freedom are small, the \(t\) distribution is more spread out and has heavier tails; as the degrees of freedom increase, the \(t\) distribution becomes closer and closer to the standard normal distribution.
Figure 11.1 shows three \(t\) distributions, with 1, 3, and 10 degrees of freedom, compared with the standard normal distribution (dashed gray). As the degrees of freedom increase, the \(t\) distribution becomes taller at its center, its tails grow lighter, and its shape approaches that of the standard normal.








Figure 11.1: Compating t-distributions with various degress of freeom to the normal distribution.





The heavier tails of the \(t\) distribution are shown more clearly in Figure 11.2, which compares the standard normal distribution to a \(t\) distribution with 4 degrees of freedom. Notice that the \(t\) distribution places more probability in the tails and less probability near the center. This difference is important because, when \(\sigma\) is unknown, we replace it with the sample standard deviation \(s.\) Since \(s\) varies from sample to sample, additional uncertainty is introduced into the inference procedure, and the heavier tails of the \(t\) distribution account for this extra uncertainty.








Figure 11.2: Comparison of the standard normal distribution and the \(t\) distribution with 4 degrees of freedom.





The amount of this additional uncertainty depends on the sample size. Small samples provide less information about \(\sigma,\) so \(s\) is a less reliable estimate and the \(t\) distribution has heavier tails; larger samples make \(s\) more stable and bring the \(t\) distribution closer to the standard normal. In mean inference, this relationship is captured directly by the degrees of freedom, \(\text{df} = n - 1\): In this way, the \(t\) distribution automatically adjusts the amount of uncertainty in the inference to match the amount of information in the sample.
Just as the standard normal distribution can be shifted and rescaled to obtain a general normal distribution with any center and standard deviation, the standard \(t\) distribution also has a more general form, written as
\[
X \sim t_{\text{df}}(\text{location}, \text{scale}),
\]
where \(\text{df}\) denotes the degrees of freedom, the location parameter determines the center of the distribution, and the scale parameter controls its spread. In mean inference, the degrees of freedom are \(n - 1,\) the location is the hypothesized population mean \(\mu_0,\) and the scale is the estimated standard error \(s/\sqrt{n},\) giving the null distribution of the sample mean stated below.






NoteWhat has a \(t\) distribution?



It is important to be clear about what is assumed to be normal and what follows a \(t\) distribution. The assumption is that the variable under study has a normal distribution in the population. Under this assumption, the statistic \(\bar{X}\) follows a \(t\) distribution. In other words, the normality assumption is about the individual measurements, while the \(t\) distribution describes the behavior of the sample mean computed from those measurements.








NoteThe Null Distribution



Under the assumptions that

the variable under study has a normal distribution in the population,
the population standard deviation \(\sigma\) is unknown and is estimated by the sample standard deviation \(s,\)
the sample size is \(n,\) and
the boundary value specified by the null hypothesis is \(\mu = \mu_0,\)

the null distribution of the sample mean \(\bar{X}\) is
\[
\bar{X} \sim t_{n-1}\left(\mu_0,\ \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\right),
\]
a \(t\) distribution with \(n - 1\) degrees of freedom, centered at \(\mu_0\) and with estimated standard error
\[
\hat\sigma_{\bar X} = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}.
\]


This result parallels the known-\(\sigma\) case, with two changes: the normal distribution is replaced by a \(t\) distribution, and because \(\sigma\) is no longer available, we replace it with the sample standard deviation \(s,\) so the scale of the distribution is the estimated standard error \(\hat\sigma_{\bar X} = s/\sqrt{n}\) rather than the known standard error \(\sigma/\sqrt{n}.\)
As in the known-\(\sigma\) case, the distribution is centered at \(\mu_0\) when the null hypothesis is true, and sample means far from \(\mu_0\) constitute evidence against \(H_0.\)
For instance, in the sleep example, suppose the null hypothesis is \(H_0: \mu \geq 7\) and we have a sample of size \(n = 15\) with sample standard deviation \(s = 1.2\) hours. Then \(\bar{X}\) follows a \(t\) distribution with \(n - 1 = 14\) degrees of freedom, centered at 7 hours and with estimated standard error \(1.2/\sqrt{15} \approx 0.310\) hours.
We can also standardize the sample mean by subtracting its null-hypothesis center \(\mu_0\) and dividing by its estimated standard error \(s/\sqrt{n}\):
\[
T = \frac{\bar{X} - \mu_0}{s/\sqrt{n}}.
\]
When \(H_0\) is true, this standardized statistic has a standard Student \(t\) distribution with \(n - 1\) degrees of freedom,
\[
T \sim t_{n-1}.
\]
This distribution, like the standard normal distribution, is centered at zero, and its shape is determined by the degrees of freedom. Rguroo reports critical regions and p-values using both the standardized statistic \(T\) and the sample mean \(\bar{X}\) on its original scale.
As in the known-\(\sigma\) case, in this text we will primarily use the null distribution of \(\bar{X}\) directly rather than its standardized version. Working on the original scale of the data allows us to interpret critical regions and p-values in the units of the problem. In the sleep example, for instance, it is more natural to reason about a sample mean of 6.4 hours relative to a hypothesized mean of 7 hours than to translate everything into the unitless \(t\) scale.






TipWhen the \(t\) and normal distributions agree



As we saw above, the \(t\) distribution becomes closer to the standard normal distribution as the degrees of freedom increase. By the time the degrees of freedom reach about 30 — that is, a sample size of roughly \(n = 30\) or more — the two distributions are nearly indistinguishable, and the critical values and p-values they produce are essentially the same. For this reason, with large samples it makes little practical difference whether one uses the \(t\) distribution or the normal distribution, and the resulting inference is usually nearly identical. We nonetheless recommend using the \(t\) distribution whenever \(\sigma\) is unknown, regardless of sample size: it is always at least as appropriate as the normal, and it requires no judgment about whether the sample is “large enough.”



Example 11.6 (Adélie Flipper Length) Recall the Adélie penguin flipper-length example. We wish to investigate whether the mean flipper length among Adélie penguins in the Palmer Archipelago differs from the reference value of 188 mm.
The hypotheses are
\[
\begin{cases}
H_0: \mu = 188 \\
H_a: \mu \neq 188
\end{cases}
\]
Use the raw flipper-length data for Adélie penguins in the PalmerPenguins dataset. Assume that Adélie flipper lengths are normally distributed in the population. Since the population standard deviation \(\sigma\) is unknown, use Rguroo to obtain the sample size \(n\) and sample standard deviation \(s.\)
What is the null distribution of \(\bar{X}\)?







Tip🔎 Solution





In this example, \(H_0: \mu = 188\) with the boundary value of \(\mu_0 = 188.\) Since the population standard deviation \(\sigma\) is unknown, we estimate it using the sample standard deviation \(s,\) and the null distribution of \(\bar{X}\) is a Student \(t\) distribution.
From Rguroo, the Adélie flipper-length data give
\[
n = 151
\]
and
\[
s = 6.539 \text{ mm}.
\]
Therefore, the degrees of freedom are
\[
n - 1 = 150,
\]
and the estimated standard error is
\[
\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{6.539}{\sqrt{151}} \approx 0.532.
\]
Thus, the null distribution is
\[
\bar{X} \sim t_{150}\left(188,\ \frac{6.539}{\sqrt{151}}\right).
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\bar{X} \sim t_{150}(188,\ 0.532).
\]
So, when \(H_0\) is true, sample means from samples of size 151 are modeled by a Student \(t\) distribution centered at 188 mm, with estimated standard error approximately 0.532 mm.

title: 11  Statistical Inference for Means
text:
11.3 The p-value Approach
To measure how strongly the observed data provide evidence against \(H_0\) and in favor of \(H_a,\) we use a quantity called the p-value. This section develops the p-value approach to hypothesis testing. An equivalent alternative, the critical region approach, is developed in Section 11.4.
Conceptually, the p-value measures how strongly the evidence in our observed sample favors the alternative hypothesis, assuming that the null hypothesis is true. As in the proportion setting, we develop the idea of the p-value through the \(H_a\) support: the set of values of the sample mean \(\bar{X}\) that are at least as favorable to the alternative hypothesis as the value we actually observed.
To make this concrete, recall that our observed sample mean is denoted \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}},\) and that we evaluate evidence using the null distribution of \(\bar{X}.\) This null distribution is \(N\!\left(\mu_0,\, \sigma/\sqrt{n}\right)\) when \(\sigma\) is known, and \(t_{n-1}\!\left(\mu_0,\, s/\sqrt{n}\right)\) when \(\sigma\) is unknown; in both cases, the probabilities below are computed under the appropriate distribution. The \(H_a\) support depends on the form of the alternative hypothesis. The callout that follows summarizes the \(H_a\) support and the corresponding p-value for each type of alternative hypothesis.






Notep-value for the One-Sample Test of \(\mu\)



In each case, the p-value is computed under the null distribution of \(\bar{X},\) which depends on whether \(\sigma\) is known:

When \(\sigma\) is known: \(\bar{X} \sim N\!\left(\mu_0,\, \sigma/\sqrt{n}\right).\)
When \(\sigma\) is unknown: \(\bar{X} \sim t_{n-1}\!\left(\mu_0,\, s/\sqrt{n}\right).\)

All probabilities below are computed assuming the boundary value \(\mu = \mu_0.\)








Alternative Hypothesis
\(H_a\) Support
p-value




\(H_a: \mu > \mu_0\)
\(\bar{X} \geq \bar{x}_{\text{obs}}\)
\(P\!\left(\bar{X} \geq \bar{x}_{\text{obs}}\right)\)


\(H_a: \mu < \mu_0\)
\(\bar{X} \leq \bar{x}_{\text{obs}}\)
\(P\!\left(\bar{X} \leq \bar{x}_{\text{obs}}\right)\)


\(H_a: \mu \neq \mu_0,\) with \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} < \mu_0\)
at least as far below \(\mu_0\) as \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}},\) or equally far above
\(2 \times P\!\left(\bar{X} \leq \bar{x}_{\text{obs}}\right)\)


\(H_a: \mu \neq \mu_0,\) with \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} \geq \mu_0\)
at least as far above \(\mu_0\) as \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}},\) or equally far below
\(2 \times P\!\left(\bar{X} \geq \bar{x}_{\text{obs}}\right)\)





In each figure below, the curve shows the null distribution of \(\bar{X},\) centered at \(\mu_0\) (dashed line), and the triangle marks the observed sample mean \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}}\); the area of the shaded region is the p-value. Figure 11.3 shows the one-sided cases, where the shading is a single tail beyond \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}}.\) Figure 11.4 shows the two-sided case: shading appears in both tails, one beyond \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}}\) itself and one an equal distance away on the opposite side of \(\mu_0\) (marked with a lighter triangle) — together, these represent all sample means at least as far from \(\mu_0\) as the one we observed. Panel (a) shows this when \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}}\) falls below \(\mu_0,\) and panel (b) when it falls at or above \(\mu_0,\) matching the two \(H_a: \mu \neq \mu_0\) rows in the table above.








Figure 11.3: The p-value for a one-sided alternative hypothesis.













Figure 11.4: The p-value for a two-sided alternative hypothesis, depending on which side of \(\mu_0\) the observed sample mean falls.











In each case, the p-value is the probability, computed under the null distribution, of observing a sample mean at least as favorable to \(H_a\) as the one actually observed.



Once the p-value has been computed, the decision rule is the same regardless of the form of the alternative hypothesis: reject \(H_0\) if the p-value is less than the significance level \(\alpha,\) and fail to reject \(H_0\) otherwise.
Intuitively, a small p-value means that the observed sample mean would be unusual under the null hypothesis, providing evidence against the null hypothesis. A p-value larger than \(\alpha\) means that the observed sample mean is reasonably consistent with the null hypothesis, and we have insufficient evidence to reject it.

11.3.1 Worked Example: \(\sigma\) Known
We now apply the p-value approach to the SAT example. As noted earlier, the SAT setting is one of the rare cases in which the population standard deviation \(\sigma\) can reasonably be treated as known (here, \(\sigma = 113\) points, computed from the scores of more than 2 million students). The remaining three running examples — sleep, commute time, and Adélie penguin flipper length — are taken up in Section 11.3.2, where we treat \(\sigma\) as unknown and use the Student \(t\) distribution.

Example 11.7 (SAT Math Scores at CSUF) We return to the SAT setting introduced in Example 11.1. Recall that the national mean math SAT score for the high school graduating class of 2025 was 508 points, with a standard deviation of 113 points, and that we wished to investigate whether the mean math SAT score among incoming CSUF freshmen in fall 2025 was higher than the national mean. A random sample of \(n = 40\) incoming CSUF freshmen yielded a sample mean of \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 542\) points.
The hypotheses are \[
\begin{cases}
H_0: \mu \leq 508 \\
H_a: \mu > 508
\end{cases}
\] where \(\mu\) denotes the mean math SAT score among incoming CSUF freshmen in fall 2025. Assume that the population of math SAT scores is normally distributed, and treat the population standard deviation as known with \(\sigma = 113\) points. Perform a test of hypothesis at the \(\alpha = 0.05\) significance level by answering the following questions:

What is the null distribution of \(\bar{X}\)?
State a probability statement that defines the p-value for this test, and describe it in words.
Use Rguroo to obtain the p-value, interpret it in the context of the problem, and state whether you reject or fail to reject \(H_0\) at \(\alpha = 0.05\) significance level.
Give your decision.








Tip🔎 Solution





a. The null distribution is
\[\bar{X}\sim N\left(508, \frac{113}{\sqrt{40}}\right)\approx N\left(508,17.867 \right)
\]
b. The p-value is the probability of observing a sample mean greater than or equal to our observed value of \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 542\) given that the true value of the population mean is \(\mu = 508.\) This can be written mathematically as
\[\text{p-value} = P(\bar{X} \geq 542).\]

11.3.2 Worked Examples: \(\sigma\) Unknown
We now turn to the more realistic setting in which the population standard deviation \(\sigma\) is unknown and is estimated from the sample by \(s.\) The three running examples in this section — sleep hours, commute time, and Adélie penguin flipper length — all use the Student \(t\) distribution as the null distribution of \(\bar{X}.\) Each example reuses the setup introduced earlier in the chapter; we now carry out the p-value part of the hypothesis test. (The critical region part of each of these same examples is taken up in Section 11.4.2.)

Example 11.8 (Sleep Hours Among University Students) We return to the sleep setting introduced in Example 11.2. Recall that the recommended minimum nightly sleep for young adults is 7 hours, and that we wished to investigate whether the mean nightly sleep among students at our university is less than 7 hours. A random sample of \(n = 15\) students yielded a sample mean of \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 6.4\) hours and a sample standard deviation of \(s = 1.2\) hours.
The hypotheses are \[
\begin{cases}
H_0: \mu \geq 7 \\
H_a: \mu < 7
\end{cases}
\] where \(\mu\) denotes the mean nightly sleep, in hours, among students at our university. Assume that the population of nightly sleep hours is normally distributed. Because the population standard deviation \(\sigma\) is unknown, we estimate it from the sample by \(s = 1.2\) hours and use the Student \(t\) distribution. Perform a test of hypothesis at the \(\alpha = 0.01\) significance level by answering the following questions:

What is the null distribution of \(\bar{X}\)?
State a probability statement that defines the p-value for this test, and describe it in words.
Use Rguroo to obtain the p-value, interpret it in the context of the problem, and state whether you reject or fail to reject \(H_0\) at \(\alpha = 0.01\) level.
Give your decision.








Tip🔎 Solution





a. Because \(\sigma\) is unknown, the null distribution of \(\bar{X}\) is a Student \(t\) distribution with \(n - 1 = 14\) degrees of freedom, centered at \(\mu_0 = 7\) with estimated standard error \(s/\sqrt{n} = 1.2/\sqrt{15} \approx 0.3098\) hours:
\[
\bar{X}\sim t_{14}\left(7,\ \frac{1.2}{\sqrt{15}}\right)\approx t_{14}\!\left(7,\ 0.3098\right).
\]
b. The p-value is the probability of observing a sample mean less than or equal to our observed value of \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 6.4,\) given that the true value of the population mean is \(\mu = 7.\) This can be written mathematically as
\[
\text{p-value} = P(\bar{X} \leq 6.4),
\]
with the probability computed under the \(t_{14}(7,\ 0.3098)\) null distribution.
c. Click to expand the box below to see how to use the Mean Inference function in Rguroo to answer this question.

Both the Test of Hypothesis table and the P-value Graph in the Rguroo output show the p-value is approximately \(0.0366 \approx 3.7\%.\) This means that if the true population mean is in fact 7 hours, then the probability of having observed a sample mean of 6.4 hours or less in a sample of size 15 is approximately 3.7%. Because this probability is larger than the significance leve \(\alpha = 0.01,\) there is not sufficient evidence to reject \(H_0\) at \(\alpha = 0.01\) significance level.

Example 11.9 (Commute Time in a Metropolitan Area) We return to the commute setting introduced in Example 11.3. Recall that the national mean one-way commute time for U.S. workers in 2023 was 26.8 minutes, and that we wished to investigate whether the mean one-way commute time among workers in our metropolitan area differs from the national mean. A random sample of \(n = 15\) commuters yielded a sample mean of \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 24.8\) minutes and a sample standard deviation of \(s = 9.6\) minutes.
The hypotheses are \[
\begin{cases}
H_0: \mu = 26.8 \\
H_a: \mu \neq 26.8
\end{cases}
\] where \(\mu\) denotes the mean one-way commute time, in minutes, among workers in our metropolitan area. Assume that the population of commute times is normally distributed. Perform a test of hypothesis at the \(\alpha = 0.10\) significance level by answering the following questions:

What is the null distribution of \(\bar{X}\)?
State a probability statement that defines the \(p\)-value for this test, and describe it in words.
Use Rguroo to obtain the \(p\)-value, interpret it in the context of the problem, and state whether you reject or fail to reject \(H_0\) at \(\alpha = 0.10\) significance level.
Give your decision.








Tip🔎 Solution





a. Because \(\sigma\) is unknown, the null distribution of \(\bar{X}\) is a Student \(t\) distribution with \(n - 1 = 14\) degrees of freedom, centered at \(\mu_0 = 26.8\) with estimated standard error \(s/\sqrt{n} = 9.6/\sqrt{15} \approx 2.4787\) minutes:
\[
\bar{X}\sim t_{14}\left(26.8,\ \frac{9.6}{\sqrt{15}}\right)\approx t_{14}\!\left(26.8,\ 2.4787\right).
\]
b. Because the test is two-sided, a sample mean that is far from 26.8 in either direction is evidence against \(H_0.\) The \(p\)-value is therefore the probability, under the null distribution, of observing a sample mean at least as far from 26.8 as our observed value of \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 24.8.\) Since 24.8 is 2 units below 26.8, this means a sample mean of 24.8 or less, or equally far above at 28.8 or more. This can be written mathematically as
\[
\text{p-value} = P(\bar{X} \leq 24.8) + P(\bar{X} \geq 28.8).
\]
Because the null \(t\) distribution is symmetric about 26.8, this is equal to
\[
\text{p-value} = 2 \times P(\bar{X} \leq 24.8),
\]
with the probability computed under the \(t_{14}(26.8,\ 2.4787)\) null distribution.
c. The steps for using Rguroo’s Mean Inference function are the same as those in Example 11.7. To see the differences in the One Population Mean Inference dialog click to open the box below:

Both the Test of Hypothesis table and the P-value Graph in the Rguroo output show the p-value is approximately \(0.4332 \approx 43.3\%.\) This means that if the true population mean is in fact 26.8 minutes, then the probability of observing a sample mean at least as far from 26.8 as 24.8 is approximately 43.3%. Because this probability is large, and in particular is greater than 10%, there is insufficient evidence to reject \(H_0.\)

H_a: \mu \neq 188
\end{cases}
\] where \(\mu\) denotes the mean flipper length, in millimeters, of Adélie penguins in the Palmer Archipelago. Assume that the population of Adélie flipper lengths is normally distributed. Perform a test of hypothesis at the \(\alpha = 0.05\) significance level by answering the following questions:

Use Rguroo to obtain the p-value, interpret it in the context of the problem, and state whether you reject or fail to reject \(H_0\) at \(\alpha = 0.05\) significane level.

a. Because \(\sigma\) is unknown, the null distribution of \(\bar{X}\) is a Student \(t\) distribution with \(n - 1 = 150\) degrees of freedom, centered at \(\mu_0 = 188\) with estimated standard error \(s/\sqrt{n} = 6.539/\sqrt{151} \approx 0.5321\) mm:
\[

\]

\]

\[

\]

title: 11  Statistical Inference for Means
text:
11.4 The Critical Region Approach
An equivalent way to decide between \(H_0\) and \(H_a\) — alongside the p-value approach of Section 11.3 — is the critical region approach. Rather than summarizing the evidence in a single probability, this approach identifies, in advance of seeing the data, the set of values of \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}}\) that would lead us to reject \(H_0.\)
To implement the critical region approach for testing hypotheses about \(\mu,\) we need a rule that ensures the probability of a Type I error, when \(\mu\) equals the boundary value \(\mu_0,\) is equal to a given significance level \(\alpha.\) That is, the critical region must satisfy \[
P(\text{Rejecting } H_0) = \alpha,\; \text{ assuming $\mu=\mu_0$}.
\] The form of the critical region depends on the alternative hypothesis: large values of \(\bar{X}\) are evidence against \(H_0\) when \(H_a\) points to large values of \(\mu,\) small values of \(\bar{X}\) are evidence against \(H_0\) when \(H_a\) points to small values of \(\mu,\) and values of \(\bar{X}\) far from \(\mu_0\) in either direction are evidence against \(H_0\) when \(H_a\) allows departure in either direction. As with the p-value, all critical values are found using the null distribution of \(\bar{X}\): \(N\!\left(\mu_0,\, \sigma/\sqrt{n}\right)\) when \(\sigma\) is known, and \(t_{n-1}\!\left(\mu_0,\, s/\sqrt{n}\right)\) when \(\sigma\) is unknown. The callout that follows summarizes the critical region in each of these cases.






NoteCritical Region for the One-Sample Test of \(\mu\)



All critical values are found using the null distribution of \(\bar{X},\) which depends on whether \(\sigma\) is known:

When \(\sigma\) is known: \(\bar{X} \sim N\!\left(\mu_0,\, \sigma/\sqrt{n}\right).\)
When \(\sigma\) is unknown: \(\bar{X} \sim t_{n-1}\!\left(\mu_0,\, s/\sqrt{n}\right).\)









Alternative Hypothesis
Critical Region
Critical Value Condition




\(H_a: \mu > \mu_0\)
\(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} \geq c\)
\(P(\bar{X} \geq c) = \alpha\)


\(H_a: \mu < \mu_0\)
\(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} \leq c\)
\(P(\bar{X} \leq c) = \alpha\)


\(H_a: \mu \neq \mu_0\)
\(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} \leq c_1\) or \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} \geq c_2\)
\(P(\bar{X} \leq c_1) = P(\bar{X} \geq c_2) = \alpha/2\)





In each figure below, the curve is the null distribution of \(\bar{X},\) centered at \(\mu_0\) (dashed line); the solid line marks the critical value, and the shaded region is the critical (rejection) region — if \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}}\) falls there, we reject \(H_0.\) Figure 11.8 shows the one-sided cases, where a single critical value \(c\) marks off one tail. Figure 11.9 shows the two-sided case: \(\alpha\) is split evenly between two critical values, \(c_1\) and \(c_2,\) one in each tail.








Figure 11.8: The critical region for a one-sided alternative hypothesis.













Figure 11.9: The critical region for a two-sided alternative hypothesis.





In the critical region approach, we reject \(H_0\) in favor of \(H_a\) if the observed sample mean \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}}\) falls in the rejection region; otherwise, we fail to reject \(H_0.\)
Because both the p-value and the critical region approaches rely on the same null distribution and answer the same underlying question — how unusual is the observed sample mean under \(H_0\)? — they always lead to the same decision: rejecting \(H_0\) using the critical region at significance level \(\alpha\) is equivalent to obtaining a p-value less than \(\alpha.\)

11.4.1 Worked Example: \(\sigma\) Known
We now apply the critical region approach to the SAT example. As noted earlier, the SAT setting is one of the rare cases in which the population standard deviation \(\sigma\) can reasonably be treated as known (here, \(\sigma = 113\) points, computed from the scores of more than 2 million students). The remaining three running examples — sleep, commute time, and Adélie penguin flipper length — are taken up in Section 11.4.2, where we treat \(\sigma\) as unknown and use the Student \(t\) distribution.

Example 11.11 (SAT Math Scores at CSUF) We return to the SAT setting introduced in Example 11.1. Recall that the national mean math SAT score for the high school graduating class of 2025 was 508 points, with a standard deviation of 113 points, and that we wished to investigate whether the mean math SAT score among incoming CSUF freshmen in fall 2025 was higher than the national mean. A random sample of \(n = 40\) incoming CSUF freshmen yielded a sample mean of \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 542\) points.
The hypotheses are \[
\begin{cases}
H_0: \mu \leq 508 \\
H_a: \mu > 508
\end{cases}
\] where \(\mu\) denotes the mean math SAT score among incoming CSUF freshmen in fall 2025. Assume that the population of math SAT scores is normally distributed, and treat the population standard deviation as known with \(\sigma = 113\) points. Perform a test of hypothesis at the \(\alpha = 0.05\) significance level by answering the following questions:

What is the null distribution of \(\bar{X}\)?
Using a significance level of \(\alpha = 0.05,\) use Rguroo’s Mean Inference function to obtain the critical region. Interpret the critical region in the context of the problem, and using the observed value, state whether you reject or fail to reject \(H_0.\)
Give your overall conclusion.








Tip🔎 Solution





a. The null distribution is
\[\bar{X}\sim N\left(508, \frac{113}{\sqrt{40}}\right)\approx N\left(508,17.867 \right)
\]
b. Click to expand the box below to see how to use the Mean Inference function in Rguroo to answer this question.

Pop S.d.: 113, the population standard deviation.

In the text box \(\mu\) = Mean of enter a label for the parameter. For this example we enter CSUF SAT Math Scores.

Leave the Significance Level textbox at the default value of 0.05.
In the Alternative Hypothesis \(\mu\) dropdown, select > and enter 508, the value stated in \(H_a.\)
Select the z-statistic checkbox to use the normal distribution.

Click the  button to open the Advanced Features dialog. In the Test of Hypothesis section select Critical Region Graph. (Rguroo can also produce a p-value graph from this same setup; we use that output separately in Section 11.3.)
Click the preview icon  to view the output.
Click the  button and save the result as CSUFSAT.







TipRguroo One-Population Mean Inference dialogs










Rguroo setup for the CSUF SAT Math one-sample mean hypothesis test.
















TipRguroo Output: CSUF SAT example






 




The right-hand side plot of the Critical Region Graph in the Rguroo output displays the critical region in the observed data scale. As shown, the critical value for a significance level of \(\alpha =0.05\) is 537.39 and thus the critical region is \(\bar{X} >537.39.\) Thus, if an observed sample mean is larger than 537.39, we would reject \(H_0.\)
Our observed sample mean is \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 542\) (shown by the green triangle) falls in the rejection region since it is greater than 537.39. Therefore we reject \(H_0\) at 5% level of significance.
c. The final decision is that based on the observed sample mean of 542, there is sufficient evidence at 5% significance level that the mean SAT math scores of CSUF students is more than the national average.





11.4.2 Worked Examples: \(\sigma\) Unknown
We now turn to the more realistic setting in which the population standard deviation \(\sigma\) is unknown and is estimated from the sample by \(s.\) The three running examples in this section — sleep hours, commute time, and Adélie penguin flipper length — all use the Student \(t\) distribution as the null distribution of \(\bar{X}.\) Each example reuses the setup introduced earlier in the chapter; we now carry out the critical region part of the hypothesis test. (The p-value part of each of these same examples was taken up in Section 11.3.2. To illustrate the method at a variety of significance levels, this example uses \(\alpha = 0.01\) instead of the \(\alpha = 0.05\) used in the p-value version.)

Example 11.12 (Sleep Hours Among University Students) We return to the sleep setting introduced in Example 11.2. Recall that the recommended minimum nightly sleep for young adults is 7 hours, and that we wished to investigate whether the mean nightly sleep among students at our university is less than 7 hours. A random sample of \(n = 15\) students yielded a sample mean of \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 6.4\) hours and a sample standard deviation of \(s = 1.2\) hours.
The hypotheses are \[
\begin{cases}
H_0: \mu \geq 7 \\
H_a: \mu < 7
\end{cases}
\] where \(\mu\) denotes the mean nightly sleep, in hours, among students at our university. Assume that the population of nightly sleep hours is normally distributed. Because the population standard deviation \(\sigma\) is unknown, we estimate it from the sample by \(s = 1.2\) hours and use the Student \(t\) distribution. Perform a test of hypothesis at the \(\alpha = 0.01\) significance level by answering the following questions:

What is the null distribution of \(\bar{X}\)?
Using a significance level of \(\alpha = 0.01,\) use Rguroo’s Mean Inference function to obtain the critical region. Interpret the critical region in the context of the problem, and using the observed value, state whether you reject or fail to reject \(H_0.\)
Give your overall conclusion.








Tip🔎 Solution





a. Because \(\sigma\) is unknown, the null distribution of \(\bar{X}\) is a Student \(t\) distribution with \(n - 1 = 14\) degrees of freedom, centered at \(\mu_0 = 7\) with estimated standard error \(s/\sqrt{n} = 1.2/\sqrt{15} \approx 0.3098\) hours:
\[
\bar{X}\sim t_{14}\left(7,\ \frac{1.2}{\sqrt{15}}\right)\approx t_{14}\!\left(7,\ 0.3098\right).
\]
b. Click to expand the box below to see how to use the Mean Inference function in Rguroo to answer this question.






Note One-Population mean hypothesis test - Sleep example





The steps for using Rguroo’s Mean Inference function are the same as those in Example 11.11, with the following differences in the One Population Mean Inference dialog:

Sample Mean: 6.4, the value of \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}}.\)
Sample S.d.: 1.2, the sample standard deviation \(s.\) (Leave Pop S.d. empty since \(\sigma\) is unknown.)
Sample Size: 15, the size of the sample \(n.\)
In the text box \(\mu\) = Mean of enter the label Nightly Sleep.
Change the Significance Level textbox to 0.01.
In the Alternative Hypothesis \(\mu\) dropdown, select < and enter 7, the value stated in \(H_a.\)
Select the t-statistic checkbox (instead of z-statistic) to use the \(t\) distribution.







TipRguroo One-Population Mean Inference dialog













Figure 11.10: Rguroo setup for the Nightly Sleep one-sample t-test (α = 0.01).

















TipRguroo Output: Sleep example






     





The right-hand side plot of the Critical Region Graph in the Rguroo output displays the critical region in the observed data scale. The critical value for a significance level of \(\alpha = 0.01\) is 6.1868, and because the alternative hypothesis is of the form less than (\(H_a: \mu < 7\)), the critical region is \(\bar{X} \leq 6.1868.\) Thus, if an observed sample mean is less than 6.1868, we would reject \(H_0.\)
Our observed sample mean is \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 6.4\) (shown by the green triangle), which does not fall in the rejection region since it is greater than 6.1868. Therefore, we fail to reject \(H_0\) at the \(\alpha = 0.01\) level of significance.
c. The final decision is that, based on the observed sample mean of 6.4 hours, there is insufficient evidence at the \(\alpha = 0.01\) significance level to conclude that the mean nightly sleep among students at our university is less than the recommended 7 hours.




Example 11.13 (Commute Time in a Metropolitan Area) We return to the commute setting introduced in Example 11.3. Recall that the national mean one-way commute time for U.S. workers in 2023 was 26.8 minutes, and that we wished to investigate whether the mean one-way commute time among workers in our metropolitan area differs from the national mean. A random sample of \(n = 15\) commuters yielded a sample mean of \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 24.8\) minutes and a sample standard deviation of \(s = 9.6\) minutes.
The hypotheses are \[
\begin{cases}
H_0: \mu = 26.8 \\
H_a: \mu \neq 26.8
\end{cases}
\] where \(\mu\) denotes the mean one-way commute time, in minutes, among workers in our metropolitan area. Assume that the population of commute times is normally distributed. Perform a test of hypothesis at the \(\alpha = 0.10\) significance level by answering the following questions:

What is the null distribution of \(\bar{X}\)?
Using a significance level of \(\alpha = 0.10,\) use Rguroo’s Mean Inference function to obtain the critical region. Interpret the critical region in the context of the problem, and using the observed value, state whether you reject or fail to reject \(H_0.\)
Give your overall conclusion.








Tip🔎 Solution





a. Because \(\sigma\) is unknown, the null distribution of \(\bar{X}\) is a Student \(t\) distribution with \(n - 1 = 14\) degrees of freedom, centered at \(\mu_0 = 26.8\) with estimated standard error \(s/\sqrt{n} = 9.6/\sqrt{15} \approx 2.4787\) minutes:
\[
\bar{X}\sim t_{14}\left(26.8,\ \frac{9.6}{\sqrt{15}}\right)\approx t_{14}\!\left(26.8,\ 2.4787\right).
\]
b. The steps for using Rguroo’s Mean Inference function are the same as those in Example 11.11. To see the differences in the One Population Mean Inference dialog click to open the box below.

Because the alternative hypothesis is two-sided, \(H_a: \mu \neq 26.8,\) the significance level \(\alpha = 0.10\) is split evenly between the two tails, with \(0.05\) in each. This produces two critical values, approximately \(c_1 = 22.434\) and \(c_2 = 31.166,\) and the critical region is \(\bar{X} \leq 22.434\) or \(\bar{X} \geq 31.166.\) Thus, we would reject \(H_0\) if an observed sample mean is less than 22.434 or greater than 31.166.
Our observed sample mean is \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 24.8\) (shown by the green triangle), which does not fall in either part of the rejection region since it lies between 22.434 and 31.166. Therefore, we fail to reject \(H_0\) at the \(\alpha = 0.10\) level of significance.
