title: 11  Statistical Inference for Means
section: 11.5 Confidence Interval for a Population Mean
text:
11.5 Confidence Interval for a Population Mean
In the previous sections, the sample mean \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}}\) played a central role: we used it to test a single candidate value \(\mu_0\) for the population mean. The sample mean is also our best single-number guess for the unknown population mean. This single-number guess is called a point estimate of \(\mu.\) In the commute-time setting of Example 11.3, our sample of \(n = 15\) commuters produced \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 24.8\) minutes. We offer 24.8 minutes as the point estimate of the mean one-way commute time \(\mu\) among workers in our metropolitan area.
A point estimate has an obvious limitation. The sample mean \(\bar{X}\) varies from sample to sample, so \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}}\) will rarely equal \(\mu\) exactly. The report “our point estimate is 24.8 minutes” leaves an important question unanswered: how close to \(\mu\) is 24.8 likely to be? Could \(\mu\) be 22? 28? 32? Reporting just \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 24.8\) tells the reader nothing about the accuracy of the estimate.
A more informative report is a range of plausible values for \(\mu,\) constructed so that the long-run reliability of the construction is known. This range is called a confidence interval for \(\mu.\) As introduced in Section 9.7 and applied to proportions in Section 10.8, the construction rests on a single idea called test inversion. We already know how to test, for any candidate value \(\mu_0,\) whether the data are consistent with \(\mu = \mu_0.\) The confidence interval is the collection of candidate values that survive the test — the values for which a two-sided test would fail to reject \(H_0: \mu = \mu_0\) at significance level \(\alpha.\)
To see what this means in numbers, consider the commute data in Example 11.3. Based on the observed sample mean \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 24.8,\) a two-sided test of \(H_0: \mu = 26.8\) at \(\alpha = 0.05\) would fail to reject the value 26.8, so 26.8 is a plausible value for the population mean. On the other hand, a two-sided test of \(H_0: \mu = 32\) at \(\alpha = 0.05\) is rejected since the value 32 is too far from \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 24.8,\) so 32 is not a plausible value for the population mean. If we repeat this process for many possible values of \(\mu,\) the values that are not rejected form an interval. The endpoints of this interval are the two boundary values where the test switches from “fail to reject” to “reject.” This is illustrated graphically in Figure 11.13. As we will formally define this shortly, the interval \((19.48, 30.12)\) is called a 95% confidence interval for the commute times, providing a set of plausible values for the population mean commute time.






Figure 11.13: A confidence interval as an inverted test, illustrated for the mean of commute data.









NoteConfidence Interval for \(\mu\) by Test Inversion



A \((1-\alpha) \times 100\%\) confidence interval for \(\mu\) is the set of values \(\mu_0\) for which a two-sided test of \(H_0: \mu = \mu_0\) at significance level \(\alpha\) fails to reject. The significance level \(\alpha\) and the confidence level \((1-\alpha) \times 100\%\) are complementary: \(\alpha = 0.05\) gives a 95% confidence interval, \(\alpha = 0.10\) gives a 90% interval, and so on.








NoteConfidence Intervals and Two-Sided Tests



A two-sided hypothesis test and a confidence interval at matching levels lead to the same decision. For any candidate value \(\mu_0\):

If \(\mu_0\) lies outside the \((1-\alpha) \times 100\%\) confidence interval, a two-sided test of \(H_0: \mu = \mu_0\) at significance level \(\alpha\) rejects \(H_0.\)
If \(\mu_0\) lies inside the \((1-\alpha) \times 100\%\) confidence interval, a two-sided test of \(H_0: \mu = \mu_0\) at significance level \(\alpha\) fails to reject \(H_0.\)

This equivalence is a direct consequence of the test-inversion construction: the confidence interval is, by definition, the collection of values \(\mu_0\) that the two-sided test does not reject. The equivalence applies only to two-sided tests; a one-sided test may reject a value that lies inside the corresponding two-sided confidence interval.


Every confidence interval for \(\mu\) that we construct in this chapter has the same general form:
\[
\left(\text{point estimate} - \text{margin of error},\
\text{point estimate} + \text{margin of error}\right)\]
The margin of error is the largest plausible difference between the point estimate and the true value of \(\mu,\) at the stated confidence level. It is the product of a critical value and the standard error of the point estimate:
\[
\text{margin of error} \;=\; (\text{critical value}) \times (\text{standard error}).
\]
The critical value depends on the desired confidence level and on the sampling distribution of \(\bar{X}\); the standard error measures how much \(\bar{X}\) varies from sample to sample. Both depend on whether \(\sigma\) is known, as we see in the next two subsections.
For the commute example, the margin of error becomes \(t^*_{14} \cdot (9.6/\sqrt{15}).\) With 95% confidence, \(t^*_{14} = 2.145,\) giving margin of error \(\approx 2.145 \times 2.479 \approx 5.32\) minutes, and the interval \((24.8 - 5.32,\ 24.8 + 5.32),\) or \((19.48,\ 30.12).\) We work through this example in detail below.
Figure 11.14 shows the anatomy of this confidence interval, using the commute example. The observed sample mean \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 24.8\) sits at the center; the margin of error, \(me \approx 5.32,\) extends equally to either side; subtracting and adding it from \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}}\) gives the endpoints 19.48 and 30.12 that bound the 95% confidence interval.








Figure 11.14: Anatomy of a confidence interval for the population mean.





The assumption from the hypothesis-testing sections continues to apply: the variable under study has a normal distribution in the population. The form of the resulting interval depends on whether the population standard deviation \(\sigma\) is known. We treat the two cases separately in the next two subsections. Conditions under which the normality assumption can be relaxed are discussed in Section 11.7.

11.5.1 Confidence Interval When \(\sigma\) Is Known
When the population standard deviation \(\sigma\) is known and the variable under study has a normal distribution in the population, the sample mean \(\bar{X}\) has a normal sampling distribution centered at \(\mu\) with standard deviation \(\sigma/\sqrt{n}.\) The \((1-\alpha) \times 100\%\) confidence interval for \(\mu\) takes the form
\[
\left(\bar{X} - z^* \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}},\ \ \bar{X} + z^* \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right),
\]
where \(z^*\) is the critical value from the standard normal distribution corresponding to the desired confidence level.
The interval above is a random interval. Its endpoints depend on the random variable \(\bar{X},\) so the whole interval shifts from sample to sample. By construction, the probability that this random interval contains \(\mu\) is \((1-\alpha) \times 100\%\):
\[
P\!\left(\bar{X} - z^* \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} \;\leq\; \mu \;\leq\; \bar{X} + z^* \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right) \;=\; 1 - \alpha.
\]






NoteConfidence Interval for \(\mu,\) \(\sigma\) Known



When the variable under study has a normal distribution in the population and \(\sigma\) is known, the \((1-\alpha) \times 100\%\) confidence interval for \(\mu\) is
\[
\left(\bar{X} - z^* \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}},\ \ \bar{X} + z^* \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right),
\]
where \(z^* \cdot \sigma/\sqrt{n}\) is the margin of error and \(z^*\) is the critical value from the standard normal distribution corresponding to the confidence level \((1-\alpha) \times 100\%.\) To compute the interval from a specific sample, replace \(\bar{X}\) with the observed value \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}}.\)


The critical values most commonly used for the standard normal distribution are given in the table below. For example, a 95% confidence interval uses \(\alpha = 0.05\) and \(z^* = 1.960.\) The critical value \(z^*\) is the number of standard deviations from the mean that captures the middle \((1-\alpha) \times 100\%\) of the standard normal distribution.









Confidence Level
\(\alpha\)
\(z^*\)

1.645

Example 11.15 (SAT Math Scores at CSUF: Confidence Interval) We return to the SAT setting introduced in Example 11.1. Note that the hypothesis test in Example 11.7 was one-sided (\(H_a: \mu > 508\)), but a confidence interval is always built from a two-sided test (Section 11.5). So here we set that alternative aside and construct a two-sided 95% confidence interval for \(\mu,\) which answers a different question — a plausible range of values for \(\mu\) — than the one-sided test did.
The national mean math SAT score for the high school graduating class of 2025 was 508 points, with a standard deviation of \(\sigma = 113\) points. A random sample of \(n = 40\) incoming CSUF freshmen in fall 2025 yielded a sample mean of \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 542\) points. Assume that the population of math SAT scores is normally distributed and that \(\sigma = 113\) is known.

What is the sampling distribution of \(\bar{X}\)?
Use Rguroo to construct a 95% confidence interval for the mean math SAT score \(\mu\) among incoming CSUF freshmen in fall 2025. Report the margin of error and the interval.
Interpret the interval in the context of the problem.








Tip🔎 Solution





a. The sampling distribution of \(\bar{X}\) is
\[
\bar{X} \sim N\!\left(\mu,\ \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right) = N\!\left(\mu,\ \frac{113}{\sqrt{40}}\right) \approx N(\mu,\ 17.867),
\]
centered at the unknown population mean \(\mu\) with standard error \(113/\sqrt{40} \approx 17.867\) points.
b. The following box describes how to obtain the confidence interval using Rguroo’s Mean Inference function.






Note Confidence Interval for a Population Mean — SAT example






Open the Analytics toolbox in Rguroo.
From the Analysis dropdown, select Mean Inference → One Population. This opens the One Population Mean Inference dialog.
In the Data Summary section of the dialog, enter the following:

Sample Mean: 542, the observed sample mean \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}}.\)
Pop S.d.: 113, the known population standard deviation \(\sigma.\)
Sample Size: 40, the sample size \(n.\)
In the text box \(\mu\) = Mean of enter the label Math SAT Score.

Click the Confidence Interval tab and specify:

In the Confidence Level textbox, enter 0.95.
In the Methods section, select the z-statistic checkbox (since \(\sigma\) is known).

Click the preview icon  to view the output.
Click the  button and save the result as SATCI.







TipRguroo dialog for the SAT confidence interval













Figure 11.15: Rguroo setup for the SAT one-population mean confidence interval.

















TipRguroo Output: SAT Math Scores at CSUF






  
  




The Normal-Based Confidence Interval table in the Rguroo output contains all the information for answering this question:

The margin of error reported by Rguroo is approximately \(35.02\) points, and the 95% confidence interval for \(\mu\) is
\[
(506.98,\ 577.02) \text{ points}.
\]
c. Interpretation: We are 95% confident that the true mean math SAT score among incoming CSUF freshmen in fall 2025 is between 506.98 and 577.02 points.




The confidence interval \((507,\ 577)\) computed above came from one particular sample. The probability statement earlier in this section — that the random interval contains \(\mu\) with probability \((1-\alpha)\times100\%\) — is best understood through repeated sampling.
Suppose we draw many independent samples of size \(n = 40\) from the population of CSUF SAT scores, compute \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}}\) for each, and form the 95% interval \(\left(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} - 35,\ \bar{x}_{\text{obs}} + 35\right)\) every time, where 35 is the margin of error. The intervals shift from sample to sample because \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}}\) does. Some intervals capture the true mean \(\mu,\) others miss. Figure 11.16 shows the result of one such simulation. Each of the twenty intervals is drawn as a horizontal segment centered at its own \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}}\); the vertical line marks the fixed (but unknown) true mean \(\mu.\) Intervals that capture \(\mu\) are drawn in blue, and intervals that miss are drawn in red. Roughly 1 in 20 — that is, 5% — misses \(\mu,\) as we would expect for a 95% method; in this particular simulation, exactly 1 of the 20 intervals misses.






Figure 11.16: Twenty 95% confidence intervals from twenty independent samples of size \(n = 40.\)



Before the data are collected, the interval is random: it is centered at the random variable \(\bar{X},\) and the probability that it contains \(\mu\) is 95%. Once we collect the data and compute \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 542,\) we plug it in for \(\bar{X}\) to obtain the specific numerical interval \((507,\ 577).\) This specific interval either contains the true \(\mu\) or it does not, and we cannot tell which. The method that produced it captures \(\mu\) in 95% of repeated samples.


11.5.2 Confidence Interval When \(\sigma\) Is Unknown
When the population standard deviation \(\sigma\) is unknown and the variable under study has a normal distribution in the population, we estimate \(\sigma\) by the sample standard deviation \(s\) and use the Student \(t\) distribution in place of the normal (Section 11.2.2). The form of the confidence interval is the same as in the known-\(\sigma\) case, with two substitutions: the sample standard deviation \(s\) replaces \(\sigma,\) and the critical value \(t^*_{n-1}\) from the Student \(t\) distribution with \(n - 1\) degrees of freedom replaces \(z^*.\)






NoteConfidence Interval for \(\mu,\) \(\sigma\) Unknown



When the variable under study has a normal distribution in the population and \(\sigma\) is unknown, the \((1-\alpha) \times 100\%\) confidence interval for \(\mu\) is
\[
\left(\bar{X} - t^*_{n-1} \cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}},\ \ \bar{X} + t^*_{n-1} \cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\right),
\]
where \(t^*_{n-1} \cdot s/\sqrt{n}\) is the margin of error and \(t^*_{n-1}\) is the critical value from the Student \(t\) distribution with \(n - 1\) degrees of freedom, corresponding to the confidence level \((1-\alpha) \times 100\%.\) To compute the interval from a specific sample, replace \(\bar{X}\) with the observed value \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}}.\)


The critical value \(z^*\) takes the same value regardless of sample size. The critical value \(t^*_{n-1},\) by contrast, depends on the degrees of freedom \(n - 1.\) The following table compares the 95% critical values for \(z^*\) and \(t^*_{n-1}\) at several common sample sizes:

The \(t\) critical value is noticeably larger than the normal value \(z^* = 1.960\) for small samples, and the difference produces a wider interval — the extra width reflects the additional uncertainty introduced by estimating \(\sigma\) from the data. The values approach \(z^* = 1.960\) as \(n\) grows: by \(n = 30\) the difference is already small, and by \(n = 100\) the two are essentially identical. This reflects the broader fact, discussed in Section 11.2.2, that the \(t\) distribution approaches the standard normal as the degrees of freedom increase. Rguroo computes \(t^*_{n-1}\) and reports the margin of error automatically, so we do not look up these values by hand in practice.


Example 11.16 (Commute Time in a Metropolitan Area: Confidence Interval) We return to the commute setting introduced in Example 11.3. A random sample of \(n = 15\) commuters yielded a sample mean of \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 24.8\) minutes and a sample standard deviation of \(s = 9.6\) minutes. Assume that the population of commute times is normally distributed.

What is the sampling distribution of \(\bar{X}\)?
Use Rguroo to construct a 95% confidence interval for the mean one-way commute time \(\mu\) among workers in our metropolitan area. Report the margin of error and the interval.
Interpret the interval in the context of the problem.








Tip🔎 Solution





a. The population standard deviation \(\sigma\) is unknown and is estimated by \(s = 9.6.\) The sampling distribution of \(\bar{X}\) is a Student \(t\) distribution with \(n - 1 = 14\) degrees of freedom, centered at \(\mu\) with estimated standard error \(s/\sqrt{n} = 9.6/\sqrt{15} \approx 2.479\) minutes:
\[
\bar{X} \sim t_{14}\!\left(\mu,\ \frac{9.6}{\sqrt{15}}\right) \approx t_{14}(\mu,\ 2.479).
\]
b. The Rguroo steps follow those in Example 11.15. The differences in the One Population Mean Inference dialog are these:

Sample Mean: 24.8, Sample S.d.: 9.6 (leave Pop S.d. empty since \(\sigma\) is unknown), Sample Size: 15.
In the text box \(\mu\) = Mean of enter the label Commute Times.
In the Methods section of the Confidence Interval tab, select the t-statistic checkbox.







TipRguroo dialog for the Commute confidence interval













Figure 11.17: Rguroo setup for the Commute one-population mean confidence interval.














TipRguroo Output: Commute Time in a Metropolitan Area






  
  




From the t-Based Confidence Interval table in the Rguroo output, the margin of error reported by Rguroo is approximately \(5.32\) minutes, and the 95% confidence interval for \(\mu\) is
\[
(19.48,\ 30.12) \text{ minutes}.
\]
c. Interpretation: We are 95% confident that the true mean one-way commute time among workers in our metropolitan area is between 19.48 and 30.12 minutes.
Note. The value 26.8 (the national mean) lies inside the 95% confidence interval \((19.48,\ 30.12).\) This is consistent with the failure to reject \(H_0: \mu = 26.8\) in the two-sided hypothesis test of Example 11.9.




Example 11.17 (Flipper Length of Adélie Penguins: Confidence Interval) We return to the penguin setting introduced in Example 11.4. The Palmer Penguins dataset contains flipper length measurements for \(n = 151\) Adélie penguins, with sample mean \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = 189.95\) mm and sample standard deviation \(s = 6.539\) mm. Assume that the population of Adélie flipper lengths is normally distributed.

What is the sampling distribution of \(\bar{X}\)?
Use Rguroo with the palmerpenguins_Adelie dataset to construct a 95% confidence interval for the mean flipper length \(\mu\) of Adélie penguins in the Palmer Archipelago. Report the margin of error and the interval.
Interpret the interval in the context of the problem.








Tip🔎 Solution





a. The population standard deviation \(\sigma\) is unknown and is estimated by \(s = 6.539.\) The sampling distribution of \(\bar{X}\) is a Student \(t\) distribution with \(n - 1 = 150\) degrees of freedom, centered at \(\mu\) with estimated standard error \(s/\sqrt{n} = 6.539/\sqrt{151} \approx 0.5321\) mm:
\[
\bar{X} \sim t_{150}\!\left(\mu,\ \frac{6.539}{\sqrt{151}}\right) \approx t_{150}(\mu,\ 0.5321).
\]
b. The Rguroo steps follow those in Example 11.16, with the raw palmerpenguins_Adelie dataset and the variable flipper_length_mm selected. The sample mean, sample standard deviation, and sample size are populated automatically from the data.






TipRguroo dialog for the Adélie flipper-length confidence interval

As shown in the t-Based Confidence Interval table in the Rguroo table, the margin of error reported by Rguroo is approximately \(1.052\) mm, and the 95% confidence interval for \(\mu\) is
\[
(188.90,\ 191.00) \text{ mm}.
\]
c. Interpretation: We are 95% confident that the true mean flipper length of Adélie penguins in the Palmer Archipelago is between 188.90 and 191.00 mm.
Note. The reference value \(\mu_0 = 188\) lies outside the 95% confidence interval \((188.90,\ 191.00).\) This is consistent with the rejection of \(H_0: \mu = 188\) in the two-sided hypothesis test of Example 11.10.





11.5.3 Homework for Section 11.5

CO2 Emissions The Kyoto Protocol, signed in 1997, required participating countries to begin reducing their carbon emissions; it became enforceable in February 2005. In 2004, the mean CO2 emission, computed by averaging each country’s per-capita emission rate across countries, was 4.87 metric tons per capita. The dataset Emission contains a random sample of per-capita CO2 emissions in 2010, in metric tons per capita, for a sample of countries. We wish to estimate the mean CO2 emission per capita across countries in 2010. Assume that the population of CO2 emissions is normally distributed. Because the population standard deviation \(\sigma\) is unknown, it is estimated from the sample, and the Student \(t\) distribution is used. Import the Emission dataset into Rguroo from the book’s Rguroo dataset repository and use the variable y2010. The first six rows of the dataset are shown in Table 11.1.


What is the sampling distribution of \(\bar{X}\)?
Use Rguroo to construct a 99% confidence interval for the mean CO2 emission \(\mu\) in 2010. Report the margin of error and the interval.
Interpret the interval in the context of the problem.
Using the confidence interval, determine whether the mean CO2 emission in 2010 differs from the 2004 mean of 4.87 metric tons per capita. Is your conclusion consistent with a two-sided test of \(H_0: \mu = 4.87\) at the \(\alpha = 0.01\) significance level?


 The dataset for this exercise is available in the Rguroo dataset repository Intro to Stats with Rguroo, with the dataset name Emission.
Code book for Dataset Emission is given here.


Mercury Concentration The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) sets 1.0 mg/kg as the allowable amount of mercury in fish that is consumed. The dataset Mercury contains a standardized, age-adjusted measure of mercury concentration, in mg/kg, in largemouth bass for a sample of 53 Florida lakes (one value per lake). We wish to estimate the mean mercury concentration across Florida lakes. Assume that the population of mercury concentrations is normally distributed. Because the population standard deviation \(\sigma\) is unknown, it is estimated from the sample, and the Student \(t\) distribution is used. Import the Mercury dataset into Rguroo from the book’s Rguroo dataset repository and use the variable mercury. The first six rows of the dataset are shown in Table 11.2.


What is the sampling distribution of \(\bar{X}\)?
Use Rguroo to construct a 90% confidence interval for the mean mercury concentration \(\mu\) across Florida lakes. Report the margin of error and the interval.
Interpret the interval in the context of the problem.
Using the confidence interval, determine whether the mean mercury concentration across Florida lakes differs from the allowable amount of 1.0 mg/kg. Is your conclusion consistent with a two-sided test of \(H_0: \mu = 1.0\) at the \(\alpha = 0.10\) significance level?


 The dataset for this exercise is available in the Rguroo dataset repository Intro to Stats with Rguroo, with the dataset name Mercury.
Code book for Dataset Mercury is given here.


Cereal Sugar The amount of sugar in a Krispy Kreme glazed donut is 10 g. The dataset Sugar_children contains the amount of sugar, in grams, in a sample of cereals geared toward children. We wish to estimate the mean amount of sugar in children’s cereal. Assume that the population of sugar amounts is normally distributed. Import the Sugar_children dataset into Rguroo from the book’s Rguroo dataset repository and use the variable sugar. This dataset was obtained by filtering the full Sugar dataset for cereals geared toward children. The first six rows of the dataset are shown in Table 11.3.


What is the sampling distribution of \(\bar{X}\): (i) assuming, based on manufacturer quality-control records, that \(\sigma = 2.5\) g is known; (ii) assuming \(\sigma\) is unknown and estimated from the sample by \(s\)?
Use Rguroo to construct a 95% confidence interval for the mean amount of sugar \(\mu\) in children’s cereal: (i) using the z-statistic method with \(\sigma = 2.5\); (ii) using the t-statistic method with \(\sigma\) unknown. Report the margin of error and the interval in each case.
Interpret each interval in the context of the problem.
Using each confidence interval, determine whether the mean amount of sugar in children’s cereal differs from the 10 g found in a glazed donut. Is your conclusion consistent with a two-sided test of \(H_0: \mu = 10\) at the \(\alpha = 0.05\) significance level in each case? Compare the two intervals — which is narrower, and why?


 The dataset for this exercise is available in the Rguroo dataset repository Intro to Stats with Rguroo, with the dataset name Sugar_children.
Code book for Dataset Sugar_children is given here.


Pulse Rate The dataset Pulse_females contains several variables for each subject, including pulse rates measured before exercise and after the subject ran in place for one minute. This dataset included data only for females. The mean pulse rate after running for one minute among females who do not drink alcohol is 97 beats per minute. We wish to estimate the mean pulse rate after running among females who do drink alcohol. Assume that the population of pulse rates is normally distributed and that, based on prior exercise-physiology research, the population standard deviation is known to be \(\sigma = 9\) beats per minute. Import the Pulse_females dataset into Rguroo from the book’s Rguroo dataset repository and use the variable pulse_after to obtain the sample size \(n\) and sample mean \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}}.\) The first six rows of the dataset are shown in Table 11.4.


What is the sampling distribution of \(\bar{X}\)?
Use Rguroo to construct a 95% confidence interval for the mean pulse rate after running \(\mu\) among females who drink alcohol. Report the margin of error and the interval.
Interpret the interval in the context of the problem.
Using the confidence interval, determine whether the mean pulse rate after running among females who drink alcohol differs from 97 beats per minute. Note that the test in the previous section was one-sided (\(H_a: \mu > 97\)), while the confidence interval corresponds to a two-sided test; comment on whether the two conclusions agree and why they may differ.


 The dataset for this exercise is available in the Rguroo dataset repository Intro to Stats with Rguroo, with the dataset name Pulse_females.
Code book for Dataset Pulse_females is given here.


Economic Dynamism Economic dynamism is an index of productive growth, measured on a scale from 0 (worst) to 100 (best). The dataset Economics contains economic data for many countries. Countries that are considered high-income have a mean economic dynamism of 60.29. We wish to estimate the mean economic dynamism of middle-income countries. Assume that the population of economic dynamism values is normally distributed. Because the population standard deviation \(\sigma\) is unknown, it is estimated from the sample, and the Student \(t\) distribution is used. Import the Middle_economies dataset into Rguroo from the book’s Rguroo dataset repository and use the variable ED. The first six rows of the dataset are shown in Table 11.5.


What is the sampling distribution of \(\bar{X}\)?
Use Rguroo to construct a 95% confidence interval for the mean economic dynamism \(\mu\) of middle-income countries. Report the margin of error and the interval.
Interpret the interval in the context of the problem.
Using the confidence interval, determine whether the mean economic dynamism of middle-income countries differs from the high-income mean of 60.29. Note that the test in the previous section was one-sided (\(H_a: \mu < 60.29\)), while the confidence interval corresponds to a two-sided test; comment on whether the two conclusions agree and why they may differ.


 The dataset for this exercise is available in the Rguroo dataset repository Intro to Stats with Rguroo, with the dataset name Middle_economies.
Code book for Dataset Middle_economies is given here.


Prenatal Care In 1999, the mean percentage of women receiving prenatal care, computed by averaging each country’s percentage across countries, was 80.1%. The dataset Fert_prenatal contains the percentage of women receiving prenatal care in a sample of countries over several years. We wish to estimate the mean percentage of women receiving prenatal care across countries in 2009. Assume that the population of percentages is normally distributed. Import the Fert_prenatal dataset into Rguroo from the book’s Rguroo dataset repository and use the variable p2009. The first six rows of the dataset are shown in Table 11.6.


What is the sampling distribution of \(\bar{X}\): (i) assuming, based on WHO records, that \(\sigma = 15\) percentage points is known; (ii) assuming \(\sigma\) is unknown and estimated from the sample by \(s\)?
Use Rguroo to construct a 95% confidence interval for the mean percentage \(\mu\) of women receiving prenatal care in 2009: (i) using the z-statistic method with \(\sigma = 15\); (ii) using the t-statistic method with \(\sigma\) unknown. Report the margin of error and the interval in each case.
Interpret each interval in the context of the problem.
Using each confidence interval, determine whether the mean percentage of women receiving prenatal care in 2009 differs from the 1999 mean of 80.1%. Is your conclusion consistent with a two-sided test of \(H_0: \mu = 80.1\) at the \(\alpha = 0.05\) significance level in each case? Compare the two intervals — which is narrower, and why?


 The dataset for this exercise is available in the Rguroo dataset repository Intro to Stats with Rguroo, with the dataset name Fert_prenatal.
Code book for Dataset Fert_prenatal is given here.


Maintaining Balance Maintaining balance may become harder with age. In a study of steadiness, elderly subjects stood on a force platform and reacted to an unpredictable noise; the platform measured how much each subject swayed, in millimeters, in the forward/backward direction. The dataset sway_elderly contains the forward/backward sway measurements for the elderly subjects. The mean forward sway of younger people is 18.125 mm. We wish to estimate the mean forward/backward sway among elderly subjects. Assume that the population of sway measurements is normally distributed and that, based on prior balance research, the population standard deviation is known to be \(\sigma = 6\) mm. Import the sway_elderly dataset into Rguroo from the book’s Rguroo dataset repository and use the variable FBSway to obtain the sample size \(n\) and sample mean \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}}.\) This dataset was obtained by filtering the full Sway dataset for elderly subjects. The first six rows of the dataset are shown in Table 11.7. The codebook for this dataset is here.


What is the sampling distribution of \(\bar{X}\)?
Use Rguroo to construct a 95% confidence interval for the mean forward/backward sway \(\mu\) among elderly subjects. Report the margin of error and the interval.
Interpret the interval in the context of the problem.
Using the confidence interval, determine whether the mean sway among elderly subjects differs from 18.125 mm. Note that the test in the previous section was one-sided (\(H_a: \mu > 18.125\)), while the confidence interval corresponds to a two-sided test; comment on whether the two conclusions agree and why they may differ.


 The dataset for this exercise is available in the Rguroo dataset repository Intro to Stats with Rguroo, with the dataset name sway_elderly.
Code book for Dataset sway_elderly is given here.

title: 11  Statistical Inference for Means
text:
11.6 Checking the Normality Assumption
As we will see in Section 11.7, the role of the normality assumption diminishes as the sample size increases. For larger samples (often \(n > 30\)), the inferential procedures developed in this chapter remain approximately valid under moderate departures from normality, though severe skewness or outliers can still affect their accuracy. For smaller samples, the assumption that the population distribution is approximately normal plays a more central role in the validity of both the normal and \(t\)-based procedures, and checking it is important.
In some applications, the plausibility of the normality assumption is supported by subject-matter knowledge and prior experience with the variable being studied. When raw data are available, we can also assess the assumption directly from the sample. In this section, we introduce two commonly used approaches: a graphical method based on a normal probability plot and a formal hypothesis test known as the Shapiro–Wilk test. Both methods are available in Rguroo.
A normal probability plot (also called a Q-Q plot, short for quantile-quantile plot) assesses normality by plotting the ordered values from the sample against the values we would expect to see if the data came from a normal distribution. If the population distribution really is normal, the plotted points should fall close to a straight line. Systematic departures from a straight line — a curve, an S-shape, or points that drift away in the tails — indicate that the data do not come from a normal distribution. Rguroo’s normal probability plot also displays a pair of dashed bands around the reference line; these bands indicate the range in which the points would typically fall if the data were normal. Points that stray outside the bands are evidence of departure from normality.
The Shapiro–Wilk test assesses normality formally through a hypothesis test. A large p-value, for example greater than 0.05, indicates that the data are consistent with a normal distribution, whereas a small p-value provides evidence against normality.
To assess normality in Rguroo, open the One Population Mean Inference as you did in the worked examples earlier in the chapter, select your dataset and variable, and check the boxes labeled Normal Probability Plot and Test of Normality. As an example, Figure 11.19 shows the dialog with the palmerpenguins_Adelie dataset and the variable flipper_length_mm selected, both normality assessment options checked.








Figure 11.19: Rguroo settings for generating a normal probability plot and conducting a Shapiro–Wilk test of normality.





The normal probability plot for these data is shown Figure 11.20. As you can see all data points follow a straight line closely and they are all within the dashed band. This indicates that the data for Adélie flipper lengths is normaly distributed.








Figure 11.20: Normal probability plot indicating that the flipper length data are approximately Adélie .





A few points outside the bands does not necessarily indicate non-normality, especially in larger samples where some scatter is expected. When the plot is ambiguous — most points on the line, but a few outliers — the Shapiro–Wilk test can supply a more formal assessment.
Figure 11.21 shows the Rguroo output for the Shapiro-Wilk test for the same data. The test reports a W-statistic of 0.993 and a p-value of 0.720. The W-statistic is part of the test calculation, but we do not need to interpret it directly here. The important value is the p-value. Since 0.720 is large, the data do not give evidence against the normality assumption. This agrees with the normal probability plot, so it is reasonable to treat the Adélie flipper length data as approximately normal.








Figure 11.21: Shapiro–Wilk test results indicating that the flipper length data are consistent with a normal distribution.





It is instructive to see an example of a normal probability plot and Shapiro-Wilk test that indicate a departure from normality. Figure 11.22 shows the normal probability plot for the variable flipper_length_mm for all the species in the palmerpenguins. The points deviate from the straight reference line, in both the lower and upper tails, and many points are outside the dashed confidence bands. This suggests that the distribution of flipper lengths for all penguins is not normal. The Shapiro-Wilk test for these data, shown in Figure 11.23, reports a W-statistic of 0.915 and a p-value of \(3.5\times 10^{-9}\) (3.5 times 10 to the power minus nine), providing strong evidence against the assumption of normality for the all species combined flipper length data.








Figure 11.22: Normal probability plot indicating that the flipper length data for all penguins are not Adélie .













Figure 11.23: Shapiro–Wilk test results indicating that the flipper length data for all penguins are not consistent with a normal distribution.





Together, the normal probability plot and the Shapiro–Wilk test provide complementary ways to check the normality assumption. The plot reveals the shape of the departure (skewness, heavy tails, outliers); the test offers a numerical summary. When both agree, the conclusion is clear. When they disagree — for instance, when a Shapiro–Wilk test rejects normality but the plot shows only a few mild departures — it is reasonable to favor the visual evidence, since the test can be sensitive to minor deviations in large samples. In small samples, the test may have low power to detect real departures, so the plot remains essential. The next section discusses situations when the normality assumption is not satisfied.

title: 11  Statistical Inference for Means
section: 11.7 Large-Sample Mean Inference: Dropping the Normality Assumption
text:
11.7 Large-Sample Mean Inference: Dropping the Normality Assumption
Every method in this chapter so far has rested on one assumption: the variable under study has a normal distribution in the population. For small samples, this assumption matters, and we check it using the methods of Section 11.6.
For large samples, the normality assumption can be dropped, by the Central Limit Theorem: when \(n\) is large, the sampling distribution of \(\bar{X}\) is approximately normal whatever the shape of the population. As a rule of thumb, \(n \geq 30\) is large enough; strongly skewed populations or those with extreme outliers may need more, and already-symmetric populations need less.
This section matters only when you are unwilling to assume the population is normal. If the population can reasonably be assumed normal, keep using the methods of the earlier sections — \(z\) when \(\sigma\) is known, \(t\) when \(\sigma\) is unknown — regardless of how large the sample is; those methods are already exact and there is nothing to gain by switching. The normal approximation described here is an alternative for when that assumption is not available.
When \(\sigma\) is known, the sampling distribution of \(\bar{X}\) is approximately \(N(\mu_0,\ \sigma/\sqrt{n}),\) and we proceed as in Section 11.5.1. When \(\sigma\) is unknown, we replace it with \(s\); for a large sample \(s\) is a reliable estimate of \(\sigma,\) and the sampling distribution of \(\bar{X}\) is approximately \(N(\mu_0,\ s/\sqrt{n}).\) In both cases we use the normal distribution — critical regions, p-values, and confidence intervals are obtained exactly as in the known-\(\sigma\) sections, just with an approximate rather than exact justification.
As shown in Section 11.2.2, the Student \(t\) distribution approaches the standard normal as the degrees of freedom increase. So even when the population is not assumed normal, continuing to use \(t\) for a large sample gives essentially the same answer as switching to \(z\) — this is why it is common practice to simply keep using \(t\) whenever \(\sigma\) is unknown, at any sample size, and treat the normal approximation here as a good enough alternative, not a required one.
The Adélie penguin example (Example 11.10, Example 11.17, \(n = 151\)) and the SAT example (Example 11.7, Example 11.15, \(n = 40\)) were both analyzed assuming a normal population, so \(t\) and \(z\) respectively were the right and exact choice there regardless of sample size. Their large sample sizes do mean, however, that had we not wanted to assume normality, the normal-approximation method of this section would have given nearly identical results.






Note Rguroo: Large-Sample Mean Inference



The large-sample analysis follows the same steps as the earlier mean inference examples, with one change: in the Methods section of the One Population Mean Inference dialog, select the z-statistic checkbox instead of the t-statistic checkbox. Sample Mean, Sample S.d. (or Pop S.d. when \(\sigma\) is known), Sample Size, the alternative hypothesis, and the confidence level are all entered exactly as before. This single change applies to both hypothesis tests and confidence intervals.








NoteLarge-Sample Mean Inference



When the sample is large (as a rule of thumb, \(n \geq 30\)) and we are not assuming the population is normal, the Central Limit Theorem makes the sampling distribution of \(\bar{X}\) approximately normal regardless of the population’s shape:

When \(\sigma\) is known, \(\bar{X}\) is approximately \(N(\mu_0,\ \sigma/\sqrt{n}),\) and the confidence interval is \(\left(\bar{X} - z^* \cdot \sigma/\sqrt{n},\ \ \bar{X} + z^* \cdot \sigma/\sqrt{n}\right).\)
When \(\sigma\) is unknown, replace \(\sigma\) with \(s\): \(\bar{X}\) is approximately \(N(\mu_0,\ s/\sqrt{n}),\) and the confidence interval is \(\left(\bar{X} - z^* \cdot s/\sqrt{n},\ \ \bar{X} + z^* \cdot s/\sqrt{n}\right).\)

In both cases, use the standard normal critical value \(z^*\) (the z-statistic method in Rguroo). If the population can be assumed normal, use \(z\) or \(t\) as in the earlier sections instead — this large-sample method is not needed.

title: 11  Statistical Inference for Means
section: 11.8 Comparing Two Means with Paired Measurements
text:
11.8 Comparing Two Means with Paired Measurements
So far in this chapter we have drawn inferences about a single population mean. We now turn to comparing two means. Many questions take this form: comparing the mean SAT Math scores of incoming CSUF freshmen and incoming Cal Poly students, the mean blood pressure of patients who receive a new drug and those who receive a placebo, the mean flipper lengths of Adélie and Gentoo penguins, or the mean ages of individuals who agree versus disagree with legalizing marijuana.
Although all of these involve comparing two means, the structure of the data can differ. In some studies, the observations in one group are unrelated to the observations in the other. A student’s SAT score at CSUF is not naturally linked to any particular student’s score at Cal Poly, and an Adélie penguin is not paired with a specific Gentoo penguin. Data of this kind are called independent groups, and we take them up in Section 11.9.
In other studies, each observation in one group is naturally linked to an observation in the other. We might measure a person’s blood pressure before and after taking a drug, or compare the cholesterol levels of identical twins when one twin receives a treatment and the other does not. Here the observations come in pairs, and the two measurements within a pair are related. Data of this kind are called paired measurements (or dependent samples), and they are the subject of this section.
Inference for paired data reduces to a one-mean problem: instead of working with the two sets of measurements, we work with the difference between each pair. We introduce the idea with a blood pressure example, then state the general procedure.
A researcher wants to determine whether a 6-week exercise program lowers systolic blood pressure. Ten participants are selected, and each person’s blood pressure is measured before the program and again after completing the program. Because the same individuals are measured twice, this is a matched-pairs design (See Chapter 1). The analysis is based on the differences between the two measurements for each participant.

The matched-pairs analysis focuses on the differences rather than on the two columns separately. Once the differences have been computed, the original measurements play no further role in the analysis.
A negative difference indicates that the participant’s blood pressure decreased after completing the exercise program. Since the difference is defined as
\[
\text{Difference} = \text{After} - \text{Before},
\]
we interpret the sign as follows:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{After} < \text{Before}
&\Rightarrow \text{negative difference} \\
&\Rightarrow \text{blood pressure decreased},\\[6pt]
\text{After} > \text{Before}
&\Rightarrow \text{positive difference} \\
&\Rightarrow \text{blood pressure increased},\\[6pt]
\text{After} = \text{Before}
&\Rightarrow \text{zero difference} \\
&\Rightarrow \text{no change}.
\end{aligned}
\]
For example, Participant 1 has
\[
139 - 142 = -3,
\]
so this person’s blood pressure decreased by 3 units.
Let’s denote the observed mean difference by \(\bar{d}_{\text{obs}}\). In this example, there are \(n = 10\) paired observations, and the sum of the differences is \(-10\) mmHg. Therefore,
\[
\bar{d}_{\text{obs}} = \frac{-10}{10} = -1 \text{ mmHg}.
\] This indicates that on average, participants experienced a decrease of 1 mmHg in systolic blood pressure after the exercise program. To determine whether this is statistically significant, we ask whether an average difference of \(-1\) mmHg is large enough, relative to the sample-to-sample variability, to provide evidence of a real decrease in the population mean blood pressure. We answer this by performing a hypothesis test or constructing a confidence interval for the mean difference, using the same methods as for one mean but applied to the differences.
Let \(D\) denote the difference for a randomly selected pair (for example, After − Before), with population mean \(\mu_D.\) For a sample of \(n\) pairs, let \(\bar{D}\) denote the sample mean of the differences and \(\sigma_D\) the population standard deviation of the differences. Assuming the pair differences are approximately normally distributed, the sampling distribution of \(\bar{D}\) is
\[
\bar{D} \sim N\!\left(\mu_D,\ \frac{\sigma_D}{\sqrt{n}}\right).
\]
As in the one-mean case, if \(\sigma_D\) is unknown we estimate it with the sample standard deviation \(s_D\) of the differences, and
\[
\bar{D} \sim t_{n-1}\!\left(\mu_D,\ \frac{s_D}{\sqrt{n}}\right).
\]






NoteThe Normality Assumption Applies to the Differences



In paired inference, the normality assumption is about the pair differences \(D,\) not about the two sets of measurements separately. We assume the differences are approximately normally distributed in the population. The before-measurements and after-measurements need not be normal themselves, and we never analyze them separately once the differences have been computed.


Every method from the one-mean sections carries over to paired data by substituting the paired-data quantities for their one-mean counterparts:









One-mean quantity
Paired-data counterpart




Variable \(X\)
Pair difference \(D\)


Population mean \(\mu\)
Mean difference \(\mu_D\)


Boundary value \(\mu_0\)
\(\mu_{D,0}\) (typically 0)


Sample mean \(\bar{X}\)
Mean of differences \(\bar{D}\)


Observed value \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}}\)
\(\bar{d}_{\text{obs}}\)


Population SD \(\sigma\)
SD of differences \(\sigma_D\)


Sample SD \(s\)
SD of differences \(s_D\)






The general procedure — the hypothesis forms, the null distribution, and the confidence interval — is summarized in the box below.
In a paired test, the boundary value is almost always 0, since the usual question is whether there is any mean difference between the paired measurements. In symbols, this value is written as \(\mu_{D,0} = 0\), where \(\mu_D\) represents the population mean difference and the subscript 0 indicates the value specified by the null hypothesis. In the blood pressure example, the researcher wants to know whether the exercise program lowers systolic blood pressure. With the difference defined as After − Before, a decrease corresponds to a negative difference, so this is a test of
\[
\begin{cases} H_0: \mu_D \geq 0 \\ H_a: \mu_D < 0. \end{cases}
\]
The direction of the alternative depends on how the difference is defined. Had we defined the difference as Before − After, a decrease in blood pressure would correspond to a positive difference, and the same research question would give \(H_a: \mu_D > 0.\) Either convention is correct, as long as the alternative hypothesis is stated to match it.






NotePaired-Difference Inference



Let \(D\) denote the pair difference (for example, After − Before), with population mean difference \(\mu_D.\) For a sample of \(n\) pairs, let \(\bar{D}\) be the sample mean of the differences and \(s_D\) the sample standard deviation of the differences. Assume the pair differences are approximately normally distributed in the population. The boundary value of the null hypothesis is taken to be \(\mu_{D,0} = 0,\) so the hypotheses are one of
\[
\text{Case 1: } \begin{cases} H_0: \mu_D \leq 0 \\ H_a: \mu_D > 0 \end{cases}
\qquad
\text{Case 2: } \begin{cases} H_0: \mu_D \geq 0 \\ H_a: \mu_D < 0 \end{cases}
\]
\[
\text{Case 3: } \begin{cases} H_0: \mu_D = 0 \\ H_a: \mu_D \neq 0 \end{cases}
\]
Null distribution of \(\bar{D}.\)

When \(\sigma_D\) is known: \[
\bar{D} \sim N\!\left(0,\ \frac{\sigma_D}{\sqrt{n}}\right).
\]
When \(\sigma_D\) is unknown, it is estimated by \(s_D\): \[
\bar{D} \sim t_{n-1}\!\left(0,\ \frac{s_D}{\sqrt{n}}\right).
\]

Confidence interval for \(\mu_D.\) The \((1-\alpha)\times 100\%\) confidence interval is
\[
\left(\bar{D} - z^* \cdot \frac{\sigma_D}{\sqrt{n}},\ \ \bar{D} + z^* \cdot \frac{\sigma_D}{\sqrt{n}}\right) \quad (\sigma_D \text{ known}),
\]
\[
\left(\bar{D} - t^*_{n-1} \cdot \frac{s_D}{\sqrt{n}},\ \ \bar{D} + t^*_{n-1} \cdot \frac{s_D}{\sqrt{n}}\right) \quad (\sigma_D \text{ unknown}),
\]
where \(z^*\) and \(t^*_{n-1}\) are the critical values for confidence level \((1-\alpha)\times 100\%.\) To compute the interval from a specific sample, replace \(\bar{D}\) with its observed value \(\bar{d}_{\text{obs}}.\)


To analyze paired data in Rguroo, we can either provide the raw data and let Rguroo compute the differences internally, or enter summary statistics for the differences directly. When raw data are provided, the two measurements are stored in separate columns — for example, Before and After — with each row corresponding to a single pair. Table 11.8 illustrates this format.

Dataset Name: BP_Pairs_Wide
This dataset contains systolic blood pressure measurements collected from 10 participants before and after completing a 6-week exercise program. The data are organized in a wide format suitable for paired-sample analysis, where each row corresponds to a single participant and the two measurements form a matched pair.

Before: Systolic blood pressure measured before the exercise program (in mmHg)

Source

Tip🔎 Solution





a. The parameter of interest is the population mean difference \(\mu_D\) between the paired measurements, where \(D\) is defined as After − Before. The research question asks whether the program lowers blood pressure; since \(D = \text{After} - \text{Before}\), lower after-program values make the differences negative, so the alternative hypothesis is \(H_a: \mu_D < 0\). The null and alternative hypotheses are:
\[
\begin{cases}
H_0: \mu_D \geq 0 \\
H_a: \mu_D < 0
\end{cases}
\]
b. We begin by setting up the problem in Rguroo. Click to expand the box below to see how to use the Mean Inference function in Rguroo to answer this question.






Note Rguroo: Paired t-test






Open the Analytics toolbox in Rguroo.
From the Analysis dropdown, select Mean Inference –> One & Two Population. This opens the One & Two Population Mean Inference dialog.
In the dialog, select the BP_Paired_wide dataset from the dropdown menu.
From the Variable 1 dropdown, select the variable After and from the Variable 2 dropdown, select the variable Before. This tells Rguroo to compute the differences as After − Before. The summary statistics for each variable appears under Population 1 and Population 2 in the Summary tab.
Select the Paired Data checkbox to indicate that the data are paired measurements. This tells Rguroo to compute the differences. Once this box is checked, the summary statistics for the differences appear under the Paired Differences section of the Summary tab.

Under the null hypothesis, the test statistic \(\bar D\) is approximately a Student \(t\) distribution with \(n-1 = 19\) degrees of freedom, centered at 0, with standard error \(s_D/\sqrt{n} = 62/\sqrt{20} \approx 13.86.\) That is, \[
\bar{D} \sim t_{19}\!\left(0,\ 13.86\right).
\]
c. From the Rguroo output the p-value is approximately 0.010. Since this is less than the significance level of 0.05, we reject \(H_0.\) There is sufficient evidence that the prep course increases mean SAT scores.



As in the one-mean case, the normality condition is less important when the number of pairs is large. By the Central Limit Theorem, when there are many pairs, the sampling distribution of \(\bar{D}\) is approximately normal even if the individual differences are not perfectly normal. In practice, the paired \(t\)-procedures are often reasonably robust, especially when there are no strong outliers or extreme skewness in the differences.

title: 11  Statistical Inference for Means
section: 11.9 Comparing Two Means with Independent Groups
text:
11.9 Comparing Two Means with Independent Groups
We now turn to the second setting introduced at the start of Section 11.8: two independent groups, where the observations in one group are unrelated to those in the other. Unlike the paired case, the two samples need not even be the same size, and there is no pairing of individual observations across groups. The paired approach of reducing to a single sample of differences is therefore unavailable, and we need a different approach.
As in the one-sample and paired cases, we begin by introducing the notation and assumptions for inference about two means with independent groups. We then describe the methods for hypothesis testing and confidence interval construction, and illustrate them with examples and Rguroo analyses.
Table 11.15 summarizes the notation used when comparing two independent population means. The parameter of interest is the difference in population means, \(\mu_1-\mu_2.\) We estimate this parameter using the difference in sample means, \(\bar{X}_1-\bar{X}_2,\) whose observed value is \(\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2.\)









Table 11.15: Notation for comparing two independent population means.

As in the one-sample case, we will have two versions of the methods for comparing two means, depending on whether the population standard deviations \(\sigma_1\) and \(\sigma_2\) are known or unknown. We also begin with the assumption that the two populations are normally distributed. We present the sampling distributions, hypothesis testing procedures, and confidence interval formulas for each case in the subsections that follow.
The parameter of interest throughout is the difference \(\mu_1 - \mu_2,\) and the natural estimator is the difference in sample means \(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2.\) Because the two samples are independent, the variance of the difference is the sum of the two individual variances. This single fact — variances add for independent samples — is what distinguishes the standard error here from the one-sample and paired cases, and it drives the formulas in the subsections below.

11.9.1 The Case When the Population Standard Deviations Are Known
When both population standard deviations \(\sigma_1\) and \(\sigma_2\) are known and both populations are normally distributed, the difference in sample means \(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2\) has a normal sampling distribution. It is centered at the true difference \(\mu_1 - \mu_2,\) and its standard error combines the two population standard deviations:
\[
\text{SE}(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) = \sqrt{\frac{\sigma_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{\sigma_2^2}{n_2}}.
\]
The two variances are added, not subtracted, because the samples are independent. Under the null hypothesis, the boundary value of the difference is typically \(\mu_1 - \mu_2 = 0,\) corresponding to equal population means.






NoteTwo Independent Means, \(\sigma_1\) and \(\sigma_2\) Known



When both populations are normally distributed and \(\sigma_1\) and \(\sigma_2\) are known, the difference in sample means has the sampling distribution
\[
\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2 \sim N\!\left(\mu_1 - \mu_2,\ \sqrt{\frac{\sigma_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{\sigma_2^2}{n_2}}\right).
\]
Hypotheses. The boundary value is typically \(\mu_1 - \mu_2 = 0,\) giving one of the three forms
\[
\begin{cases} H_0: \mu_1 - \mu_2 \leq 0 \\ H_a: \mu_1 - \mu_2 > 0 \end{cases}
\qquad
\begin{cases} H_0: \mu_1 - \mu_2 \geq 0 \\ H_a: \mu_1 - \mu_2 < 0 \end{cases}
\qquad
\begin{cases} H_0: \mu_1 - \mu_2 = 0 \\ H_a: \mu_1 - \mu_2 \neq 0. \end{cases}
\]
Confidence interval. The \((1-\alpha)\times 100\%\) confidence interval for \(\mu_1 - \mu_2\) is
\[
\left((\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) - z^* \cdot \text{SE},\ \ (\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) + z^* \cdot \text{SE}\right),
\]
where \(z^*\) is the standard normal critical value for confidence level \((1-\alpha)\times 100\%,\) and
\[
\text{SE} = \sqrt{\frac{\sigma_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{\sigma_2^2}{n_2}}.
\]
To compute the interval from a specific sample, replace \(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2\) with its observed value \(\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2.\)


As in the one-mean case, the known-\(\sigma\) setting is mostly of conceptual value, since the population standard deviations are rarely known in practice. The realistic case, in which \(\sigma_1\) and \(\sigma_2\) are estimated from the data, is taken up next.


11.9.2 The Case When the Population Standard Deviations Are Unknown
When the population standard deviations are unknown, we estimate them separately from the data using the sample standard deviations \(s_1\) and \(s_2,\) making no assumption about whether the two population variances are equal. The standard error of \(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2\) becomes the estimated standard error
\[
\widehat{\text{SE}}(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) = \sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{s_2^2}{n_2}}.
\]
As in the one-mean case, replacing the unknown standard deviations with sample estimates introduces additional uncertainty, and the sampling distribution of \(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2\) is approximated by a Student \(t\) distribution rather than a normal. The degrees of freedom are computed from the two sample sizes and standard deviations by a formula that statistical software evaluates automatically; the resulting value need not be a whole number. We do not compute the degrees of freedom by hand. Rguroo reports the degrees of freedom along with the critical values and p-values.






NoteTwo Independent Means, \(\sigma_1\) and \(\sigma_2\) Unknown



When both populations are normally distributed and \(\sigma_1\) and \(\sigma_2\) are unknown, the difference in sample means has the approximate sampling distribution
\[
\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2 \sim t_{\text{df}}\!\left(\mu_1 - \mu_2,\ \sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{s_2^2}{n_2}}\right),
\]
where the degrees of freedom \(\text{df}\) are computed from the data by software.
Hypotheses. The boundary value is typically \(\mu_1 - \mu_2 = 0,\) giving one of the three forms
\[
\begin{cases} H_0: \mu_1 - \mu_2 \leq 0 \\ H_a: \mu_1 - \mu_2 > 0 \end{cases}
\qquad
\begin{cases} H_0: \mu_1 - \mu_2 \geq 0 \\ H_a: \mu_1 - \mu_2 < 0 \end{cases}
\qquad
\begin{cases} H_0: \mu_1 - \mu_2 = 0 \\ H_a: \mu_1 - \mu_2 \neq 0. \end{cases}
\]
Confidence interval. The \((1-\alpha)\times 100\%\) confidence interval for \(\mu_1 - \mu_2\) is
\[
\left((\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) - t^*_{\text{df}} \cdot \widehat{\text{SE}},\ \ (\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) + t^*_{\text{df}} \cdot \widehat{\text{SE}}\right),
\]
where \(t^*_{\text{df}}\) is the Student \(t\) critical value for confidence level \((1-\alpha)\times 100\%\) on the software-computed degrees of freedom, and
\[
\widehat{\text{SE}} = \sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{s_2^2}{n_2}}.
\]
To compute the interval from a specific sample, replace \(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2\) with its observed value \(\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2.\)


This is the version used in nearly all practical two-group comparisons. The known-\(\sigma\) formulas of Section 11.9.1 are the conceptual special case; the unknown-\(\sigma\) formulas here are what we apply to real data.


11.9.3 The Case of Equal Population Variances
The unknown-\(\sigma\) method of Section 11.9.2 makes no assumption about how the two population standard deviations compare: \(\sigma_1\) and \(\sigma_2\) may be equal or unequal, and each is estimated separately by its own sample standard deviation. In some studies, however, there is good reason to believe the two populations have the same standard deviation, even though its common value is unknown. For example, when two groups differ only in the treatment they receive and are otherwise drawn from similar populations, it is often reasonable to assume their spreads are equal.
When the two population variances can be assumed equal, \(\sigma_1 = \sigma_2 = \sigma,\) we no longer estimate two separate standard deviations. Instead, we combine the information from both samples into a single estimate of the common standard deviation, called the pooled standard deviation:
\[
s_p = \sqrt{\frac{(n_1 - 1)s_1^2 + (n_2 - 1)s_2^2}{n_1 + n_2 - 2}}.
\]
The pooled standard deviation is a weighted average of the two sample variances, with more weight given to the larger sample. Using \(s_p\) in place of the two separate estimates, the estimated standard error of \(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2\) becomes
\[
\widehat{\text{SE}}(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) = s_p \sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}}.
\]
Because the common variance is estimated from the data, the sampling distribution of \(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2\) is again a Student \(t\) distribution. Unlike the unequal-variance case, however, the degrees of freedom are now a simple whole number: \(n_1 + n_2 - 2.\)






NoteTwo Independent Means, Equal Population Variances



When both populations are normally distributed with equal but unknown variances, \(\sigma_1 = \sigma_2,\) the difference in sample means has the sampling distribution
\[
\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2 \sim t_{\,n_1 + n_2 - 2}\!\left(\mu_1 - \mu_2,\ s_p \sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}}\right),
\]
where the pooled standard deviation is
\[
s_p = \sqrt{\frac{(n_1 - 1)s_1^2 + (n_2 - 1)s_2^2}{n_1 + n_2 - 2}}.
\]
Hypotheses. The boundary value is typically \(\mu_1 - \mu_2 = 0,\) giving one of the three forms
\[
\begin{cases} H_0: \mu_1 - \mu_2 \leq 0 \\ H_a: \mu_1 - \mu_2 > 0 \end{cases}
\qquad
\begin{cases} H_0: \mu_1 - \mu_2 \geq 0 \\ H_a: \mu_1 - \mu_2 < 0 \end{cases}
\qquad
\begin{cases} H_0: \mu_1 - \mu_2 = 0 \\ H_a: \mu_1 - \mu_2 \neq 0. \end{cases}
\]
Confidence interval. The \((1-\alpha)\times 100\%\) confidence interval for \(\mu_1 - \mu_2\) is
\[
\left((\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) - t^*_{\,n_1 + n_2 - 2} \cdot \widehat{\text{SE}},\ \ (\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) + t^*_{\,n_1 + n_2 - 2} \cdot \widehat{\text{SE}}\right),
\]
where \(t^*_{\,n_1 + n_2 - 2}\) is the Student \(t\) critical value for confidence level \((1-\alpha)\times 100\%\) on \(n_1 + n_2 - 2\) degrees of freedom, and
\[
\widehat{\text{SE}} = s_p \sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}}.
\]
To compute the interval from a specific sample, replace \(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2\) with its observed value \(\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2.\)


The equal-variance method and the unequal-variance method of Section 11.9.2 answer the same question and use the same hypotheses; they differ only in how the standard error and degrees of freedom are computed. When the two population variances really are equal, the equal-variance method is slightly more powerful, since it uses a single pooled estimate and a larger degrees of freedom. When the variances are not equal, however, the equal-variance method can be misleading, while the unequal-variance method remains valid. We return to the question of which method to use once both have been illustrated with an example.
In Rguroo, the choice between the two methods is made with a single checkbox. The unequal-variance method is obtained as described in Section 11.9.2; to use the equal-variance method instead, select the Equal Variances option in the One & Two Population Mean Inference dialog. All other steps — selecting the variables, specifying the hypotheses or confidence level, and choosing the t-statistic method — are unchanged.

Example 11.22 (Comparing Two Independent Means - Marijuana Legalization and Age) Recall the GSS2024 dataset, a subset of the 2024 General Social Survey (GSS) conducted by NORC at the University of Chicago. After removing observations with missing values, the dataset contains information on \(n = 399\) individuals.
Although the dataset includes many variables, we focus on two variables:

age, which records the respondent’s age in years.
Grass, which indicates whether the respondent supports legalizing marijuana (Yes) or does not support legalizing marijuana (No).

Our goal is to investigate whether respondents who support legalizing marijuana tend to be younger, on average, than respondents who do not support legalization.
a. Let \(\mu_1\) denote the mean age of respondents who do not support legalizing marijuana (No), and let \(\mu_2\) denote the mean age of respondents who support legalizing marijuana (Yes). State the null and alternative hypotheses for testing whether the mean age of respondents who support legalization is less than the mean age of respondents who do not support legalization.
b. Set up the problem in Rguroo’s Mean Inference function to perform a hypothesis test comparing the mean ages of the two independent groups using the GSS2024 dataset. From the output, obtain the mean age for each group and the observed difference between the sample means.
c. From the output, obtain the standard error and degrees of freedom used in the test. Then state the sampling distribution of the test statistic under the null hypothesis.
d. Determine the critical value for the test in the scale of the data at the \(\alpha=0.05\) significance level. Does the observed difference between the sample means fall in the rejection region?
e. State the p-value and determine whether you should reject or fail to reject the null hypothesis.
f. Interpret the results in the context of the relationship between age and support for legalizing marijuana.

 The dataset for this example is available in the Rguroo dataset repository Intro to Stats with Rguroo, with the dataset name GSS2024.
Code book for Dataset GSS2024 is given here.








Tip🔎 Solution





a. The null and alternative hypotheses for testing whether the mean age of respondents who support legalization is less than the mean age of respondents who do not support legalization are:
\[\begin{cases} H_0: \mu_1 \leq \mu_2 \\ H_a: \mu_1 > \mu_2 \end{cases}\]
where \(\mu_1\) is the mean age of respondents who do not support legalizing marijuana (No), and \(\mu_2\) is the mean age of respondents who support legalizing marijuana (Yes).
This can also be expressed as: \[
\begin{cases} H_0: \mu_1 - \mu_2 \leq 0 \\ H_a: \mu_1 - \mu_2 > 0 \end{cases}
\]
b. Click to expand the box below to see how to set up the problem in Rguroo’s Mean Inference function.

In the Summary tab, a. under the Population 1 section, from the Level dropdown, select the level No. b. under the Population 2 section, from the Level dropdown, select the level Yes.
Select the Population 1-2 tab, and select the Hypothesis Test sub-tab to specify the hypothesis test settings. a. In the Alternative Hyp \(\mu_1-\mu_2\) dropdown, select the option > and type in 0 in the corresponding textbox. b. In the Significance Level field, enter 0.05 (this is the default). c. Select the t-statistic checkbox to specify that the test should be based on the Student \(t\) distribution.
Under the Assumptions section, select [Unequal variances] to indicate that the variances of the two populations are not assumed to be equal.
Click the  button to open the Advanced Features dialog. In the Test of Hypothesis and Simulation Methods section, select P-value Graph and Critical Region Graph. This will instruct Rguroo to give results for both critical regions and p-value.
Click the preview icon  to view the output.
Click the  button and save the result as GSS2024_Grass_Age.







TipRguroo One & Two Population Mean Inference dialogs for two independent means with GSS2024 dataset

TipRguroo Output: Marijuana Legalization and Age






 




Referring to the Rguroo output Data Summary table, the mean age for respondents who do not support legalizing marijuana (No) is approximately 56.642 years, and the mean age for respondents who support legalizing marijuana (Yes) is approximately 51.394 years. Therefore, the observed difference between the sample means is approximately \(56.642 - 51.394 = 5.248\) years.
c. From the Rguroo output Test of Hypothesis - t-Test table, the standard error of the difference in sample means is approximately 2.076 years, and the degrees of freedom used in the test is approximately 191.1. The sampling distribution of the test statistic under the null hypothesis is approximately t-distributed with center at 0, standard error 2.076 and 191.1 degrees of freedom: \[
\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2 \sim t_{191.1}\!\left(0,\ 2.076\right).
\]
d. The left panel of the Rguroo output Critical Region Graph: t-Test, shows the critical value for the test in the scale of the data. This value at the \(\alpha = 0.05\) significance level is approximately 3.432. Since the observed difference between the sample means (5.248) is greater than the critical value (3.432), it falls in the rejection region, and we reject the null hypothesis.
e. The Test of Hypothesis: t-test table and the P-value Graph: t-Test in the Rguroo output show a p-value of 0.0061. Since this value is less than \(\alpha = 0.05\), we reject the null hypothesis.
f. We reject the null hypothesis and conclude that there is sufficient evidence at the \(\alpha = 0.05\) level of significance that the mean age of those who do not support legalization of marijuana is greater than that of those who support legalization.

From the Rguroo output, the observed difference in sample means is \(\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2 = 56.642 - 51.394 = 5.248\) years. The margin of error is approximately 4.096 years, and the 95% confidence interval for \(\mu_1 - \mu_2\) is approximately

\[
(1.154,\ 9.343) \text{ years}.
\]

We are 95% confident that the true difference in mean age between respondents who do not support legalizing marijuana and those who do is between approximately 1.15 and 9.34 years. Because the entire interval is positive, the respondents who do not support legalization are, on average, older than those who support it, by somewhere between about 1 and 9 years.
The value 0 lies outside the 95% confidence interval \((1.153,\ 9.343).\) A two-sided test of \(H_0: \mu_1 - \mu_2 = 0\) versus \(H_a: \mu_1 - \mu_2 \neq 0\) at \(\alpha = 0.05\) would therefore reject \(H_0,\) indicating that the mean ages of the two groups differ.










NoteChoosing a Method for Two Independent Means



Two questions determine which method to use.
1. Are the population standard deviations known?

Known \(\sigma_1\) and \(\sigma_2\) (rare in practice): use the normal-based method of Section 11.9.1, with critical value \(z^*.\)
Unknown \(\sigma_1\) and \(\sigma_2\) (the usual case): estimate them from the data and use a \(t\)-based method. Proceed to question 2.

2. Can the two population variances be assumed equal?

No, or unsure (the safer default): use the unequal-variance method of Section 11.9.2. The standard error is \(\sqrt{s_1^2/n_1 + s_2^2/n_2},\) and software computes the degrees of freedom (generally not a whole number). This method performs almost as well as the equal-variance method even when the variances happen to be equal, which is why many statistical software packages, including Rguroo, use it by default.
Yes, with good reason: use the equal-variance method of Section 11.9.3. The standard error uses the pooled standard deviation \(s_p,\) and the degrees of freedom are \(n_1 + n_2 - 2.\) A common rule of thumb is that this assumption is reasonable when neither sample standard deviation is more than about twice the other.

Large samples. When both samples are large (as a rule of thumb, \(n_1 \geq 30\) and \(n_2 \geq 30\)), the normality assumption is not needed, and the normal-based large-sample method of Section 11.10 applies, with critical value \(z^*.\)
When in doubt, use the unequal-variance \(t\) method. It requires no assumption about equal variances, performs almost as well as the equal-variance method when the variances are in fact equal, and is the default in most software, including Rguroo.

title: 11  Statistical Inference for Means
text:
11.10 The Large-Sample Case
As in the one-mean case, the assumption that the two populations are normally distributed can be relaxed when both samples are large. By the Central Limit Theorem, when \(n_1\) and \(n_2\) are both large (as a rule of thumb, each at least 30), the difference in sample means \(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2\) is approximately normally distributed regardless of the shape of the two population distributions. The methods of this section then apply as approximations.
As before, this large-sample method is most useful when normality cannot be assumed. If both populations can reasonably be assumed normal, the \(t\)-based methods of Section 11.9.2 or Section 11.9.3 remain the correct choice regardless of sample size — a large \(n\) does not by itself justify switching from \(t\) to \(z.\) The method of this section is for the case where normality is in doubt but the samples are large enough for the Central Limit Theorem to apply.
When the population standard deviations are unknown, we replace them with the sample standard deviations \(s_1\) and \(s_2,\) just as in the one-mean large-sample case. For large samples these are reliable estimates, and the difference in sample means is approximately
\[
\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2 \sim N\!\left(\mu_1 - \mu_2,\ \sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{s_2^2}{n_2}}\right).
\]
In Rguroo, the only change from the unknown-\(\sigma\) procedure is to select the z-statistic method rather than the t-statistic method, exactly as in the one-mean large-sample case (Section 11.7). Because the \(t\) distribution is nearly identical to the normal for large degrees of freedom, the two methods give essentially the same critical regions, p-values, and confidence intervals when normality does hold — but when normality cannot be assumed, the \(z\)-based method here is the one that remains justified.






NoteLarge-Sample Inference for Two Independent Means



When both samples are large (as a rule of thumb, \(n_1 \geq 30\) and \(n_2 \geq 30\)), the Central Limit Theorem makes \(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2\) approximately normal regardless of the shape of the two populations, so the normality assumption is not needed. When \(\sigma_1\) and \(\sigma_2\) are unknown, replace them with \(s_1\) and \(s_2.\) The difference in sample means then has the approximate sampling distribution
\[
\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2 \sim N\!\left(\mu_1 - \mu_2,\ \sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{s_2^2}{n_2}}\right).
\]
Hypotheses. The boundary value is typically \(\mu_1 - \mu_2 = 0,\) giving one of the three forms
\[
\begin{cases} H_0: \mu_1 - \mu_2 \leq 0 \\ H_a: \mu_1 - \mu_2 > 0 \end{cases}
\qquad
\begin{cases} H_0: \mu_1 - \mu_2 \geq 0 \\ H_a: \mu_1 - \mu_2 < 0 \end{cases}
\qquad
\begin{cases} H_0: \mu_1 - \mu_2 = 0 \\ H_a: \mu_1 - \mu_2 \neq 0. \end{cases}
\]
Confidence interval. The \((1-\alpha)\times 100\%\) confidence interval for \(\mu_1 - \mu_2\) is
\[
\left((\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) - z^* \cdot \text{SE},\ \ (\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2) + z^* \cdot \text{SE}\right),
\]
where \(z^*\) is the standard normal critical value for confidence level \((1-\alpha)\times 100\%,\) and
\[
\text{SE} = \sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{s_2^2}{n_2}}.
\]
To compute the interval from a specific sample, replace \(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2\) with its observed value \(\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2.\)



Example 11.24 (Household Income: Large-Sample Test) The nhanes dataset contains household income information for a sample of U.S. residents. We wish to investigate whether mean household income differs between males and females. Let \(\mu_1\) be the mean household income for males and \(\mu_2\) the mean household income for females. We treat the two groups as independent. Because both groups are large, we can use the large-sample method without assuming that household incomes are normally distributed.
Import nhanes dataset from the book’s Rguroo dataset repository. Use hhincomemid as the numerical variable and gender as the BY factor, with male as Population 1 and female as Population 2. The first rows are shown in Table 11.16, and the codebook is here.

State the null and alternative hypotheses in terms of \(\mu_1-\mu_2\).
Use Rguroo to obtain the sample size and mean income for each group. Check that both sample sizes are large enough for the large-sample method.
State the approximate sampling distribution of \(\bar{X}_1-\bar{X}_2\) under \(H_0\).
Report the p-value and interpret the result in context.








Tip🔎 Solution





a. The research question asks whether the two population means differ, so the alternative hypothesis is two-sided:
\[
\begin{cases}
H_0: \mu_1-\mu_2=0 \\
H_a: \mu_1-\mu_2\neq 0
\end{cases}
\]
b. Click to expand the box below to see how to set up the test in Rguroo.

In the Data section, select nhanes. Select Variable, choose hhincomemid, and select gender as the BY Factor.
In the Summary tab, set Population 1 to male and Population 2 to female.

Select the z-statistic method and the Unequal variances option.
Preview the output and save it as nhanes_Income_Large_Sample.

Enter the summary statistics for the two groups - large sample.





Specify the hypothesis test settings.


Rguroo setup for test of hypothesis , large-sample using the normal approximation, with unequal variances.












TipRguroo Output: Large-Sample Household Income Test






 




As shown in the Rguroo output, the sample consists of \(n_1=61\) males and \(n_2=64\) females. Both sample sizes exceed 30, therefore the large-sample method is appropriate. The sample means are approximately \(\bar{x}_1=\$61{,}557.4\) and \(\bar{x}_2=\$53{,}007.8\), giving an observed difference of \(\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2=\$8{,}549.6\).
c. Using the sample standard deviations, the estimated standard error is approximately \(\$5{,}627.15\). This value id reported in the table Test of Hypothesis: z-Test in the Rguroo output.At the boundary value specified by \(H_0\), the sampling distribution of the difference in sample means is
\[
\bar{X}_1-\bar{X}_2 \ {\sim}\ N(0,\ 5627.15).
\]
d. The two-sided p-value is approximately \(0.129\). Since \(0.129>0.01\), we fail to reject \(H_0\). These data do not provide sufficient evidence at the \(\alpha=0.01\) significance level that mean household income differs between males and females.
